question: What does section 6 of the Data Protection Act 2018 say?
statements: Section 6 of the Data Protection Act 2018 is headed "Meaning of 'controller'" and qualifies the definition of "controller" in Article 4(1)(7) of the UK GDPR rather than creating a free-standing definition.

Section 6(2) provides that where personal data is processed only for purposes, and by means, required by an enactment, the person on whom the obligation to process the data is imposed by that enactment is the controller.
Section 6(1) makes the UK GDPR definition of "controller" have effect subject to section 6(2), section 209 and section 210 of the Act.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

Section 6 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (c. 12) is a short interpretive provision headed **"Meaning of 'controller'"**. It does **not** create a free-standing definition; instead it qualifies the definition of "controller" in Article 4(1)(7) of the UK GDPR, making it subject to subsection (2), section 209 and section 210, and it provides that where personal data is processed **only** for purposes, and by means, *required by an enactment*, the person on whom that statutory obligation falls is the controller. It sits in **Part 2 (general processing), Chapter 2** of the Act (Chapter 2 now headed "The UK GDPR"), and is in force as amended by the EU Exit Regulations 2019 and, in consequence, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Full text of section 6 (as retrieved in current revised form)

> **Section 6 — Meaning of "controller"**
>
> (1) The definition of "controller" in Article 4(1)(7) of the UK GDPR has effect subject to—
>    (a) subsection (2),
>    (b) section 209, and
>    (c) section 210.
>
> (2) For the purposes of the UK GDPR, where personal data is processed only—
>    (a) for purposes for which it is required by an enactment to be processed, and
>    (b) by means by which it is required by an enactment to be processed,
> the person on whom the obligation to process the data is imposed by the enactment (or, if different, one of the enactments) is the controller.

([Data Protection Act 2018, s.6](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/6))

#### 2.2 Effect

**(a) A modifier, not a definition.** Section 6 operates only on the UK GDPR's own definition of "controller" (Art. 4(1)(7)). This reciprocal relationship is confirmed on the UK GDPR side: the EU Exit Regulations amended Article 4(7) so that, after "determined", the words referring to Union/Member State law were replaced with "**(but see section 6 of the 2018 Act)**" ([SI 2019/419, Sch. 1, para. 6(3)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/419/schedule/1)).

**(b) The statutory-duty rule (s.6(2)).** Where *both* the purposes and the means of processing are mandated by an enactment, controllership is allocated by statute to the person bearing that obligation, displacing the ordinary "determines the purposes and means" test. This is a drafting pattern repeated across the Act:
- **Part 3 (law enforcement processing):** s.32(1)–(2) — "controller" means the *competent authority* which determines purposes and means, or which is the controller by virtue of the equivalent enactment rule ([s.32](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/32)).
- **Part 4 (intelligence services processing):** s.83(1)–(2), in materially identical terms ([s.83](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/83)).

**(c) Section 6 is subject to ss.209 and 210.** Subsection (1)(b)–(c) subordinates the definition to those two sections. Note: the retrieval did not return the text of ss.209–210, and the available database extract therefore does not confirm their subject-matter beyond the fact that both were amended by SI 2019/419 (Sch. 2, paras. 88–89) to substitute "UK GDPR" for "GDPR" in s.209(2)–(4) and s.210(2)–(3). **The available database does not contain, in the material retrieved, the operative text of sections 209 and 210.**

#### 2.3 Definitions established / interaction with other definitions

Section 6 is one of four controllership provisions signposted by the Act's central definitions section:

> s.3(6): "'Controller' and 'processor', in relation to the processing of personal data to which … Part 2, Part 3 or Part 4 applies, have the same meaning as in that … Part (**see sections 5, 6, 32 and 83** and see also subsection (14)(d))."
> ([s.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/3))

Related definitional architecture:
- **s.5 ("Definitions")** — terms used in Part 2 and in the UK GDPR bear their UK GDPR meaning, read with any Part 2 provision modifying that meaning, and subject to any express contrary provision and s.204 ([s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/5)). Section 6 is precisely such a modifying provision.
- **s.3(10)** — "the UK GDPR" means Regulation (EU) 2016/679 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of s.3 of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 ([s.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/3)).
- **s.206** — index of defined expressions (s.3(15)).
- Note s.6 defines *only* "controller"; there is no "processor" limb in Part 2 (contrast s.32(3) and s.83(3), which each define "processor" for Parts 3 and 4 respectively).

#### 2.4 Place within the structure of the Act

| Level | Location |
|---|---|
| Part | **Part 2 — General processing** |
| Chapter | **Chapter 2** — originally "The GDPR", now headed "**The UK GDPR**" |
| Cross-heading | Italic heading immediately before s.6, originally "The GDPR", now "**The UK GDPR**" |
| Neighbouring sections | s.4 (processing to which Part applies), s.5 (definitions), s.6, s.7 (public authorities/bodies), s.8 (lawfulness: public interest) |

The structural evidence comes from the amending instrument: SI 2019/419, Sch. 2, para. 5 is headed "**Part 2 (general processing)**" and, within it, para. 7 directs "For the heading of **Chapter 2** substitute 'The UK GDPR'"; para. 8 directs "In the **italic heading before section 6**, for 'GDPR' substitute 'UK GDPR'"; para. 9 then amends s.6 itself ([SI 2019/419, Sch. 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/419/schedule/2)).

Note also that Chapter 3 of Part 2 (the "applied GDPR" regime, ss.21–28) was substantially dismantled by the same Regulations, and Schedule 6 (which had applied the GDPR to non-EU-law processing) was omitted (SI 2019/419, Sch. 2, paras. 27–36, 96; and see [Sch. 6 DPA 2018](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/schedule/6), now shown as repealed).

#### 2.5 Amendments since enactment

**(1) SI 2019/419 — the EU Exit Regulations (in force IP completion day)**

- **Schedule 2, para. 9:** "In **section 6(1) and (2)**, for 'GDPR' substitute '**UK GDPR**'."
- **Schedule 2, para. 8:** italic heading before s.6 amended in the same way.
([The Data Protection, Privacy and Electronic Communications (Amendments etc) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019, Sch. 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/419/schedule/2))

Commencement of those amendments: "Subject to paragraph (3), they come into force on exit day" ([SI 2019/419, reg. 1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/419/regulation/1)). Regulation 4 is the operative provision ("Schedule 2 amends the 2018 Act") ([reg. 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/419/regulation/4)).

**(2) Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.67(2) — consequential renumbering**

> s.67(2): "In consequence of the amendment made by subsection (1)(a), **in section 6 of the 2018 Act (meaning of 'controller'), for '4(7)' substitute '4(1)(7)'**."
([Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.67](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2025/18/section/67))

This is purely consequential on s.67(1)(a) restructuring Article 4 of the UK GDPR (the existing text becoming Article 4(1), with new paragraphs (2)–(5) on research and statistical purposes). The revised text of s.6 retrieved from the database already reads "Article 4(1)(7)".

**(3) Commencement status of the 2025 amendment.** Section 67 is **not** among the provisions brought into force on passing or after two months by s.142(2)–(4) of the 2025 Act; it therefore "comes into force on such day as the Secretary of State may by regulations appoint" ([DUAA 2025, s.142](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2025/18/section/142)). The available database does not record the commencement regulations for s.67, so I cannot confirm from the API whether the "4(1)(7)" substitution is fully commenced or is displayed as a prospective/revised amendment.

**(4) Prospective amendments.** No further amendment to s.6 itself was located. However, two prospective changes to the wider Part 1/Part 2 definitional framework in which s.6 operates are recorded:
- **s.3(8A)** inserting "the Commission" (Information Commission) — DUAA 2025, s.117 ([s.117](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2025/18/section/117)) — and the abolition of the office of Information Commissioner with consequential omission of s.3(8) ([s.118](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2025/18/section/118)).
- Amendments to s.83 (Part 4 controllership) inserting a new subsection (A1) covering intelligence services and qualifying competent authorities under designation notices ([DUAA 2025, s.90](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2025/18/section/90)).

These do not alter the text of s.6 but affect the surrounding definitional context.

#### 2.6 Case law interpreting section 6

**The available database does not contain information on this specific issue.** The LEX tools accessible here index UK primary and secondary legislation only; they do not return judicial decisions. No case law interpreting s.6 can be verified from the retrieved data, and no citations are supplied from outside the tool output.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent:** United Kingdom. The metadata for both the Act and s.6 records `extent: ["United Kingdom"]`.
- **Status of the Act:** `revised` (i.e. the text held incorporates effected amendments) — [ukpga/2018/12](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12).
- **Status of s.6:** In force, in the amended form set out above. Section 6 has not been repealed or omitted (contrast, e.g., s.9 and Sch. 6, which SI 2019/419 omitted outright).
- **Amending instruments' status:** SI 2019/419 — `revised`, extent UK; DUAA 2025 (c. 18) — `revised`, extent UK.
- **Caveat:** the API output does not carry per-section commencement/"prospective" annotations, so the precise commencement date of the DUAA 2025 s.67(2) substitution should be verified against the commencement regulations before reliance.

question: What powers of direction do the Scottish Ministers have in relation to Health Boards in Scotland?
statements: Section 2(5) of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978 gives the Scottish Ministers a general power of direction, under which each Health Board shall act subject to, and in accordance with, such regulations as may be made and such directions as may be given.
Directions under section 2(5) may be made or given generally or to meet the circumstances of a particular area or matter.
The section 2(5) power reaches both the purposes for which a Health Board was constituted and any function otherwise conferred on the Board by or under the 1978 Act or the 2021 Act.
Section 78A allows the Scottish Ministers to direct that specified functions be performed by another body or person where a service is failing.

Section 105(6) and (7) provide that a direction may be varied or revoked by subsequent directions made in like manner, and may be given either generally or in specified cases subject to exceptions and conditions.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The Scottish Ministers hold a **broad general power of direction** over Health Boards under **section 2(5) of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978**: in carrying out the purposes for which they were constituted, and in exercising any function otherwise conferred on them by or under that Act or the 2021 Act, each Health Board "shall act subject to, and in accordance with, such regulations as may be made, and such directions as may be given" by the Scottish Ministers — and those directions "may be made or given generally or to meet the circumstances of a particular area or matter". That general power is supplemented by two targeted powers engaged by failure: **section 78A** (direct that specified functions be performed by another body or person where a service is failing) and **section 77** (declare a body in default after an inquiry, whereupon its members vacate office). **Section 105(6)–(7)** supplies the general machinery: any direction may be varied or revoked by subsequent directions made in like manner, and may be given either generally or in specified cases subject to exceptions and conditions.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The constitutional starting point — Health Boards exercise the Ministers' own functions

Health Boards are not autonomous statutory bodies with functions of their own. Under **s.2(1)(a)**, the Scottish Ministers "shall by order constitute … boards for such areas as he may by order determine, **for the purpose of exercising such of his functions relating to the health service as he may so determine**", and for making arrangements on his behalf for the provision of the services in Part II. Special Health Boards are constituted on the same footing under **s.2(1)(b)**, again "for the purpose of exercising such of his functions … as he may so determine" ([NHS (Scotland) Act 1978, s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/2)).

This is the doctrinal basis for the breadth of the direction power that follows: a Health Board is exercising delegated ministerial functions, and s.2(8) confirms that it does so "notwithstanding that it is exercising functions on behalf of the Secretary of State" (while remaining liable in its own name).

#### 2.2 The general power of direction — s.2(5)

> **s.2(5):** "In carrying out the purposes mentioned in subsection (1) and in exercising any function otherwise conferred on them by or under this Act or by or under the 2021 Act each Health Board shall act subject to, and in accordance with, such regulations as may be made, and such directions as may be given, by the Secretary of State; and such regulations and directions may be made or given generally or to meet the circumstances of a particular area or matter."
> ([s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/2))

Four features of the retrieved text are worth drawing out:

1. **Its reach is not confined to the delegated functions.** It bites both on "the purposes mentioned in subsection (1)" *and* on "any function **otherwise** conferred on them by or under this Act or by or under the 2021 Act". A function given to a Health Board directly by statute is therefore still exercisable only subject to ministerial direction.
2. **It is mandatory in form.** The Board "shall act subject to, and in accordance with" the directions. The text creates a duty of compliance rather than a duty to have regard — contrast the guidance provisions at 2.5 below.
3. **It is expressly both general and particular.** Directions "may be made or given generally or to meet the circumstances of a particular area or matter" — so a direction may be issued to all Boards at large or to one Board about one matter.
4. **No procedural conditions appear on the face of the subsection.** The retrieved text imposes no consultation, writing, or publication requirement on a s.2(5) direction. (See the caveat at 2.6.)

**Directions as to schemes of functions (s.2(6)–(7)).** Regulations under s.2(5) "shall make provision requiring each Health Board to submit … a scheme for the exercise of their functions", which the Ministers may approve with or without modifications, and may themselves make if a Board fails to do so (s.2(6)). Under **s.2(7)**, a Board "may at any time, **and if directed by the Secretary of State shall**, within such period as he may specify, submit a new scheme for the exercise of their functions". This is a discrete, expressly conferred power of direction over the Board's own scheme of delegation ([s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/2)).

#### 2.3 Direction on service failure — s.78A

Section 78A applies where it is a function of a body or person under the 1978 Act or the 2021 Act to provide or secure the provision of a service, and the Scottish Ministers consider that the body "has failed, is failing or is likely to fail" either to provide the service or "to provide it to a standard which they regard as acceptable" (s.78A(1)).

> **s.78A(2):** "The Scottish Ministers may, where they consider it necessary for the purpose of ensuring the provision of the service in question to a standard which they regard as acceptable, **direct that specified functions** of the body or person … **be performed, for a specified period and to a specified extent**, by— (a) a body falling within subsection (4), or (b) one or more persons falling within subsection (5)."
> ([s.78A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/78A))

Key features from the retrieved text:

- **The trigger is anticipatory and subjective.** "has failed, is failing or is **likely to fail**", and the standard is one "which **they regard** as acceptable" — the judgement is the Ministers' own.
- **Who may be directed to step in.** A Health Board, a Special Health Board, the Agency or HIS (s.78A(4)); or an employee of any of those bodies, a member of the staff of the Scottish Administration, or an employee of a local authority (s.78A(5)).
- **Compliance is compulsory.** "An appointed person **must comply** with a direction given under subsection (2)" (s.78A(7)).
- **Acts of the appointee are attributed to the failing body.** Anything done or omitted by the appointed person in performing the specified functions "is to be regarded as done or omitted by" the original body (s.78A(9)), and a third party dealing in good faith and for value need not inquire into the appointee's powers (s.78A(10)).
- **Cost falls on the failing body** unless the direction says otherwise (s.78A(8)).
- **The direction is revisable.** "The Scottish Ministers may vary or withdraw a direction given under subsection (2)" (s.78A(11)).

Note that s.78A is a power to **re-allocate the performance of functions**, not merely to instruct the failing body — it is the more intrusive of the two failure powers in operational terms, though it does not disturb the body's membership.

#### 2.4 Default powers — s.77

Where the Ministers are of the opinion, "on representations made to him or otherwise", that a Health Board (or an NHS trust, the Dental Estimates Board, or HIS) has **failed to carry out any functions** conferred or imposed by or under the 1978 Act or the 2021 Act, "or have in carrying out those functions **failed to comply with any regulations, schemes, proposals or directions** relating to those functions", they may — **after holding an inquiry** — make an order declaring the body to be in default (s.77(1)).

The consequence is severe and automatic: "the members of the body shall **forthwith vacate their office**", and the order must provide for the appointment or election of new members and may authorise a person to act in the body's place in the interim (s.77(2)) ([s.77](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/77)).

Two points of contrast with s.78A:
- **Non-compliance with a direction is itself a default trigger.** Section 77(1) expressly reaches a failure "to comply with any … directions", which is the enforcement route standing behind s.2(5).
- **Section 77 carries a procedural precondition that s.78A does not** — an inquiry must be held first.

#### 2.5 The general machinery for directions — s.105

Section 105 governs orders, regulations and directions under the Act. Two subsections bear directly on directions:

> **s.105(6):** "Where under any provision of this Act— (a) power to make an order may be exercisable, or **(b) directions may be given**, or (c) schemes may be made, that provision includes **power to vary or revoke** the order or direction or scheme … by subsequent order or subsequent directions or subsequent scheme made in the like manner and subject to the same provisions."
>
> **s.105(7):** "Any power conferred by this Act to make regulations, orders **or directions** may be exercised— (a) either in relation to **all cases** to which the power extends, or in those cases subject to exceptions, or in relation to any **specified cases or classes of case**, and (b) subject to such other exceptions or conditions as the Secretary of State thinks fit, and shall include power to make such supplementary, incidental, consequential, transitory, transitional or saving provision as appears … to be expedient."
> ([s.105](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/105))

Importantly, the statutory-instrument and parliamentary-procedure requirements in s.105(1)–(4) are directed at **orders and regulations**, not directions: s.105(1) makes "any power to make orders and regulations … exercisable by statutory instrument", and s.105(2) subjects statutory instruments to annulment. Directions are not brought within that machinery by the retrieved text. This is what makes the s.2(5) power administratively rapid — a direction requires no instrument and no parliamentary process.

#### 2.6 Boundaries of the direction power — what the retrieved material does *not* support

- **Guidance is not direction.** Where the Act wants a "have regard" duty it says so: under **s.12IV**, HIS, every Health Board, every relevant Special Health Board and the Agency "must **have regard to** any guidance issued by the Scottish Ministers about the operation of sections 12IP to 12IU", with a duty to consult before issuing and to publish it ([s.12IV](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/12IV)). This is a materially weaker obligation than s.2(5) compliance, and the two should not be conflated.
- **Form and publication of s.2(5) directions.** The retrieved provisions do not state that a direction must be in writing or published. **The available database does not contain, in the material retrieved, any provision imposing a general form, notification or publication requirement on directions under the 1978 Act.** Any assertion that s.2(5) directions must be in writing should be verified before reliance.
- **Judicial control.** Case law on the limits of these powers is out of scope in this research mode and none was retrieved.

#### 2.7 Why the provisions read "Secretary of State"

The 1978 Act is a pre-devolution enactment and its text still refers throughout to "the Secretary of State". Two provisions of the Scotland Act 1998 convert those references:

- **s.53(1)–(2)(c):** functions "conferred on a Minister of the Crown by any **pre-commencement enactment**" are, "so far as they are exercisable **within devolved competence**, … exercisable by the Scottish Ministers instead of by a Minister of the Crown". A "pre-commencement enactment" includes an Act passed before the Scotland Act 1998 (s.53(3)(a)), which the 1978 Act is ([Scotland Act 1998, s.53](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/53)).
- **s.117:** so far as necessary for or in consequence of the exercise of a function by a member of the Scottish Government within devolved competence, any pre-commencement enactment "shall be read as if references to a Minister of the Crown (however described) were or included references to the Scottish Ministers" ([Scotland Act 1998, s.117](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/117)).

Consistently with this, the more recently inserted provisions of the 1978 Act — s.77's reference to HIS, s.78A and s.12IV — name "the Scottish Ministers" directly on their face.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978 (ukpga/1978/29) is recorded with extent `["United Kingdom"]` and the Scotland Act 1998 (ukpga/1998/46) likewise. Note that the *extent* of the 1978 Act as a UK Act is distinct from its **application**, which is to the health service in Scotland; the powers described operate on Scottish Health Boards only.
- **Status.** Both Acts are recorded as `revised` — i.e. the text held incorporates effected amendments. The retrieved s.2, s.77, s.78A, s.105 and s.12IV texts all show amendment (the "2021 Act" references in ss.2(5), 77(1) and 78A, and the s.12IV staffing provisions, are later insertions).
- **Devolved competence.** The transfer under Scotland Act 1998 s.53 operates only "so far as [the functions] are exercisable within devolved competence". Health is a devolved matter, but the qualification is on the face of the provision and is not disapplied by anything retrieved.
- **Caveat on section numbering.** The provision returned at `…/ukpga/1978/29/section/2CA` carries the internal heading "Section 2CB) … Functions of Health Boards outside Scotland". The URI and the text's own numbering disagree, so the citation for that provision should be checked against legislation.gov.uk directly before it is relied on. It is not material to the direction powers described above.
- **Currency.** The API output does not carry per-section commencement or "prospective" annotations, so the in-force position of the most recently inserted provisions should be confirmed against the relevant commencement instruments before reliance.

question: What is the process for making and reviewing an Integration Joint Board's strategic plan?
statements: The making and reviewing of an integration joint board's strategic plan is governed by Part 2 of the Public Bodies (Joint Working) (Scotland) Act 2014, sections 29 to 38.

Section 29 requires the strategic plan to set out the arrangements for carrying out the integration functions and how those arrangements are intended to achieve the national health and wellbeing outcomes, and to divide the area into two or more localities with the arrangements set out separately for each.
Section 33 prescribes a three-stage consultative sequence with the strategic planning group and wider consultees, proposals then a first draft then a second draft, before the plan may be finalised.
Section 37(1)(a) requires the board to review the effectiveness of the strategic plan before the expiry of each three-year relevant period, and section 37(1)(b) permits a review at any other time.
Section 38 allows the constituent authorities acting jointly to direct the board to prepare a replacement strategic plan, and the board must comply with such a direction.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The process is governed by **Part 2 of the Public Bodies (Joint Working) (Scotland) Act 2014 (asp 9)**, ss.29–38. An integration joint board ("IJB") must prepare a strategic plan setting out the arrangements for carrying out the integration functions and how they will achieve the national health and wellbeing outcomes, divided by locality (**s.29**). Preparation runs through a **prescribed three-stage consultative sequence** with its strategic planning group and then a wider body of consultees — proposals, first draft, second draft — before the plan may be finalised (**s.33**), and it must be published together with a statement of the action taken (**s.35**). The board **must review the plan's effectiveness before the expiry of each three-year "relevant period"** (**s.37(1)(a), (10)**), having regard to the integration delivery principles and the national health and wellbeing outcomes and seeking the views of its strategic planning group (**s.37(2)**); it *may* review at any other time (**s.37(1)(b)**). Following a review it *may* prepare a replacement plan (**s.37(3)**), and the constituent authorities acting jointly *may direct* it to do so in the circumstances in **s.38**, with which it **must comply**.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Who is under the duty

The Act imposes the duty on the "integration authority" for the area of a local authority (**s.29(1)**). Under **s.59**, where functions are delegated under the integration model in s.1(4)(a), the integration authority **is the integration joint board** established under the scheme ([s.59](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/59)). The provisions below therefore apply to an IJB directly.

"**Constituent authority**" means each local authority and the Health Board which prepared the integration scheme in pursuance of which the IJB was, or is to be, established (**s.61**) ([s.61](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/61)). That definition matters at three points: information provision (s.34), consultation on the second draft (s.33(5)(a)), and the power to direct a replacement plan (s.38).

#### 2.2 The duty to prepare, and what the plan must contain (s.29)

A strategic plan is a document —
- setting out **the arrangements for carrying out the integration functions** for the local authority's area over the period of the plan (s.29(2)(a));
- setting out **how those arrangements are intended to achieve, or contribute to achieving, the national health and wellbeing outcomes** (s.29(2)(b)); and
- including such other material as the integration authority thinks fit (s.29(2)(c)).

The s.29(2)(a) provision **must** include provision dividing the local authority's area into **two or more localities** and setting out **separately** the arrangements for each locality (**s.29(3)**) ([s.29](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/29)).

Timing of the first plan: it must be prepared **before the integration start day** (s.29(5)), which for an IJB is the day functions are delegated to it (s.29(6)(a)). Where functions are to be delegated before the day prescribed under s.9(3), the first plan must specify the day on which functions are to be delegated (s.29(4)).

#### 2.3 What the board must have regard to (s.30, s.31, s.5)

When preparing a strategic plan the integration authority **must have regard to**:
- **the integration delivery principles** (s.30(2)(a), defined in s.31); and
- **the national health and wellbeing outcomes** (s.30(2)(b), made under s.5).

It must also have regard to the effect its proposed arrangements may have on services, facilities or resources used in relation to arrangements in **another** integration authority's strategic plan, whether already prepared or under preparation, where the periods overlap (**s.30(3)–(4)**) ([s.30](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/30)).

The **integration delivery principles** (s.31(1)) are that the main purpose of services provided in pursuance of integration functions is to improve service-users' wellbeing, and that so far as consistent with that purpose the services should so far as possible be integrated from the service-user's point of view; take account of the particular needs, characteristics and circumstances of different service-users and of service-users in different parts of the area; respect service-users' rights and dignity; take account of participation in the community; protect and improve safety; improve quality; be **planned and led locally in a way which is engaged with the community** (including service-users, those who look after them and those involved in providing health or social care); best anticipate needs and prevent them arising; and make the best use of available facilities, people and other resources ([s.31](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/31)).

The **national health and wellbeing outcomes** are prescribed by the Scottish Ministers by regulations under **s.5(1)**, after consulting each local authority, each Health Board, each IJB then established, and representatives of the eleven groups listed in s.5(3) ([s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/5)). *The specific outcomes regulations were not retrieved in this run — see 2.9.*

#### 2.4 The strategic planning group (s.32)

**Before preparing its first strategic plan**, the integration authority must establish a "strategic planning group" (s.32(1)). For an IJB, its membership comprises:
- at least one person nominated by the **Health Board** which is a constituent authority (s.32(1)(a)(i));
- at least one person nominated by the **local authority** (or, where two or more local authorities are constituent authorities, by those authorities) (s.32(1)(a)(ii)–(iii));
- **one person in respect of each prescribed group**, being a person the authority considers representative of that group (s.32(1)(d), with the groups prescribed under s.32(2)); and
- **such other persons as the integration authority considers appropriate** (s.32(1)(e)).

During the period of any strategic plan, the group **must also** include a person to represent the interests of **each locality** set out in the plan under s.29(3)(a) (**s.32(7)**); the authority decides who is suitable and selects the representative (s.32(8)), and may select one person for two or more localities (s.32(9)).

The authority determines the group's size and (so far as not set out in s.32) the processes for appointment, removal and replacement (s.32(3)), and its procedure (s.32(11)); it may pay expenses and allowances (s.32(12)). A constituent authority may remove and replace its own nominee (s.32(5)); a member may resign at any time (s.32(6)); and **a vacancy does not affect the validity of anything the group does** (s.32(10)) ([s.32](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/32)).

#### 2.5 The staged preparation procedure (s.33) — the core of the process

Section 33 prescribes a **sequential, three-round process**. The statutory language is directive ("is to", "must"), and each round must take account of the previous one:

| Stage | What the board does | Who is consulted | Statutory basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Prepare **proposals for what the plan should contain**, and seek views on them | Strategic planning group | s.33(2) |
| 2 | Taking account of stage 1 views, prepare a **first draft** and seek views on it | Strategic planning group | s.33(3) |
| 3 | Taking account of stage 2 views, prepare a **second draft**, send a copy to the s.33(5) persons and to such others as it considers appropriate, and invite views within such period as it considers appropriate | Each constituent authority; representatives of each prescribed group; others as it considers appropriate | s.33(4) |
| 4 | **Finalise** the plan, taking account of the stage 3 views | — | s.33(7) |

The persons who **must** receive the second draft, where the integration authority is an IJB, are **each constituent authority** (s.33(5)(a)) and **persons the authority considers representative of each of the prescribed groups** (s.33(5)(d)) ([s.33](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/33)).

Two features are worth noting for compliance purposes:
- The obligation at stages 1–3 is to **seek views**; the obligation to **take account of** them is expressed separately at the start of each following stage and, for the final round, in s.33(7). Seeking views without demonstrably taking account of them would not satisfy the section.
- The consultation **period** at stage 3 is at the board's discretion ("within such period as the integration authority considers appropriate") — the Act sets no minimum.

#### 2.6 Information from constituent authorities (s.34)

A constituent authority **must** provide an IJB with such information as the board **may reasonably require** for the purpose of preparing a strategic plan (**s.34(1)**) ([s.34](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/34)). The equivalent duty applies on review under s.37(5).

#### 2.7 Publication (s.35)

**As soon as practicable after the finalisation of the plan under s.33**, the integration authority must publish its strategic plan (s.35(1)); and **at the same time** it must also publish **a statement of the action which it took in pursuance of s.33** (s.35(2)) ([s.35](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/35)). The second limb is an auditable record of the consultative process, not an optional annex.

#### 2.8 Review and replacement

**(a) Periodic review — s.37(1)(a) and (10).** The integration authority **must, before the expiry of the relevant period, review the effectiveness of its strategic plan**. "Relevant period" means the period of **3 years** beginning with the integration start day, and each subsequent period of 3 years beginning with:
- where a replacement plan is prepared following a review, **the day specified under s.37(9)** (the day the new plan's period begins); or
- where **no** replacement plan is prepared following a review, **the day on which the authority decides not to prepare one** (s.37(10)(b)).

So the three-year clock restarts from the decision point, not from the review's commencement. The authority **may** also carry out a review from time to time (s.37(1)(b)).

**(b) What a review must involve — s.37(2).** The authority must have regard to the integration delivery principles and the national health and wellbeing outcomes (s.37(2)(a)), and must **seek and have regard to the views of its strategic planning group** on (i) the effectiveness of the arrangements for carrying out the integration functions in the area, and (ii) **whether the authority should prepare a replacement strategic plan** (s.37(2)(b)). Subject to that, **the process of a review is such as the integration authority determines** (s.37(4)) — the Act prescribes the inputs, not the method.

**(c) Information on review — s.37(5)–(7).** The s.34 duty is mirrored: a constituent authority must give an IJB such information as it may reasonably require for the purpose of carrying out a review.

**(d) Replacement following review — s.37(3), (8), (9).** Following a review the authority **may** prepare a replacement plan. Where it does, **ss.30, 33, 34 and 35 apply to it as they apply to a s.29 plan** (s.37(8)) — i.e. the full considerations, three-stage consultation, information and publication requirements are repeated. The replacement plan **must specify a day on which the period of the plan is to begin** (s.37(9)) ([s.37](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/37)).

**(e) Directed replacement — s.38.** This section applies only where the integration authority **is an IJB** (s.38(1)). Where it appears to a constituent authority that the strategic plan **is preventing, or is likely to prevent, that authority from carrying out any of its functions appropriately**, or in a way which complies with the integration delivery principles and contributes to achieving the national health and wellbeing outcomes, **the constituent authorities acting jointly may direct** the IJB to prepare a replacement strategic plan (s.38(2)).

The direction:
- **must be in writing** and **include a statement summarising the reasons** for giving it (s.38(3));
- **must specify** a day by which the replacement plan must be prepared and a day on which the plan's period is to begin (s.38(4)), which the constituent authorities acting jointly may later substitute by further direction (s.38(5)); and
- **must be complied with** — "An integration authority must comply with a direction given to it under subsection (2)" (s.38(6)).

Again, **ss.30, 33, 34 and 35 apply** to a plan prepared under a s.38 direction (s.38(7)) ([s.38](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/38)).

Note the constitutional shape of s.38: the power is exercisable **only by the constituent authorities acting jointly**, not by either alone and not by the Scottish Ministers. The trigger is the effect of the plan on a **constituent authority's own functions**, not a general view that the plan is deficient.

**(f) Significant decisions taken outside the plan — s.36.** Where an integration authority proposes a significant decision about the arrangements for carrying out integration functions and intends it to take effect **other than by revising its strategic plan under s.37**, it must seek and have regard to the views of its strategic planning group and take such action as it thinks fit to secure that **users of the service** are involved in and consulted on the decision (s.36(3)–(4)). "Significant decision" means one the authority considers **might significantly affect the provision of a service** provided in pursuance of the integration functions in the area (s.36(2)) ([s.36](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/9/section/36)). This closes the obvious gap — it prevents the consultative regime being bypassed by taking major decisions outside the plan.

#### 2.9 The prescribed consultees (SSI 2014/283)

The groups prescribed for the purposes of **s.33(6)** — i.e. those whose representatives must receive the second draft under s.33(5)(d) — are, subject to reg 5, **the "standard consultees"** (reg 3) ([SSI 2014/283, reg 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/283/regulation/3)).

The **standard consultees** are listed in the Schedule: health professionals; users of health care; carers of users of health care; commercial providers of health care; non-commercial providers of health care; social care professionals; users of social care; carers of users of social care; commercial providers of social care; non-commercial providers of social care; staff of the Health Board and local authority who are not health or social care professionals; non-commercial providers of social housing; and third sector bodies carrying out activities related to health or social care ([SSI 2014/283, Schedule](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/283/schedule)). "Third sector" includes representative groups, interest groups, social enterprises and community organisations (reg 1(2)).

**Regulation 5** imposes a locality/connection qualification: users must reside in the area of the local authority which prepared the integration scheme **and** use services provided in pursuance of integration functions; carers must care for such a user; non-commercial providers of social housing and third sector bodies must operate in that area; and in any other case the consultee must operate in that area **and** provide, or be engaged in relation to, services provided in pursuance of integration functions ([SSI 2014/283, reg 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/283/regulation/5)).

**Two gaps in the retrieved material, stated rather than filled:**
- **Section 32(2) (strategic planning group membership) does not appear to be prescribed for by SSI 2014/283.** The Regulations expressly prescribe for ss.6(2)(a) and 46(4)(a) (reg 2), s.33(6) (reg 3) and s.41(4) (reg 4). **The available database does not contain, in the material retrieved, the instrument prescribing the groups for the purposes of s.32(2)**; the groups whose representatives must sit on the strategic planning group under s.32(1)(d) should therefore be confirmed against the current subordinate legislation before reliance.
- **The national health and wellbeing outcomes regulations under s.5(1) were not retrieved.** The outcomes themselves are therefore not set out above.

question: What powers does the Information Commissioner have to impose penalties for breach of data protection duties?
statements: The Information Commissioner's power to impose a financial penalty for breach of data protection duties is the penalty notice under section 155 of the Data Protection Act 2018.

Section 157 sets a higher maximum amount of £17,500,000 or 4% of an undertaking's total annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, and a standard maximum amount of £8,700,000 or 2% on the same basis.
Section 115(9) makes the section 155 penalty notice the only route by which the administrative fine powers in Articles 58(2)(i) and 83 of the UK GDPR may be exercised.

Schedule 16 imposes a mandatory procedure: a notice of intent must be given first, allowing not less than 21 days for written representations, and the penalty notice must follow within 6 months of the notice of intent.
A penalty notice may be appealed to the Tribunal, including against the amount alone under section 162(3), and the Tribunal may substitute its own decision under section 163(3).
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The Commissioner's power to impose a financial penalty is the **penalty notice** under **section 155 of the Data Protection Act 2018**, and it is the **only** route by which the administrative-fine powers in Articles 58(2)(i) and 83 of the UK GDPR may be exercised (**s.115(9)**). The maximum is tiered (**s.157**): a **higher maximum amount** of **£17,500,000 or 4% of an undertaking's total annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, whichever is higher**, and a **standard maximum amount** of **£8,700,000 or 2%**, on the same "whichever is higher" basis. For UK GDPR infringements the amount is that specified in **Article 83** — Article 83(4) matters attract the 2%/£8.7m tier and Article 83(5)–(6) matters the 4%/£17.5m tier. Imposition is subject to a **mandatory procedure in Schedule 16**: a notice of intent must be given first, with **not less than 21 days** for written representations, and the penalty notice must follow **within 6 months** of the notice of intent (or as soon as reasonably practicable thereafter); payment is due within **not less than 28 days**. A penalty notice may be **appealed to the Tribunal**, including against the amount alone (**s.162(3)**), and the Tribunal may substitute its own decision (**s.163(3)**).

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The power — s.155

If the Commissioner is **satisfied** that a person:
- **(a)** has failed or is failing as described in **s.149(2), (3), (4) or (5)**;
- **(b)** has failed to comply with **an information notice, an assessment notice, an interview notice or an enforcement notice**; or
- **(c)** has failed to comply with a duty imposed by **s.146A(6)**,

the Commissioner "**may, by written notice (a 'penalty notice'), require the person to pay to the Commissioner an amount in sterling specified in the notice**" (s.155(1)) ([s.155](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/155)).

The power is **discretionary** ("may"), and the precondition is the Commissioner's own satisfaction.

**The failures cross-referenced from s.149** ([s.149](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/149)) are:
- **s.149(2)** — a controller or processor failing to comply with: the processing principles (Chapter II UK GDPR, or Chapter 2 of Part 3 or Part 4 of the Act); provisions of or made under Articles 12–22D UK GDPR or Parts 3/4 conferring **data subject rights**; Articles 25–39 UK GDPR or ss.64–65 (**controller and processor obligations**); the duty to **communicate a personal data breach** under ss.67, 68 or 108; or the **international transfer** principles in Articles 44A–49A UK GDPR or ss.73–78 or 109.
- **s.149(3)** — a **monitoring body** failing to comply with Article 41 (monitoring of approved codes of conduct).
- **s.149(4)** — a **certification provider** which does not meet accreditation requirements, or fails to comply with Article 42 or 43, or with any other provision of the UK GDPR.
- **s.149(5)** — a **controller** failing to comply with regulations under s.137 (the charges regulations).

**Extension by regulations.** The Secretary of State may by regulations confer power to give a penalty notice in respect of *other* failures to comply with the data protection legislation, and provide whether the standard or higher maximum applies (s.155(6)); such regulations may amend ss.155–158 themselves and are subject to the **affirmative** resolution procedure (s.155(7)).

#### 2.2 The maximum amounts — s.157

> **s.157(5):** The "higher maximum amount" is — (a) in the case of an undertaking, **£17,500,000 or 4% of the undertaking's total annual worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year, whichever is higher**, or (b) in any other case, **£17,500,000**.
>
> **s.157(6):** The "standard maximum amount" is — (a) in the case of an undertaking, **£8,700,000 or 2%** of that turnover, **whichever is higher**, or (b) in any other case, **£8,700,000**.
> ([s.157](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/157))

Which tier applies:

| Infringement | Maximum | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A provision of the **UK GDPR** | The amount **specified in Article 83**; if none is specified there, the standard maximum | s.157(1) |
| **Part 3** (law enforcement processing) — failure to comply with ss.35, 36, 37, 38(1), 39(1), 40, 44–48, 50B, 50C, 52, 53, 73, 75–78 | **Higher** maximum | s.157(2)(a) |
| Any other Part 3 provision | **Standard** maximum | s.157(2)(b) |
| **Part 4** (intelligence services processing) — failure to comply with ss.86–91, 93, 94, 100 or 109 | **Higher** maximum | s.157(3)(a) |
| Any other Part 4 provision | **Standard** maximum | s.157(3)(b) |
| Failure to comply with an **information, assessment, interview or enforcement notice** | **Higher** maximum | s.157(4) |

Note the drafting of s.157(5)–(6): the turnover alternative applies **only to an undertaking**, and where it applies the maximum is **the higher** of the cash figure and the percentage — not a choice, and not a cap at the cash figure.

#### 2.3 The UK GDPR tiers — Article 83

For UK GDPR infringements the operative amounts are in **Article 83** of the retained Regulation ([Article 83](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/eur/2016/679/article/83)):

- **Article 83(4)** — up to **£8,700,000, or in the case of an undertaking up to 2% of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher**: controller/processor obligations under Articles 8, 11, 25–39, 42 and 43; certification body obligations under Articles 42–43; monitoring body obligations under Article 41(4).
- **Article 83(5)** — up to **£17,500,000, or 4%, whichever is higher**: the basic principles for processing including conditions for consent (Articles 5, 6, 7, 9); data subjects' rights (Articles 12–21); Article 22B or 22C (restrictions on and safeguards for automated decision-making); international transfers (Articles 44A–49); obligations under Parts 5 or 6 of Schedule 2 to the 2018 Act or regulations under s.16(1)(c); and non-compliance with an order, limitation on processing or suspension of data flows under Article 58(2), or failure to provide access in violation of Article 58(1).
- **Article 83(6)** — non-compliance with an order of the Commissioner under Article 58(2): the **4% / £17,500,000** tier.

**The "gravest infringement" cap.** Where a controller or processor intentionally or negligently infringes **several provisions for the same or linked processing operations**, "the total amount of the administrative fine shall not exceed the amount specified for the gravest infringement" (**Article 83(3)**). This is a material limit on aggregation and has no direct equivalent in ss.155–158.

**The overriding standard.** Article 83(1) requires the Commissioner to ensure that a fine is in each individual case "**effective, proportionate and dissuasive**" — a requirement echoed in the s.155(3)(l) factor.

#### 2.4 The mandatory relationship with the UK GDPR powers — s.115(9)

> **s.115(9):** "The Commissioner's powers under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83 of the UK GDPR (administrative fines) are exercisable **only** by giving a penalty notice under section 155."
> ([s.115](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/115))

This is the pivotal integrating provision: there is **no free-standing power to fine** under the UK GDPR in domestic law. Section 115 does the same for the other corrective powers — Article 58(2)(c)–(h) and (j) are exercisable **only** by enforcement notice under s.149 (s.115(8)), and the Article 58(1)(a) information power only by information notice under s.142 (s.115(5)). Any analysis that treats Article 83 as directly exercisable is wrong as a matter of UK law.

#### 2.5 What the Commissioner must consider — s.155(2)–(4)

When deciding **whether** to give a penalty notice **and** determining **the amount**, the Commissioner must have regard, so far as relevant:
- to the extent the notice concerns a **UK GDPR** matter — the matters listed in **Article 83(1) and (2)** (s.155(2)(a)); and
- to the extent it concerns **another** matter — the twelve factors in **s.155(3)** (s.155(2)(b)).

The s.155(3) list closely tracks Article 83(2): nature, gravity and duration of the failure; its intentional or negligent character; mitigation of damage or distress; degree of responsibility having regard to technical and organisational measures under ss.57, 66, 103 or 107; relevant previous failures; degree of co-operation; categories of personal data affected; how the infringement became known (including self-reporting); compliance with previous enforcement or penalty notices; adherence to approved codes of conduct or certification mechanisms; any other aggravating or mitigating factor including **financial benefits gained or losses avoided**; and **whether the penalty would be effective, proportionate and dissuasive**.

**Exception:** ss.155(2) and (3) do **not** apply to a decision or determination relating to a **s.149(5)** failure — i.e. non-compliance with the charges regulations (s.155(4)), which is dealt with by the fixed-penalty regime below.

#### 2.6 Procedure — Schedule 16

Schedule 16 is mandatory and its steps are sequential ([Schedule 16](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/schedule/16)):

1. **Notice of intent (para 2(1)).** "Before giving a person a penalty notice, the Commissioner **must**, by written notice (a 'notice of intent') inform the person that the Commissioner intends to give a penalty notice."
2. **Contents of the notice of intent (para 3).** Name and address; the reasons, including a description of the circumstances of the failure and, for a s.149(2) failure, the nature of the personal data involved; and **an indication of the amount proposed, including any aggravating or mitigating factors** the Commissioner proposes to take into account.
3. **Representations (para 3(3)–(5)).** The notice must state that written representations may be made and specify the period, which "**must be a period of not less than 21 days beginning when the notice of intent is given**". Where the Commissioner considers it appropriate for the person to have an opportunity to make **oral** representations, the notice must say so and specify the arrangements.
4. **The 6-month window (para 4(A2)).** Within **6 months** beginning when the notice of intent is given, "or as soon as reasonably practicable thereafter", the Commissioner must give the person either a penalty notice or **written notice of a decision not to** give one.
5. **No premature notice (para 4(1)).** A penalty notice may not be given before the time or the end of the period specified for representations; and the Commissioner **must consider** any representations made (para 4(2)).
6. **Contents of the penalty notice (para 5).** Name and address; details of the notice of intent; whether representations were received; the reasons for imposing the penalty; **the reasons for the amount, including aggravating and mitigating factors taken into account**; how to pay; **details of the rights of appeal under s.162**; and details of the Commissioner's enforcement powers.
7. **Payment (para 6).** Within the period specified, which "must be a period of **not less than 28 days** beginning when the penalty notice is given".
8. **Variation (para 7).** By a written "penalty variation notice". Critically, it **may not** reduce the payment period, **increase** the amount, or otherwise vary the notice **to the detriment** of the recipient; and any overpayment following a reduction must be repaid.
9. **Cancellation (para 8).** The Commissioner may cancel by written notice; on cancellation the Commissioner **may not take any further action** under s.155 or Schedule 16 in relation to that failure, and must repay anything already paid.
10. **Recovery (para 9).** No recovery action until the payment period has ended **and** all appeals (against the notice and any variation) have been decided or ended and the time for appealing has expired. Recovery is then: in **England and Wales** and **Northern Ireland**, as if payable under an order of the county court or High Court if that court so orders; in **Scotland**, "in the same manner as an extract registered decree arbitral bearing a warrant for execution issued by the sheriff court of any sheriffdom in Scotland".

#### 2.7 Restrictions on the power — s.156

The Commissioner **may not** give a penalty notice ([s.156](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/156)):

- **Special purposes (s.156(1)–(2)).** In reliance on s.149(2) with respect to processing for the **special purposes**, unless a **s.174 determination** has taken effect **and a court has granted leave**. A court must not grant leave unless satisfied that the Commissioner has reason to suspect a s.149(2) failure **of substantial public importance**, and that the controller or processor has had notice of the leave application in accordance with rules of court, or the case is urgent.
- **Parliament (s.156(3)).** Where the purposes and manner of the processing are determined by or on behalf of **either House of Parliament**.
- **Excluded persons (s.156(4)).** To the **Crown Estate Commissioners**, or to a person who is a controller by virtue of **s.209(4)** (controller for the Royal Household etc).
- **Joint controllers (s.156(5)).** For Part 3 or Part 4 processing where responsibilities are allocated by an arrangement under s.58 or s.104, a penalty notice in reliance on s.149(2) may be given to a controller **only if that controller is responsible for compliance** with the provision, requirement or principle in question.

#### 2.8 Fixed penalties for the charges regulations — s.158

Non-compliance with the s.137 charges regulations is dealt with separately. The Commissioner **must produce and publish** a document specifying the penalty amount, may specify different amounts for different types of failure, and the **maximum specifiable is 150% of the highest charge payable by a controller for a financial year** under the regulations, disregarding any available discount (s.158(1)–(3)). The document may be altered or replaced, must be published, requires prior consultation with the Secretary of State and such others as the Commissioner considers appropriate, and **must be laid before Parliament** (s.158(4)–(6)) ([s.158](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/158)).

#### 2.9 Published guidance — s.160

The Commissioner **must** produce and publish guidance about how the Commissioner proposes to exercise the functions in connection with information notices, assessment notices, interview notices, enforcement notices **and penalty notices** (s.160(1)), and **may** publish guidance on other Part 6 functions (s.160(2)). Section 160 goes on to prescribe the minimum content of that guidance for each notice type ([s.160](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/160)). The guidance itself is not legislation and was not retrieved; the statutory duty to have it is.

#### 2.10 Appeals — ss.162–163

A person given a **penalty notice** or a **penalty variation notice** may appeal to the **Tribunal** (s.162(1)(d)–(e)), and "may appeal to the Tribunal **against the amount** of the penalty specified in the notice, **whether or not** the person appeals against the notice" (s.162(3)) ([s.162](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/162)).

The Tribunal's powers are broad (s.163) ([s.163](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/163)):
- it **may review any determination of fact** on which the notice was based (s.163(2));
- if it considers the notice **is not in accordance with the law**, or that to the extent discretion was involved **the Commissioner ought to have exercised it differently**, it **must** allow the appeal or **substitute another notice or decision which the Commissioner could have given** (s.163(3));
- otherwise it must dismiss the appeal (s.163(4)).

This is a **full merits review**, not a rationality review — the Tribunal may substitute its own view of how the discretion should have been exercised.

#### 2.11 Distinguish: criminal penalties — s.196

Section 196 is **not** a Commissioner penalty power. It sets the penalties on **conviction** for offences under the Act ([s.196](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2018/12/section/196)):
- offences under s.119, s.173 or paragraph 15 of Schedule 15 — on summary conviction in England and Wales, **a fine**; in Scotland or Northern Ireland, **a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale**;
- offences under ss.132, 144, 148, 148C, 170, 171 or 184 — on summary conviction in England and Wales, a fine; in Scotland or Northern Ireland, **a fine not exceeding the statutory maximum**; on conviction on indictment, a fine.

The court may also order forfeiture, destruction or erasure of material connected with an offence under s.170 or s.184, subject to a third-party owner's right to be heard (s.196(4)–(5)). **The retrieved text states these penalties exactly as above; no monetary equivalent for "level 5 on the standard scale" or "the statutory maximum" appears in it, and none should be supplied from outside the retrieved material.**

The recovery provisions in Schedule 16 para 9 are expressly differentiated for England and Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.

question: How is the chair of Food Standards Scotland appointed?
statements: The chair of Food Standards Scotland is appointed by the Scottish Ministers under section 6(1)(a) of the Food (Scotland) Act 2015.
The Food (Scotland) Act 2015 requires no approval or confirmation of the chair's appointment by the Scottish Parliament.
The Act fixes no term of office for the chair: under section 6(5) membership is for such period and on such terms and conditions as the Scottish Ministers may determine.

The appointment is a regulated public appointment under the Public Appointments and Public Bodies etc. (Scotland) Act 2003, so it is governed by the code of practice of the Commissioner for Ethical Standards in Public Life in Scotland, who may under section 2(8) direct the Ministers to delay the appointment, and the Ministers must comply.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The chair is appointed by **the Scottish Ministers** under **section 6(1)(a) of the Food (Scotland) Act 2015 (asp 1)**: Food Standards Scotland consists of "a person appointed by the Scottish Ministers to chair Food Standards Scotland" together with **no fewer than 3 nor more than 7** other members, also appointed by the Scottish Ministers. The Act imposes **no requirement for Scottish Parliament approval or confirmation**, and **fixes no term of office** — membership is "for such period and on such terms and conditions as the Scottish Ministers may determine" (s.6(5)), subject to the early-ending provisions in ss.7 and 18. The appointment is nevertheless a **regulated public appointment**: s.17(4) of the 2015 Act inserted Food Standards Scotland into schedule 2 to the **Public Appointments and Public Bodies etc. (Scotland) Act 2003 (asp 4)**, so the process is governed by the **code of practice** prepared and published by the **Commissioner for Ethical Standards in Public Life in Scotland** under s.2(1) of that Act — and where the Commissioner considers the code has not been complied with in a material regard, the Commissioner **may direct the Scottish Ministers to delay making the appointment** until Parliament has considered the case, and **the Ministers must comply** (s.2(8)).

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The body and the appointing power

**Section 1** establishes "a body corporate called Food Standards Scotland or, in Gaelic, Inbhe-Bidhe Alba" ([s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/1)).

> **s.6(1):** "Food Standards Scotland is to consist of— (a) **a person appointed by the Scottish Ministers to chair Food Standards Scotland**, and (b) no fewer than 3 nor more than 7 other members appointed by the Scottish Ministers."
> ([s.6](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/6))

Three points follow directly from the text:

1. **The appointing authority is the Scottish Ministers alone.** No approval, confirmation, nomination or veto by the Scottish Parliament, by a committee, or by any other body appears on the face of s.6.
2. **The chair is a distinct appointment, not an office filled from among the members.** Section 6(1)(a) creates a separate limb from s.6(1)(b), and the board size is "3 to 7 **other** members" — so the full board is between 4 and 8 people including the chair.
3. **The chair is appointed "to chair" the body**, i.e. appointed directly to that role rather than appointed as a member and subsequently elected chair.

#### 2.2 Disqualification from appointment — s.6(2)

A person **may not be appointed** as a member if the person is:
- a member of the **Scottish Parliament**;
- a member of the **House of Commons**;
- a member of the **European Parliament**;
- an **office-holder in the Scottish Administration**;
- a **councillor** of any local authority; or
- an **employee** of any local authority.

The list applies to "a member", which by s.6(1) includes the chairing member.

#### 2.3 The manner of appointment — s.6(3)–(4)

> **s.6(3):** "The Scottish Ministers **must** make appointments of members of Food Standards Scotland in a manner which encourages **equal opportunities** and in particular the observance of the **equal opportunity requirements**."

"Equal opportunities" and "equal opportunity requirements" bear the meanings given in **Section L2 of Part 2 of Schedule 5 to the Scotland Act 1998** (s.6(4)). This is a duty on the *process* of appointment, not merely on the outcome, and it is expressed as an obligation ("must").

#### 2.4 Term, terms and conditions, remuneration — ss.6(5)–(7), 8

- **No statutory term.** "Membership is (subject to sections 7 and 18) for such period and on such terms and conditions as the Scottish Ministers may determine" (**s.6(5)**). The Act sets no minimum or maximum term for the chair; the period is set by the Ministers in the individual appointment.
- **Resignation.** A member may resign "by informing the Scottish Ministers in writing to that effect" (**s.6(6)**).
- **Re-appointment.** "A person may be re-appointed on, or after, ceasing to be a member" (**s.6(7)**). There is no statutory cap on the number of terms.
- **Remuneration.** A member is entitled to such remuneration as the Scottish Ministers may determine, and to such sums as they determine to reimburse or compensate for expenses properly incurred in exercising the member's functions; **it is for Food Standards Scotland to pay** those sums (**s.8**) ([s.8](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/8)). So the amount is set by the Ministers but borne by the body.

#### 2.5 Deputising and a vacant chair — s.6(8)–(9)

The Scottish Ministers may assign to one of the **s.6(1)(b) members**:
- **(a)** the function of **deputising** for the chair; and
- **(b)** the function of **chairing Food Standards Scotland during any period when there is no person appointed under s.6(1)(a)** — i.e. an acting chair during a vacancy.

Such an assignment runs for the period the Ministers specify, may be resigned by written notice to the Ministers, and is made and ended in accordance with terms and conditions the Ministers determine (s.6(9)).

Note the constraint: the deputy or acting chair must be an **existing member appointed under s.6(1)(b)**. The Ministers cannot use s.6(8) to install an outsider as acting chair.

#### 2.6 How the appointment ends early — ss.7 and 18

**Automatic termination (s.7(1)).** Membership **ends** if the person *becomes* any of the six disqualifying categories in s.6(2) — MSP, MP, MEP, office-holder in the Scottish Administration, councillor, or local authority employee. This is automatic; no ministerial act is required ([s.7](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/7)).

**Discretionary removal (s.7(2)).** The Scottish Ministers **may** end a person's membership if:
- **(a)** the person becomes an **undischarged bankrupt**; or
- **(b)** the Ministers are satisfied that the person —
  - **(i)** has, **without the permission of Food Standards Scotland**, been absent from its meetings for a period longer than **6 consecutive months**,
  - **(ii)** is **unable** to perform the functions of a member, or
  - **(iii)** is **unsuitable** to continue as a member.

Two features are worth noting: the absence ground turns on the *body's* permission, not the Ministers'; and grounds (ii) and (iii) are framed on the Ministers' own satisfaction, with "unsuitable" undefined in the retrieved text.

**Collective removal for serious failure (s.18).** Where the Scottish Ministers consider there has been a **serious failure** by Food Standards Scotland to exercise any of its functions, they may give it such directions as they consider appropriate to remedy the failure, having first **consulted** the body (s.18(1)–(3)). Such a direction **must be in writing** and **must include a statement summarising the reasons** for it (s.18(4)), and the Ministers **must publish** it (s.18(5)). If the body fails to comply, the Ministers may give effect to the direction themselves, exercising any of the body's functions in its place (s.18(6)), and **may end the membership of all its members** and, until new members are appointed, exercise any of its functions in its place or appoint another person to do so (s.18(7)) ([s.18](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/18)).

Section 18(7) is the only route in the retrieved material by which the chair's membership can be ended other than under s.7 — and it operates on the whole board, not on the chair individually.

#### 2.7 The appointment is a *regulated* public appointment — s.17(4)

Section 17 of the 2015 Act applied a series of public-body statutes to Food Standards Scotland by amendment. The one that governs the appointment process is **s.17(4)**:

> "In the **Public Appointments and Public Bodies etc. (Scotland) Act 2003**, in **schedule 2 (specified authorities)**, after the entry relating to the Crofting Commission insert— 'Food Standards Scotland'."
> ([s.17](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2015/1/section/17))

This is confirmed by the current text of the 2003 Act: **Food Standards Scotland appears in the retrieved schedule 2** ([PAPB (Scotland) Act 2003, schedule 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2003/4/schedule/2)).

(Section 17 also brought the body within the Ethical Standards in Public Life etc. (Scotland) Act 2000 schedule 3, the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman Act 2002 schedule 2, the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 schedule 1, the Public Services Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 schedules 8, 19 and 20, the Public Records (Scotland) Act 2011, the Regulatory Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 schedule 1 and the Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 — none of which bears directly on the appointment process.)

#### 2.8 What the regulated regime requires — PAPB (Scotland) Act 2003, s.2

Because Food Standards Scotland is a specified authority, the Ministers' appointment of its chair is subject to the statutory code regime ([PAPB (Scotland) Act 2003, s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2003/4/section/2)):

- **The code of practice (s.2(1)).** The **Commissioner for Ethical Standards in Public Life in Scotland** "is to prepare and publish a **code of practice** in respect of the making by the Scottish Ministers of any appointment or … recommendation for any appointment … to a body specified in schedule 2".
- **Its content (s.2(2)).** The code is to include guidelines as to the methods and practices to be employed, and may in particular cover **how vacancies are publicised**, **how applications are encouraged**, and **the basis on which the Ministers are to consider persons** for appointment.
- **Consultation on the code (s.2(4)).** In preparing or revising it the Commissioner must consult the Parliament and the Scottish Ministers, and invite representations from others.
- **Oversight (s.2(5)).** The Commissioner is to examine the Ministers' methods and practices in making such appointments, may examine the making of any particular appointment, and **is to investigate complaints** arising from an appointment.
- **Guidance (s.2(6)).** The Commissioner may issue guidance to the Ministers, generally or in a particular case, as to compliance with the code.
- **Enforcement (s.2(7)–(8)).** Where it appears to the Commissioner that the code **has not been complied with in a material regard**, the Commissioner has intimated that to the Ministers, and the Commissioner considers the code is unlikely to be complied with within a reasonable time (or, after a reasonable time, remains uncomplied with), the Commissioner **must report the case to the Parliament** and — **if the appointment has not yet been made** — **may direct the Scottish Ministers to delay making it until the Parliament has considered the case**. "**and the Scottish Ministers must comply with any such direction**."
- **The governing objective (s.2(9)).** The Commissioner is to exercise these functions with a view to ensuring appointments are **made fairly and openly**, and that so far as reasonably practicable **all categories of person** are afforded an opportunity to be considered.
- **Equal opportunities strategy (s.2(10)).** The Commissioner must prepare and publish a strategy for ensuring appointments are made in a manner encouraging equal opportunities, and may set targets — mirroring the duty imposed directly on the Ministers by s.6(3) of the 2015 Act.

The Ministers must also provide the Commissioner with such information as the Commissioner reasonably requires (**s.3(1)**), and may by order amend schedule 2 or adjust the Commissioner's functions in relation to appointments (**s.3(2)**), after consulting the Parliamentary corporation where the change is to the Commissioner's functions (s.3(2A)) ([s.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2003/4/section/3)).

#### 2.9 What the retrieved material does *not* establish

- **The content of the code of practice.** The code is made under s.2(1) but is **not itself legislation** and was not retrieved. The practical mechanics of a chair appointment — advertisement, selection panel composition, interview, ministerial choice from a list of appointable candidates — are matters for the code, not the Acts. **The available database does not contain the code of practice**, and its requirements should be taken from the Commissioner's own published version.
- **Any prescribed term length.** No provision fixing the chair's term was retrieved; s.6(5) leaves it to the Ministers.
- **Any parliamentary confirmation requirement.** None appears in the retrieved text of the 2015 Act. The only parliamentary involvement in the retrieved material is the Commissioner's report to the Parliament under s.2(8) of the 2003 Act, which arises only on material non-compliance with the code.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Food (Scotland) Act 2015 (asp/2015/1) and the Public Appointments and Public Bodies etc. (Scotland) Act 2003 (asp/2003/4) are both recorded with extent `["Scotland"]`. The regime applies to Scotland only.
- **Status.** Both Acts are recorded as `revised` — the text held incorporates effected amendments. The 2003 Act text shows amendment: s.2(1) now refers to the **Commissioner for Ethical Standards in Public Life in Scotland** (the office having replaced the former Commissioner for Public Appointments in Scotland named in the s.1 heading), and s.3(2A) is a later insertion.
