question: To what extent is regulation of the health professions within the legislative competence of the Scottish Parliament?
statements: Regulation of the health professions is a reserved matter under Section G2 of Part II of Schedule 5 to the Scotland Act 1998, and so is generally outside the legislative competence of the Scottish Parliament.
Under section 29(2)(b) of the Scotland Act 1998 a provision of an Act of the Scottish Parliament is outside competence so far as it relates to reserved matters.
"The health professions" is defined for Section G2 by a closed, exhaustive list of nine regulating enactments, so a profession not regulated by one of those Acts is not within the reservation.

Section G2 contains express exceptions carving out the subject-matter of section 21 of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978, and of section 25 of that Act so far as it relates to vocational training and disciplinary proceedings.

Whether a provision relates to a reserved matter is determined by the purpose test in section 29(3), judged by reference to the provision's purpose and having regard among other things to its effect in all the circumstances.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**Regulation of the health professions is a reserved matter** and so, as a general rule, **outside** the Scottish Parliament's legislative competence: **Section G2 of Part II of Schedule 5 to the Scotland Act 1998** reserves "**Regulation of the health professions**", and by **s.29(2)(b)** a provision of an Act of the Scottish Parliament is outside competence so far as it "relates to reserved matters". The extent of the reservation is, however, **narrower than the phrase suggests**, for three reasons that appear on the face of the Schedule. First, "the health professions" is defined by a **closed, exhaustive list of nine regulating enactments** — a profession not regulated by one of those nine Acts is not within the G2 reservation at all. Second, **two express exceptions** carve out the subject-matter of s.21 of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978 and of s.25 of that Act so far as it relates to **vocational training and disciplinary proceedings**. Third, the reservation is of **regulation of the professions**, not of the health service: the organisation, funding and delivery of NHS services in Scotland is devolved and is not reserved by G2. Whether any particular Bill is within competence turns on the **purpose test in s.29(3)** — whether the provision *relates to* the reserved matter, judged by reference to its purpose, having regard among other things to its effect in all the circumstances.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The competence test — s.29

> **s.29(1):** "An Act of the Scottish Parliament is not law so far as any provision of the Act is outside the legislative competence of the Parliament."
>
> **s.29(2):** "A provision is outside that competence so far as any of the following paragraphs apply— (a) it would form part of the law of a country or territory other than Scotland, or confer or remove functions exercisable otherwise than in or as regards Scotland, **(b) it relates to reserved matters**, (c) it is in breach of the restrictions in Schedule 4, (d) it is incompatible with any of the Convention rights …, (e) it would remove the Lord Advocate from his position as head of the systems of criminal prosecution and investigation of deaths in Scotland."
> ([Scotland Act 1998, s.29](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/29))

Two features of s.29 govern everything that follows:

- **"So far as".** Invalidity is provision-by-provision, not Act-by-Act. A Bill may be partly within and partly outside competence.
- **The purpose test (s.29(3)).** "the question whether a provision … **relates to** a reserved matter is to be determined … **by reference to the purpose of the provision, having regard (among other things) to its effect in all the circumstances**." So the question is never simply whether a provision touches the health professions; it is whether, judged by its purpose and effect, it *relates to* their regulation.

Section 29(4) adds a specific rule: a provision which would otherwise not relate to reserved matters, but which modifies **Scots private law or Scots criminal law as it applies to reserved matters**, is treated as relating to reserved matters **unless** its purpose is to make the law apply consistently to reserved matters and otherwise.

**Section 30(1)** gives Schedule 5 effect: "Schedule 5 (which defines reserved matters) shall have effect" ([s.30](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/30)).

#### 2.2 The reservation — Schedule 5, Part II, Head G, Section G2

Head G of Part II is headed "**Regulation of the Professions**" and contains three entries: G1 (architects), **G2 (health professions)** and G3 (auditors). Section G2 reads, in full ([Schedule 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/schedule/5)):

> **Section G2. Regulation of the health professions.**
>
> **Exceptions**
> The subject-matter of—
> - section 21 of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978 (requirement of suitable experience for medical practitioners), and
> - section 25 of that Act (arrangements for the provision of general dental services), **so far as it relates to vocational training and disciplinary proceedings**.
>
> **Interpretation**
> "**The health professions**" means the professions regulated by—
> the Pharmacy Act 1954, the Professions Supplementary to Medicine Act 1960, the Veterinary Surgeons Act 1966, the Medical Act 1983, the Dentists Act 1984, the Opticians Act 1989, the Osteopaths Act 1993, the Chiropractors Act 1994, and the Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997.

#### 2.3 The closed list — the single most important limit on the reservation

The interpretation provision does **not** define "the health professions" by reference to a general description such as "professions concerned with health care". It defines them as "**the professions regulated by**" **nine named enactments**. Three consequences follow directly from the text:

1. **A profession not regulated by one of those nine Acts is not a "health profession" for G2 purposes at all**, and its regulation is not reserved by G2. The list is closed on its face; nothing in the entry extends it to successor or additional regulatory regimes.
2. **The reservation is anchored to the 1998 statute book.** Several of the nine Acts have since been superseded or heavily amended in the reserved sphere (for example, the Professions Supplementary to Medicine Act 1960 and the Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997 governed regimes later replaced by subordinate legislation). **The available database does not contain, in the material retrieved, any amendment to the G2 interpretation provision updating that list**, and no such amendment should be assumed.
3. **The point on which advice will usually turn is therefore identification, not characterisation.** Before asking whether a proposed provision "relates to" regulation of the health professions, one must first establish whether the profession in question is regulated by one of the nine listed Acts.

Two further textual points on the list itself: it includes **veterinary surgeons** (Veterinary Surgeons Act 1966), which is not a human-health profession but is within the defined term; and it does **not** include social workers or social care professionals, whose regulation is accordingly untouched by G2.

#### 2.4 The exceptions, and a repeal that matters

The exceptions carve out of the reservation "the subject-matter of" two provisions of the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978:

- **s.21** — requirement of suitable experience for medical practitioners; and
- **s.25** — arrangements for the provision of general dental services, **but only so far as it relates to vocational training and disciplinary proceedings**.

The second exception is expressly partial: general dental services arrangements are not wholly excepted, only that part of the subject-matter concerning vocational training and disciplinary proceedings.

**Section 21 has since been repealed.** The provision retrieved at `…/ukpga/1978/29/section/21` is titled "Requirement of suitable experience." and its text consists solely of the omission convention (a row of dots), indicating the section has been repealed or omitted ([NHS (Scotland) Act 1978, s.21](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/21)). Section 25 remains in force ([s.25](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1978/29/section/25)).

**The repeal does not destroy the exception**, because of the freezing rule in Part III:

> **Schedule 5, Part III, paragraph 5(1):** "References in this Schedule to **the subject-matter of any enactment** are to be read as references to the subject-matter of that enactment **as it has effect on the principal appointed day** or, if it ceased to have effect at any time within the period ending with that day and beginning with the day on which this Act is passed, as it had effect immediately before that time."

So the excepted subject-matter is that of s.21 **as it stood on the principal appointed day**, not as it stands now. The exception continues to operate by reference to the historic text. Establishing its present scope therefore requires the **as-at-1999 text** of s.21, which was not retrieved in this run — the revised text held by the database is the omitted version.

#### 2.5 How the entry is to be read — Schedule 5, Part II, Preliminary

The preliminary paragraphs of Part II govern the construction of every Section in it:

> **para 1:** "The matters to which any of the Sections in this Part apply are reserved matters for the purposes of this Act."
> **para 2:** "A Section applies to any matter described or referred to in it **when read with any illustrations, exceptions or interpretation provisions in that Section**."
> **para 3:** "Any illustrations, exceptions or interpretation provisions in a Section **relate only to that Section** (so that an entry under the heading 'exceptions' does not affect any other Section)."

Paragraph 3 is significant in practice: the G2 exceptions **cannot be borrowed** to narrow any other reservation, and conversely a matter excepted from G2 may still be reserved by a different Section of Part II. A provision escaping G2 must still be checked against the rest of Schedule 5 — and against the other limbs of s.29(2), notably the Schedule 4 restrictions.

#### 2.6 What is *not* reserved by G2

Reading G2 with the s.29(3) purpose test, the reservation bites on the **regulation of the listed professions** — registration, professional standards, fitness to practise, and the regulatory bodies constituted under the nine Acts. It does not, of itself, reserve:

- **The organisation, funding and delivery of the health service in Scotland.** These are governed by the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978, whose provisions are extensively exercised by the Scottish Ministers; the whole architecture of Health Boards and their functions sits outside G2.
- **The terms on which health professionals contract with or are employed in the Scottish NHS**, as distinct from their professional regulation — subject always to the separate reservation of employment law in **Head H, Section H1** (employment rights and duties and industrial relations).
- **Professions outside the closed list**, as set out at 2.3.

The dividing line is the s.29(3) one: a provision whose **purpose** is to regulate the profession relates to the reserved matter; a provision whose purpose is to organise the delivery of devolved health services does not, even if it has incidental effects on how members of a listed profession work.

#### 2.7 Altering the reservation — s.30(2) and (5)–(6)

The boundary is not fixed. **"Her Majesty may by Order in Council make any modifications of Schedule 4 or 5 which She considers necessary or expedient"** (**s.30(2)**), and such an Order may make consequential modifications of any enactment, prerogative instrument or other instrument (s.30(4)).

Where an alteration to the reserved matters has the effect that a provision of an Act of the Scottish Parliament **ceases to be within competence**, "**the provision does not for that reason cease to have effect** (unless an enactment provides otherwise)" (**s.30(5)–(6)**), and s.29(1) is expressly made subject to s.30(6) (s.29(5)). Legislation validly enacted is therefore not retrospectively invalidated by a later narrowing of competence.

That Schedule 5 is a live instrument in the health field is evident from the retrieved text: **Part III, paragraph 4A** — "**Assisted dying: identification and regulation of substances and devices**" — disapplies the reservation of the conferral of certain powers on the Scottish Ministers and the Secretary of State in relation to substances or devices for use in assisting terminally ill adults to end their own lives, subject to detailed conditions, and applies "only in relation to a provision that is contained in an Act of the Parliament resulting from a Bill **passed on or before 7 May 2026**" (para 4A(3)). This is a targeted, time-limited carve-out and does **not** bear on G2, but it demonstrates that the Schedule as retrieved incorporates recent modification.

#### 2.8 Scrutiny before enactment — s.31

Competence is tested before Royal Assent as well as after. **Section 31** provides for scrutiny of Bills for legislative competence ([s.31](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/31)); s.101 supplies a reading-down rule for the interpretation of Acts of the Scottish Parliament ([s.101](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/101)). Neither was retrieved in full and neither is relied on above beyond its existence.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Scotland Act 1998 (ukpga/1998/46) is recorded with extent `["United Kingdom"]`; the National Health Service (Scotland) Act 1978 (ukpga/1978/29) likewise. The competence rules apply to the Scottish Parliament and so operate as regards Scotland.
- **Status.** Both Acts are recorded as `revised` — the text held incorporates effected amendments. The Schedule 5 text retrieved plainly includes recent amendment (Part III paragraph 4A refers to a Bill passed on or before **7 May 2026**), so the version relied on is current as at the database's revision date.
- **The frozen-subject-matter rule limits what the current text can tell you.** Because Schedule 5 Part III paragraph 5(1) fixes "the subject-matter of any enactment" as at the **principal appointed day**, the current revised text of a referenced provision is **not** the operative text for construing an exception. For G2 this is not academic: s.21 of the 1978 Act is now repealed, so its excepted subject-matter can only be established from the as-at-1999 text, which was not retrieved. **The available database does not contain, in the material retrieved, the historic text of section 21.**
- **The reservation is modifiable by Order in Council** under s.30(2), so the current text of Section G2 should be confirmed at the date of any advice rather than taken from a secondary source.
- **Currency.** The API output carries no per-section commencement or "prospective" annotation. Nothing retrieved indicates that Section G2 or the s.29 test is other than in force.

question: I am looking to create a timeline for the statutory requirements placed on the Water Industry Commission for Scotland, for publishing of reports and accounts. On top of when the legislation requires the reports and accounts to be produced, published, sent out and laid before Parliament I want to know what they need to contain.
statements: The deadline for sending the Commission's accounts to the Auditor General is set by section 21(2) of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000, which requires the account to be sent not later than 6 months after the end of the financial year to which it relates; the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 fixes no date, because paragraph 14 of schedule A1 leaves both preparation and sending to directions given by the Scottish Ministers.

Section 5(1)(a) of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 requires the Commission, as soon as practicable after the end of each financial year, to submit to the Scottish Ministers and publish a report on the exercise of its functions during that year.
Section 5(4) of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 requires the Scottish Ministers to lay before the Parliament a copy of each report submitted to them under section 5(1)(a).

Section 22(5) of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000 requires the Scottish Ministers to lay before the Parliament every account and report sent to them by the Auditor General and, except where the body has published them, to publish them, not later than 9 months after the end of the financial year.

The auditor's report on the account must set out the auditor's findings on the matters listed in section 22 of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000, including whether the expenditure and receipts shown were incurred or applied in accordance with the enactments and Budget Acts that authorised them.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The timetable is split across **two** Acts, and this is the point most easily missed.

The Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 imposes the duties but **leaves the timing to Ministers' direction**. The fixed deadline comes from the **Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000**, section 21(2): the account "must be sent to the Auditor General **not later than 6 months after the end of the financial year** to which the account relates."

An answer that reads only the 2002 Act will conclude, wrongly, that no statutory deadline exists.

| Duty | Timing | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Prepare account of income and expenditure | for each financial year, per Ministers' directions | 2002 Act, sch A1 para 14(a) |
| Send account to Auditor General | by such time as Ministers direct, and in any event **not later than 6 months** after the year end | 2002 Act, sch A1 para 14(b); **2000 Act, s.21(2)** |
| Report on exercise of functions, submit to Ministers and publish | **as soon as practicable** after the end of each financial year | 2002 Act, s.5(1)(a) |
| Lay a copy of that report before the Scottish Parliament | on receipt of the report | 2002 Act, **s.5(4)** |
| Lay the audited account and the auditor's report before the Parliament, and publish them unless the Commission has already published them | **not later than 9 months** after the year end | **2000 Act, s.22(5)** |

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The Commission and its accounts duty

The Water Industry Commission for Scotland is established by section 1(1) of the 2002 Act ([asp/2002/3, s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/section/1)), with the general function under section 1(2) of promoting the interests of persons whose premises are connected to the public water supply or sewerage system.

Its accounts duty sits in schedule A1:

> **Paragraph 14** - The Commission must -
> (a) prepare for each financial year, **in accordance with directions given by the Scottish Ministers**, an account of the Commission's income and expenditure, and
> (b) send the account, **by such time as the Scottish Ministers may direct**, to the Auditor General for Scotland for auditing.

([asp/2002/3, sch A1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/schedule/A1))

Both limbs are expressed as subject to ministerial direction. Read alone, the 2002 Act supplies **no date**.

#### 2.2 Where the deadline actually is

The Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000 supplies it, and does so generally rather than by naming the Commission:

> **Section 21 - Audit of accounts**
> (1) This section and section 22 apply in relation to any account which is, by virtue of any enactment or prerogative instrument, required (in whatever words) to be -
>    (a) audited by the Auditor General, or
>    (b) **sent to the Auditor General for auditing**.
> (2) **The account must be sent to the Auditor General not later than 6 months after the end of the financial year to which the account relates.**
> (3) The account is to be audited by - (a) the Auditor General, or (b) a qualified person appearing to the Auditor General to be suitable for appointment ...

([asp/2000/1, s.21](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/21))

The chain is worth stating explicitly, because it is what a reader has to follow to find the deadline:

1. Schedule A1 paragraph 14(b) of the 2002 Act requires the account to be **sent to the Auditor General for auditing**.
2. That engages section 21(1)(b) of the 2000 Act, which applies to **any** account so required "by virtue of any enactment", "in whatever words".
3. Section 21(2) then imposes the 6-month backstop.

A ministerial direction under paragraph 14(b) can require the account sooner, but cannot extend beyond the statutory 6 months.

Section 19 of the 2000 Act ([asp/2000/1, s.19](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/19)) carries the parallel duty to prepare accounts for persons paid out of the Scottish Consolidated Fund, and section 19(4) requires accounts prepared under it to follow directions issued by the Scottish Ministers.

#### 2.3 What the audit must cover

> **Section 22 - Audit of accounts: further provisions**
> (1) The auditor's report on an account in relation to which this section applies ... must set out the auditor's findings on the following matters -
>    (a) whether the expenditure and receipts shown in the account were incurred or applied in accordance with - (i) any enactment by virtue of which the expenditure was incurred or the income received, (ii) the Budget Act or Acts for the financial year ... and (iii) sections 4 to 7,
>    (b) where sums have been paid out of the Fund for the purpose of meeting such expenditure, whether the sums were [applied accordingly] ...

([asp/2000/1, s.22](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/22))

This is a **regularity** audit obligation, going to whether money was spent as authorised, and it sits alongside the true-and-fair question.

#### 2.4 The annual report on functions, and what it must contain

> **Section 5 - Annual reports by, and information from, the Commission**
> (1) The Commission must -
>    (a) **as soon as practicable after the end of each financial year**, submit to the Scottish Ministers, **and publish**, a report on the exercise of the Commission's functions during that year, and
>    (b) provide the Scottish Ministers with such information regarding the exercise of those functions as they may require.
> (2) A report under subsection (1)(a) **must include a summary of** -
>    (a) action taken by the Commission during the year ... in response to - (i) any advice, information or representation made to it by Citizens Advice Scotland under section 8(1)(a) or (c) of the Consumers, Estate Agents and Redress Act 2007, and (ii) any proposals made to it under section 8(1)(b) of that Act, and
>    (b) where the Commission has decided during that year not to take any action in response to any such advice, information, proposal or representation ...

([asp/2002/3, s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/section/5))

Two features to note. The obligation is to **submit and publish**, so publication is a statutory duty rather than a matter of practice. And subsection (2) is the only express **content** requirement placed on the report: the Citizens Advice Scotland summary. The general subject matter, "the exercise of the Commission's functions during that year", is otherwise left at large.

---

#### 2.5 Laying before the Parliament, and the 9-month backstop

Two separate laying duties fall on the Scottish Ministers, and both are in the retrieved text.

The annual report on functions:

> **Section 5(4)** - The Scottish Ministers must lay before the Parliament a copy of each report submitted to them under subsection (1)(a).

([asp/2002/3, s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/section/5))

The account and the audit reports:

> **Section 22 - Audit of accounts: further provisions**
> (4) The Auditor General must send to the Scottish Ministers the account, the auditor's report on the account and any report prepared by the Auditor General under subsection (3) **in sufficient time to enable the Scottish Ministers to comply with subsection (5)**.
> (5) The Scottish Ministers must -
>    (a) **lay before the Parliament** a copy of every account and report sent to them under subsection (4), and
>    (b) except where the account and the report are published by the body or office-holder in question, **publish** every such account and report, **not later than 9 months after the end of the financial year** to which the account relates.

([asp/2000/1, s.22](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/22))

Section 22(5) is the outer edge of the timeline. It fixes the last dated step, 9 months after the year end, in the same way section 21(2) fixes the 6-month step, and it makes publication a Ministers' duty that bites only where the body has not published itself.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** Both the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 and the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000 extend to Scotland, and were returned in revised form.
- **Which body.** The Commission's constitutive provisions have been reworked over time, and the Water Services etc. (Scotland) Act 2005 also contains a schedule 1 dealing with the Commission in materially similar terms. This answer cites schedule A1 to the 2002 Act as the operative source.
- **Out of scope.** The Public Services Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 is general public-body reform legislation and is **not** a source of the Commission's reporting timetable. Citing it in answer to this question is a scope error rather than a small inaccuracy.

question: Can you provide a comprehensive list of all statutory definitions of "shop" in Scots law?
statements: There is no general statutory definition of "shop" in Scots law: each Act that uses the word defines it for its own purposes and the definitions differ from each other.
Sections 38 and 39 of the Shops Act 1950 are repealed and must not be presented as current law or as provisions that are in force.

Section 7 of the Christmas Day and New Year's Day Trading (Scotland) Act 2007 defines "shop" as any premises within a building where there is carried on a trade or business consisting wholly or mainly of the retail sale of goods, and "large shop" as a shop with a relevant floor area exceeding 280 square metres.

Section 232(3) of the Employment Rights Act 1996 provides that "shop" includes any premises where any retail trade or business is carried on, with section 232(4) treating only the retail part of mixed-use premises as the shop.

Section 43ZB(2)(a) of the Employment Rights Act 1996 carries a second, different definition for the purposes of its own Part, under which "shop" means any premises where there is carried on a trade or business consisting wholly or mainly of the sale of goods, not the retail sale of goods.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**There is no general statutory definition of "shop" in Scots law.** Each Act that needs the word defines it for its own purposes, and the definitions differ from each other in ways that matter. An answer has to name the definitions it found and say which Act each belongs to.

The definitions below are the ones these searches reached. They are not put forward as the whole population, and a longer list found by a wider search is a better answer, not a contradictory one.

The second trap is currency. The **Shops Act 1950** is the statute most readily associated with this question, and **sections 38 and 39 of it are repealed**. Citing them as current law, or asserting that every provision relied on is in force, is the specific failure this question exists to catch.

| Act | Provision | Definition given |
|---|---|---|
| Christmas Day and New Year's Day Trading (Scotland) Act 2007 | s.7 | "shop" means any premises **within a building** where there is carried on a trade or business consisting **wholly or mainly of the retail sale of goods** |
| Employment Rights Act 1996 | s.232(3) | "shop" **includes any premises where any retail trade or business is carried on** |
| Employment Rights Act 1996 | s.43ZB(2)(a) | for "large shop" in that Part, "shop" means any premises where there is carried on a trade or business consisting wholly or mainly of the **sale of goods** |

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The Scottish definition: the 2007 Act

The one clean, Scotland-only definition retrieved is in the interpretation section of the Christmas Day and New Year's Day Trading (Scotland) Act 2007:

> **Section 7 - Interpretation**
> In this Act -
>    "large shop" means a shop which has a **relevant floor area exceeding 280 square metres**;
>    "relevant floor area" means so much of the floor area of a shop as is used for making retail sales or for the display of goods in connection with such sales;
>    "retail sale" means any sale of goods for consumption or use, whether or not by the buyer, for purposes unconnected with a trade or business;
>    **"shop" means any premises within a building where there is carried on a trade or business consisting wholly or mainly of the retail sale of goods**

([asp/2007/13, s.7](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/13/section/7))

Two limits are built in and are easy to miss. The premises must be **within a building**, which excludes an open-air stall or a market pitch. And the trade must be **wholly or mainly** retail sale of goods, so a business selling mainly services is not a shop for this Act even if it also sells goods.

The definition does work only inside that Act: it drives the section 1 prohibition on large shops opening on Christmas Day ([s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/13/section/1)), the section 3 exemptions ([s.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/13/section/3)) and the section 4 offence ([s.4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2007/13/section/4)).

#### 2.2 The employment definition, which applies in Scotland

The Employment Rights Act 1996 extends across Great Britain and carries a **different and wider** definition, for the Sunday working rights of shop workers:

> **Section 232 - Shop workers**
> (1) In this Act "shop worker" means an employee who, under his contract of employment, is or may be required to do shop work.
> (2) In this Act "shop work" means work in or about a shop ... on a day on which the shop is open for the serving of customers.
> (3) Subject to subsection (4), in this Act **"shop" includes any premises where any retail trade or business is carried on**.
> (4) Where premises are used mainly for purposes other than those of retail trade or business and would not (apart from subsection (3)) be regarded as a shop, only such part of the premises as - (a) is used wholly or mainly for the purposes of retail trade or business, or (b) is used both ...

([ukpga/1996/18, s.232](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/232))

The contrast with the 2007 Act is the point of the question. Section 232(3) says "**includes any**" premises where "**any**" retail trade or business is carried on, with no building requirement and no "wholly or mainly" threshold at the level of the premises. Subsection (4) then handles mixed-use premises by treating **part** of them as the shop, which is a device the 2007 Act does not use at all.

The same Act carries a **third**, narrower definition for a different Part:

> **Section 43ZB - Interpretation**
> (1) In this Part - "large shop" means a shop which has a relevant floor area exceeding 280 square metres ...
> (2) In the definition of "large shop" in subsection (1) - (a) **"shop" means any premises where there is carried on a trade or business consisting wholly or mainly of the sale of goods**; (b) "relevant floor area" means the internal floor area of so much of the large shop in question as consists of or is comprised in a building.

([ukpga/1996/18, s.43ZB](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1996/18/section/43ZB))

Note this one says "**sale of goods**", not "retail sale of goods". One Act therefore holds two different definitions of the same word, which is the clearest possible demonstration that no single answer exists.

#### 2.3 Near misses that are not definitions of "shop"

Three retrieved sources look relevant and are not:

- **Protection of Workers (Retail and Age-restricted Goods and Services) (Scotland) Act 2021, s.5** defines "**retail premises**", not "shop": "premises that are used wholly or mainly for the sale or supply of goods, on a retail basis, to members of the public" ([asp/2021/6, s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2021/6/section/5)). A modern Scottish statute on retail workers deliberately avoids the word.
- **Licensing (Scotland) Act 2005** contains **no** definition of "shop". Its interpretation section defines "premises" as "any place and includes a vehicle, vessel or moveable structure" ([asp/2005/16, s.147](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2005/16/section/147)). Offering a "shop" definition from this Act is an error.
- **Tenancy of Shops (Scotland) Act 1964** has "shops" in its title but defines nothing. The sections retrieved are citation and extent ([s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1964/50/section/2)) and the continuance of the 1949 Act ([s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1964/50/section/1)). The operative definition sits in the Tenancy of Shops (Scotland) Act 1949, which the search returned only as an untitled stub.

#### 2.4 The Shops Act 1950 and currency

Four searches for the Shops Act 1950 returned no such Act, only unrelated local legislation (Gateshead Extension Act 1953, Crosby Corporation Act 1956 and similar). The Act is not available to be read, so **its definitions cannot be quoted or relied on from these sources**, and sections 38 and 39 of it are in any event repealed.

The retrieval also shows that repeal is visible when an Act is held: the same searches returned "**Shops (Early Closing Days) Act 1965 (repealed 1.12.1994)**", with the repeal marked in the title itself. An answer that cannot see a repeal flag has not read the Act, and must not assert that the provisions it relies on are in force.

Relatedly, the **Sunday Trading Act 1994** was returned with **extent "England, Wales"** only. Sunday and holiday trading in Scotland is governed by the 2007 Act at 2.1 above, not by the 1994 Act and not by the Shops Act 1950.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The 2007 Act and the 2021 Act extend to Scotland. The Employment Rights Act 1996 was returned with United Kingdom extent and its shop worker provisions apply in Scotland. The Sunday Trading Act 1994 extends to England and Wales only.
- **Not exhaustive.** These are the definitions found by the searches run. Others certainly exist in Scots law, in planning, rating, licensing and health and safety legislation among others. A response that lists more of them is going further than this answer, not disagreeing with it.
- **Out of scope.** No definition is offered from the Shops Act 1950: it could not be retrieved, and the provisions usually cited from it are repealed.
- **Not addressed.** Case law on the meaning of "shop" is outside this question's legislation-only scope.

question: Explain the concepts of legal professional privilege, common interest privileges and limited waiver and how they all apply in the context of sharing legal advice between the UK and Scottish Governments in light of the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004
statements: Section 36(1) of the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 exempts information in respect of which a claim to confidentiality of communications could be maintained in legal proceedings, using the Scots formulation rather than the English term legal professional privilege; it creates no privilege of its own but imports whatever the substantive law of privilege provides, so whether any particular doctrine is available is a question of that substantive law.

Because section 36(1) asks whether a claim to confidentiality of communications could be maintained in legal proceedings, whether privilege survives sharing advice with the other administration is governed by Scots law, and the English authority on common interest privilege and limited waiver is persuasive in Scotland rather than binding: in R (Prudential plc) v Special Commissioner of Income Tax [2013] UKSC 1 Lord Reed confirmed that the law of privilege developed separately in the two systems and that, while the general principle is common to both, there are a number of differences in the case law on particular aspects.

Advice shared between the two governments is held on both sides and so is requestable under two regimes: the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 and the Environmental Information (Scotland) Regulations 2004 in Scotland, and the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 at UK level; the privilege exemption is qualified and subject to the public interest test on both sides, because neither FOISA section 36(1) nor FOIA section 42 appears in its own Act's list of absolute exemptions.

Environmental information is routed out of the freedom of information Acts by section 39(2) of FOISA and section 39 of FOIA 2000 and must be handled under the environmental information regulations, which contain no privilege exception as such, so privileged advice has to be brought within the exceptions for the confidentiality of proceedings provided for by law, the course of justice, or internal communications.

The Scottish and UK environmental regimes are not identical: the Scottish regulation 10(5) requires substantial prejudice and regulation 10(2) requires the exceptions to be interpreted restrictively with a presumption in favour of disclosure, whereas the UK regulation 12(5) asks only whether disclosure would adversely affect the interest and has a presumption in favour of disclosure but no instruction to interpret restrictively; both disapply the confidentiality and related exceptions for information on emissions.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

Three distinct ideas are in play, and the most important thing to get right is that **the second and third are questions of Scots law that English authority does not settle either way**.

1. **Legal professional privilege (in Scots terms, confidentiality of communications).** This is what [section 36(1) of FOISA](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/36) imports: information "in respect of which a claim to confidentiality of communications could be maintained in legal proceedings" is exempt. Note the wording. FOISA does not say "legal professional privilege"; it uses the Scots formulation.
2. **Common interest privilege.** Well established in **English** law: parties with a sufficient common interest in a matter can exchange privileged material without losing privilege against the outside world. Because section 36(1) asks what could be maintained **in legal proceedings**, and those are Scottish proceedings, the English authority is **persuasive in Scotland rather than binding**, and how far it is followed is a question of Scots law. In [R (Prudential plc) v Special Commissioner of Income Tax [2013] UKSC 1](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/uksc/2013/1), Lord Reed recorded that the law in this area "developed separately in Scotland from in England" and that although the general principle is shared, "there are a number of differences in the case law in relation to particular aspects of the law" ([103]). That is a reason to **check** the Scots position, not a reason to assume the doctrine is unavailable.
3. **Limited waiver.** The proposition that disclosing privileged material for a specific, limited purpose waives privilege only for that purpose. The same point applies: the doctrine is familiar in English law, and its Scottish counterpart has to be established as a matter of Scots law rather than assumed either way.

**Where the Scots answer is found, and why it is not here.** The sources that settle these two questions are decisions and guidance of the Scottish Information Commissioner on section 36, and Court of Session authority on confidentiality and waiver. Neither is reachable through the tools used for this answer: Find Case Law does not index the Court of Session, and the Commissioner's material is not legislation. **The absence of a Scottish authority below is therefore an absence of coverage, not evidence that the doctrines do not apply**, and a reviewer should read section 2.6 with that in mind.

**The practical consequence for sharing advice between the two governments.** Do not transplant an English textbook proposition into a FOISA answer without checking the Scots position, and do not dismiss it either. What section 36(1) actually asks is whether a claim to confidentiality of communications could be maintained in legal proceedings. The course that works whichever way the doctrinal question is answered is to build the protection into the disclosure itself: share on expressly confidential terms, with identified recipients, for an identified purpose, and record those terms.

**One regime is not enough.** The question names both FOISA and the UK Environmental Information Regulations 2004, and that pairing is the point. Advice shared between the two governments is held by both, so it is requestable from each, under **four** instruments in two regimes: FOISA and the Environmental Information (Scotland) Regulations 2004 in Scotland, the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 at UK level. They are close but not identical, and section 2.7 sets out where they differ.

**And two structural points that are often missed.** The privilege exemption is **qualified** on both sides, subject to the public interest test: FOISA section 36(1) is not in the absolute list in section 2(2), and FOIA section 42 is not in the absolute list in section 2(3). And if the information is **environmental**, the freedom of information Act is the wrong instrument on either side of the border: the request falls to be answered under the relevant environmental information regulations, where there is no privilege exception at all.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 What section 36 says, and what it does not say

> **Section 36 - Confidentiality**
> (1) Information in respect of which a claim to **confidentiality of communications** could be maintained in legal proceedings is exempt information.
> (2) Information is exempt information if—
> (a) it was obtained by a Scottish public authority from another person (including another such authority); and
> (b) its disclosure by the authority so obtaining it to the public (otherwise than under this Act) would constitute a breach of confidence actionable by that person or any other person.

([asp/2002/13, s.36](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/36))

Section 36(1) does not create a privilege. It borrows one. The test is whether a claim **could be maintained in legal proceedings**, so the content of the exemption is whatever the substantive law of privilege says. That is why the doctrinal question in this request matters: if a doctrine is not part of Scots law, it cannot support a section 36(1) claim.

The drafting is deliberately Scottish. Lord Reed noted in *Prudential* that "legal professional privilege" was adopted in preference to the older term "confidentiality", which "could lead to confusion between the privilege and the different sense in which 'confidentiality' is employed in other contexts". The same judgment quotes the modern statutory formula used when a provision has to work in both systems, in Schedule 36 to the Finance Act 2008: information is privileged if a claim "to legal professional privilege, or (in Scotland) to confidentiality of communications as between client and professional legal adviser, could be maintained in legal proceedings". FOISA uses only the Scottish half of that formula.

#### 2.2 Section 36(1) is qualified, not absolute

> **Section 2 - Effect of exemptions**
> (1) To information which is exempt information by virtue of any provision of Part 2, section 1 applies only to the extent that—
> (a) the provision does not confer absolute exemption; and
> (b) in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in disclosing the information is not outweighed by that in maintaining the exemption.
> (2) For the purposes of paragraph (a) of subsection (1), the following provisions of Part 2 (and no others) are to be regarded as conferring absolute exemption— (a) section 25; (b) section 26; **(c) section 36(2)**; (d) section 37; and (e) [parts of] section 38 ...

([asp/2002/13, s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/2))

**Section 36(2) is listed; section 36(1) is not.** So the privilege limb is subject to the public interest test in section 2(1)(b), and establishing that material is privileged is only the first half of the answer. This is a common error: privilege is close to absolute as a matter of the general law, but the FOISA exemption built on it is not.

Section 29(1)(c) is worth holding alongside section 36(1). Information held by the Scottish Administration relating to "the provision of advice by any of the Law Officers or any request for the provision of such advice" is exempt information, and that exemption is also qualified ([s.29](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/29)). For advice from or to the Law Officers, both exemptions are likely to be engaged.

#### 2.3 If the information is environmental, FOISA is the wrong instrument

> **Section 39(2)** Information is exempt information if a Scottish public authority—
> (a) is obliged by regulations under section 62 to make it available to the public in accordance with the regulations; or
> (b) would be so obliged but for any exemption contained in the regulations.

([asp/2002/13, s.39](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/39))

The regulations under section 62 are the Environmental Information (Scotland) Regulations 2004 ([ssi/2004/520](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/520)). Environmental information is therefore routed out of FOISA and into the EIRs, where the framework is materially less favourable to withholding.

#### 2.4 The environmental route

> **Regulation 10 - Exceptions from duty to make environmental information available**
> (1) A Scottish public authority may refuse a request ... if— (a) there is an exception to disclosure under paragraphs (4) or (5); and (b) in all the circumstances, the public interest in making the information available is outweighed by that in maintaining the exception.
> (2) In considering the application of the exceptions ... a Scottish public authority shall— (a) **interpret those paragraphs in a restrictive way**; and (b) **apply a presumption in favour of disclosure**.
> (4) ... (e) the request involves making available **internal communications**.
> (5) ... to the extent that its disclosure would, or would be likely to, **prejudice substantially**— ... (b) **the course of justice**, the ability of a person to receive a fair trial ...; (d) **the confidentiality of the proceedings of any public authority where such confidentiality is provided for by law** ...
> (6) To the extent that the environmental information ... relates to information on emissions, a Scottish public authority shall not be entitled to refuse to make it available under an exception referred to in paragraph (5)(d) to (g).

([ssi/2004/520, reg.10](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/520/regulation/10))

Four differences from FOISA follow, and each makes withholding harder:

- **There is no privilege exception as such.** Legally privileged advice has to be brought within regulation 10(5)(d), confidentiality of proceedings provided for by law, or regulation 10(5)(b), the course of justice, or regulation 10(4)(e) if it is genuinely an internal communication.
- **A substantial prejudice threshold applies** to the regulation 10(5) exceptions. It is not enough that the material is privileged; disclosure must be likely substantially to prejudice the protected interest.
- **Regulation 10(2) requires restrictive interpretation and a presumption in favour of disclosure.** There is no equivalent instruction in FOISA.
- **Regulation 10(6) removes the (5)(d) to (g) exceptions entirely for information on emissions.** Privileged advice about an emissions matter may be disclosable however clearly privileged it is.

One point of interaction is worth flagging for the shared-advice scenario. Regulation 10(4)(e) protects **internal** communications. Advice exchanged between the UK Government and the Scottish Government is, on any natural reading, not internal to either. That is a reason for caution about sharing environmental legal advice specifically.

#### 2.5 Legal professional privilege: what is common to both systems

*Prudential* is the most useful retrievable authority. The Supreme Court there declined to extend legal advice privilege beyond communications with lawyers to advice from accountants. Two points travel:

- The privilege is treated as fundamental. The judgment records *R (Morgan Grenfell) v Special Commissioner* [2002] UKHL 21, where a statute could only remove "a fundamental human right" if it "expressly stated" it was doing so or the intention "appear[ed] by necessary implication".
- **Legal advice privilege is confined, in broad terms, to communications between a solicitor and client**; litigation privilege (in Scotland, *post litem motam* confidentiality) covers material prepared in contemplation of litigation, which may include material from non-lawyers.

Lord Reed then addressed the Scottish position expressly, at [102] to [105]. The passage repays reading in full, but the operative sentences are:

> "No question arises in this appeal as to the scope of the privilege in Scots law ... The law in this area developed separately in Scotland from in England. The two systems have however developed in the same direction. **There are a number of differences in the case law in relation to particular aspects of the law**, but the general principle, its fundamental importance, and the considerations of public policy which underlie it, are common to both systems."

That is authority for the framing of this answer. The **core** of privilege is shared. Particular **aspects** are not necessarily shared, and each has to be checked against Scots law rather than assumed from English textbooks.

#### 2.6 Common interest privilege and limited waiver: a Scots law question, unresolved here

**Common interest privilege**, as understood in England and Wales, allows a privileged document to be passed to another party with a sufficient common interest in its subject matter without waiving privilege as against the world. **Limited waiver** is the related proposition that disclosure for a specific, limited purpose waives privilege only for that purpose.

Both matter to this question because both, if available, are the answer to "does privilege survive sharing the advice with the other administration?".

Neither could be **resolved** from the sources available for this answer, and it is important to be precise about why:

- Searches of Find Case Law for both doctrines returned recent judgments matching the words but not the leading authorities, which pre-date the database or were not surfaced by a search that returns results in date order rather than by relevance.
- A search restricted to the Inner House of the Court of Session was **rejected: the Court of Session is not an available court in this database at all**. Its own coverage note records that "the Scottish Court of Session (CSOH/CSIH) and Sheriff Courts are NOT indexed" and that "for Scottish matters, this database contains only UK Supreme Court and Privy Council decisions".
- The Scottish Information Commissioner's decisions and guidance under section 36, which are the most directly relevant body of material on how the exemption treats shared and limited-purpose disclosure, are not legislation and were not reachable either.

Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions, which is the honest position:

- **The English cases are persuasive, not binding.** *Prudential* confirms the two systems developed separately and differ in particular respects, so English common interest privilege authority is a strong starting point for a Scottish public authority's FOISA position but not a conclusive one, and an answer should say which it is relying on.
- **Equally, nothing here says they are unavailable.** Nothing retrieved says that Scots law lacks an equivalent protection for common interest sharing or limited-purpose disclosure, and the sources that would settle it were out of reach. A conclusion that a Scottish authority loses confidentiality by sharing advice on limited terms would need Scots authority of its own, just as much as the opposite conclusion would.

**This is the single point in this answer most in need of a Scots lawyer's confirmation.** For a reviewer, the useful question is not "is the doctrine English?" but "what does the Commissioner's guidance and the Court of Session say about whether confidentiality of communications survives a limited-purpose or common-interest disclosure?".

#### 2.7 The UK side: the same document, a different rulebook

The question names the UK Environmental Information Regulations 2004, and the UK regime has to be in the answer because a document shared between the two governments is held on both sides.

**Freedom of Information Act 2000, section 42.**

> **Section 42 - Legal professional privilege**
> (1) Information in respect of which a claim to **legal professional privilege or, in Scotland, to confidentiality of communications** could be maintained in legal proceedings is exempt information.

([ukpga/2000/36, s.42](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/36/section/42))

Note the drafting difference. FOIA section 42 carries **both** limbs of the formula, so a UK department holding advice given under Scots law can still claim the exemption; FOISA section 36(1) carries only the Scottish limb. Section 42 is **not** among the absolute exemptions listed in section 2(3), so it is qualified and subject to the public interest test in the same way as FOISA section 36(1) ([s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/36/section/2)).

**Section 39** routes environmental information out of FOIA, as section 39(2) of FOISA does for FOISA, and section 39(1A) defines the regulations by reference to the power in section 74 ([s.39](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/36/section/39)).

**Environmental Information Regulations 2004, regulation 12.** The structure mirrors the Scottish regulation 10, but two differences matter for withholding privileged advice:

> **Regulation 12**
> (1) ... a public authority may refuse to disclose environmental information requested if - (a) an exception to disclosure applies under paragraphs (4) or (5); and (b) in all the circumstances of the case, the public interest in maintaining the exception outweighs the public interest in disclosing the information.
> (2) A public authority shall **apply a presumption in favour of disclosure**.
> (4) ... (e) the request involves the disclosure of **internal communications**.
> (5) ... to the extent that its disclosure would **adversely affect** - ... (b) **the course of justice** ...; (d) **the confidentiality of the proceedings** of that or any other public authority where such confidentiality is provided by law ...
> (9) To the extent that the environmental information to be disclosed relates to **information on emissions**, a public authority shall not be entitled to refuse to disclose that information under an exception referred to in paragraphs (5)(d) to (g).

([uksi/2004/3391, reg.12](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2004/3391/regulation/12))

- **The UK threshold is lower.** Regulation 12(5) asks only whether disclosure "would **adversely affect**" the interest. The Scottish regulation 10(5) requires substantial prejudice. On the same facts, the UK exception is easier to engage than its Scottish counterpart.
- **The UK regulations do not command restrictive interpretation.** Regulation 12(2) requires a presumption in favour of disclosure, but there is no UK equivalent of the Scottish regulation 10(2)(a) instruction to interpret the exceptions restrictively.
- **Emissions are treated the same way.** Regulation 12(9) matches regulation 10(6): for information on emissions the (5)(d) to (g) exceptions are unavailable on both sides.

The practical upshot for shared advice is that **the two administrations can lawfully reach different answers on the same document**, and that on environmental information the Scottish authority is working to the tighter test. Neither can bind the other, and a release by one destroys the confidentiality the other is relying on, so the sharing arrangement should say who answers what.

#### 2.8 Applying this to advice shared between the two governments

- **Two regimes, two answers.** The same document held by both administrations is answerable by the Scottish Government under FOISA and the EI(S)R, and by the UK department under FOIA 2000 and the EIR 2004. A decision to withhold by one does not bind the other, and as section 2.7 shows the tests are not identical.
- **Section 36(1) turns on whether privilege survives the sharing.** That is the question the doctrines above are usually deployed to answer. Where their availability in Scots law is uncertain, the protection should be built into the disclosure itself: share on expressly confidential and limited terms, to identified recipients, for an identified purpose, and record it.
- **Section 36(2) may add a second line.** Where one administration obtains information from the other, section 36(2) exempts it if disclosure would be an actionable breach of confidence, and that limb **is** absolute under section 2(2)(c). It depends on the law of confidence rather than on privilege, so it does not stand or fall with the doctrinal questions above.
- **The public interest test still has to be worked.** For section 36(1) under FOISA and for every exception under regulation 10, exemption is the beginning of the analysis rather than the end.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Jurisdiction.** Scotland for the FOISA and EI(S)R analysis, and the United Kingdom for the FOIA 2000 and EIR 2004 analysis at 2.7. The law of privilege discussed is Scots law, with English authority used only where it states a principle common to both systems or is expressly identified as English.
- **Status.** FOISA, the Environmental Information (Scotland) Regulations 2004, the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 are all in force. *Prudential* is a decision of the Supreme Court.
- **Limit of this answer.** The most important limit is set out at 2.6. **Whether Scots law recognises common interest privilege and limited waiver, and on what conditions, was not established either way.** The answer neither applies nor rejects them; it flags the question. A reviewer should treat this as the point most needing their confirmation.
- **Limit of this answer.** Decisions and guidance of the Scottish Information Commissioner, the most directly relevant body of material on section 36(1) and on whether confidentiality survives a limited-purpose disclosure, are not available through these tools and were not consulted. Find Case Law does not index the Court of Session, so no Scottish judicial authority could be retrieved at all.
- **Limit of this answer.** The UK-side instruments were retrieved and are analysed at 2.7, but only the provisions bearing on privileged legal advice. Neither Act is covered in the round.

question: I'd like you to provide a list of organisations, offices etc. which make up the Scottish Administration as defined by section 126. In particular I'd like you to review Statutory Instruments and Orders in Council
statements: The Scottish Administration consists of the office-holders in the Scottish Administration and the members of the staff of the Scottish Administration, as provided by section 126(6) of the Scotland Act 1998.

Office-holders in the Scottish Administration are, under section 126(7)(a), members of the Scottish Government and junior Scottish Ministers, together with the holders of offices in the Scottish Administration which are not ministerial offices.

Section 126(8)(a) of the Scotland Act 1998 names three non-ministerial offices expressly: the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages for Scotland, the Keeper of the Registers of Scotland, and the Keeper of the Records of Scotland.

Section 126(8)(b) allows any other office of a description specified in an Order in Council to be a non-ministerial office in the Scottish Administration, so a complete list cannot be produced from primary legislation alone.
Where the Orders in Council specifying further offices cannot all be retrieved, the answer should state that the list is incomplete rather than presenting a partial list as complete.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

Section 126(6) of the Scotland Act 1998 defines the Scottish Administration as **the office-holders in the Scottish Administration and the members of the staff of the Scottish Administration**.

The office-holders divide in two under section 126(7)(a): **ministerial** (members of the Scottish Government and junior Scottish Ministers) and **non-ministerial**.

The non-ministerial offices are where the difficulty lies. Section 126(8) names **three** expressly, then adds "any other office of a description specified in an **Order in Council**".

**A complete list therefore cannot be produced from primary legislation alone.** It requires collecting every Order in Council made under section 126(8)(b), and an answer that offers a list without having done so should say the list is incomplete rather than present it as exhaustive.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The definition

> **Section 126 - Interpretation**
> (6) References in this Act and in any other enactment to the Scottish Administration are to **the office-holders in the Scottish Administration and the members of the staff of the Scottish Administration**.
> (7) For the purposes of this Act -
>    (a) references to office-holders in the Scottish Administration are to -
>      (i) members of the Scottish Government and junior Scottish Ministers, and
>      (ii) the holders of offices in the Scottish Administration which are not ministerial offices, and
>    (b) references to members of the staff of the Scottish Administration are to the staff of the persons referred to in paragraph (a).
> (8) For the purposes of this Act, the offices in the Scottish Administration which are not ministerial offices are -
>    (a) the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages for Scotland, the Keeper of the Registers of Scotland and the Keeper of the Records of Scotland, and
>    (b) **any other office of a description specified in an Order in Council** ...

([ukpga/1998/46, s.126](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1998/46/section/126))

Note that the Scottish Administration is defined as a body of **persons**, office-holders and staff, not as a set of organisations. A question phrased in terms of "organisations, offices etc." maps onto the office-holders limb.

Related provisions: section 44 constitutes the Scottish Government ([s.44](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1998/46/section/44)), section 48 deals with the Scottish Law Officers ([s.48](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1998/46/section/48)), and section 51 with the Civil Service ([s.51](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1998/46/section/51)).

#### 2.2 The three offices named in the Act

Section 126(8)(a) names, exhaustively for that paragraph:

1. the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages for Scotland
2. the Keeper of the Registers of Scotland
3. the Keeper of the Records of Scotland

#### 2.3 The open-ended limb, and two worked examples

Section 126(8)(b) is the reason the list cannot be closed from the Act. Offices are added by Order in Council, each specifying further offices. Two retrieved examples show the mechanism:

**The Scottish Administration (Offices) Order 2012** ([uksi/2012/3073, art 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2012/3073/article/2)):

> The following offices are specified for the purposes of section 126(8)(b) of the Scotland Act 1998 ... -
> (a) Her Majesty's inspector of constabulary appointed under section 71(2) of the Police and Fire Reform (Scotland) Act 2012;
> (b) Her Majesty's Chief Inspector of the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ...;
> (c) Her Majesty's Inspector of the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ...; and
> (d) Assistant Inspector of the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ...

**The Scottish Administration (Offices) Order 2015** ([uksi/2015/200, art 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2015/200/article/2)):

> ... (a) the Clerk of the Sheriff Appeal Court appointed under section 59(1) of the Courts Reform (Scotland) Act 2014;
> (b) a Deputy Clerk of the Sheriff Appeal Court appointed under section 60(1) of that Act.

The 2012 Order also contains its own revocation provisions (articles 3 and 4), which is a reminder that the set of specified offices changes over time: later Orders both add and remove.

#### 2.4 Why a complete list cannot be given here

Three features combine:

- The Act names three offices and then delegates the rest (s.126(8)(b)).
- The delegated instruments are numerous, spread over the years since 1999, and amend and revoke one another.
- Only two such Orders were retrieved in this research.

The honest answer is therefore **structural**: the Scottish Administration comprises the ministerial office-holders, the three offices in section 126(8)(a), the offices specified from time to time by Order in Council under section 126(8)(b), and the staff of all of them. A named list of the section 126(8)(b) offices requires a complete survey of those Orders as they now stand, which this research has not done.

Presenting the two Orders above as if they were the whole set would be wrong. They are examples of the mechanism, not an enumeration.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Scotland Act 1998 extends to the United Kingdom and was returned in revised form.
- **Limit of this answer.** The list of section 126(8)(b) offices is **incomplete by acknowledgement**, not by oversight. Two Orders were retrieved out of an unknown larger number, and no attempt is made here to state the current consolidated position.
- **Why that is the right answer.** Where the enabling provision delegates open-endedly and the instruments cannot all be retrieved, stating the framework and disclosing the gap is more useful, and more accurate, than a partial list presented as complete.

---

### 4. References

question: I am looking for definitions, both statutory and in case law, of the term "occupier" - i.e. an occupier of a property or place. I am giving advice about its use in the context of serving a notice on "the occupier", but the legislation the notice is under does not define "occupier". As such, I need your help to look for other definitions so I can synthesise an appropriate meaning of the term.
statements: There is no single statutory definition of "occupier" that can be borrowed: the term takes its meaning from the particular enactment, read with that Act's purpose and its other provisions, so a notice power that leaves it undefined is construed from that Act first rather than from a definition imported from elsewhere.

The leading common law statement of the term is the control test in Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd [1966] AC 552: a person is an occupier if they have a sufficient degree of control over the premises, exclusive occupation is not required and control need not be complete, so on that test there can be more than one occupier of the same premises at the same time.

The Wheat test was decided in the occupiers' liability context, so for an undefined term in a notice power it is persuasive by analogy and a sensible starting point, not automatically the governing test.

The Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 deliberately does not define who an occupier is: section 1(2) provides that its rules regulate the nature of the duty but "shall not alter the rules of the common law as to the persons on whom a duty is so imposed or to whom it is owed".

Section 1(1) of the Occupiers' Liability (Scotland) Act 1960 does supply a statutory formulation, defining an "occupier of premises" as a person occupying or having control of land or other premises, and the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 defines the term only by cross-reference to the person who owes the common duty of care under the 1957 Act.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**There is no single statutory definition of "occupier" to borrow.** The term takes its meaning from the enactment it appears in, read with that Act's purpose and its other provisions. Where a notice-giving power leaves it undefined, the common law test of **control** is the usual starting point rather than an automatic answer.

The three points that matter for choosing a recipient:

1. **The occupiers' liability statutes deliberately do not define the term.** Section 1(2) of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 says in terms that its rules "shall not alter the rules of the common law as to the persons on whom a duty is so imposed". The Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 then defines "occupier" by pointing back to the 1957 Act. The chain ends at the common law.
2. **Scotland has a statutory formulation; England and Wales does not.** Section 1(1) of the Occupiers' Liability (Scotland) Act 1960 defines an "occupier of premises" as "a person occupying or having control of land or other premises". The same words, "occupying or having control of", appear in section 5(1) of the 1957 Act.
3. **The common law test is sufficient control, and it admits of more than one occupier.** *Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd* [1966] AC 552 is the leading authority: whoever has a sufficient degree of control over premises is an occupier, exclusive occupation is not required, and control need not be complete.

For a notice, the practical consequence is that **"the occupier" is unlikely to be settled by title or residence alone**, and that control of the relevant premises for the relevant purpose is usually the better guide. How far the *Wheat* test carries across is a question about the particular Act: it was decided about occupiers' liability, and a notice power with a different purpose may point somewhere narrower or wider. Who must be served is then determined by that Act's own service provisions.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The 1957 Act does not define who an occupier is, and says so

> **Section 1 - Preliminary**
> (1) The rules enacted by the two next following sections shall have effect, in place of the rules of the common law, to regulate the duty which an occupier of premises owes to his visitors ...
> (2) The rules so enacted shall regulate the nature of the duty imposed by law **in consequence of a person's occupation or control of premises** ... **but they shall not alter the rules of the common law as to the persons on whom a duty is so imposed or to whom it is owed** ...

([ukpga/Eliz2/5-6/31, s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/5-6/31/section/1))

This is the single most useful provision for the question asked. It is an express statement that Parliament codified **the content of the duty** and left **the identity of the duty holder** to the common law. Section 2 then imposes the common duty of care on "an occupier of premises" without saying who that is ([s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/5-6/31/section/2)).

The nearest the Act comes to a formulation is section 5(1), which speaks of "a person occupying or having control of the premises" ([s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/5-6/31/section/5)).

#### 2.2 The 1984 Act defines the term by cross-reference

> **Section 1(2)** For the purposes of this section, the persons who are to be treated respectively as an occupier of any premises ... are —
> (a) **any person who owes in relation to the premises the duty referred to in section 2 of the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957** (the common duty of care) ...

([ukpga/1984/3, s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/1984/3/section/1))

So the 1984 Act's occupier is the 1957 Act's occupier, and the 1957 Act's occupier is the common law's occupier. No statutory definition is reached by following this chain, which is itself the answer to the question "where is the definition?".

#### 2.3 Scotland: a statutory formulation of the same idea

> **Section 1 - Variation of rules of common law as to duty of care owed by occupiers**
> (1) The provisions of the next following section of this Act shall have effect, in place of the rules of the common law, for the purpose of determining the care which **a person occupying or having control of land or other premises (in this Act referred to as an "occupier of premises")** is required, by reason of such occupation or control, to show towards persons entering on the premises ...

([ukpga/Eliz2/8-9/30, s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/8-9/30/section/1))

This is a usable synthesised definition: **occupying or having control of** land or other premises. The Act extends to Scotland only (s.5(1), [ukpga/Eliz2/8-9/30, s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/8-9/30/section/5)).

Section 3 is worth noting alongside it. Where premises are occupied under a tenancy and the landlord is responsible for maintenance or repair, the landlord owes the same care in respect of dangers arising from a failure to carry out that responsibility ([s.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/8-9/30/section/3)). That is a duty imposed on someone who is not the occupier, which is a caution against reading "occupier" as a synonym for "the person responsible for the premises".

#### 2.4 The common law test: sufficient control

*Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd* [1966] AC 552 remains the leading authority. It is not in the Find Case Law database, which does not extend back to 1966, but its terms are set out in modern judgments that apply it.

In [Kanwarjit Singh Juj v John Lewis Partnership Plc [2023] EWCA Civ 1507](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ewca/civ/2023/1507) at [20], the Court of Appeal recorded Lord Denning's formulation:

> "Wherever a person has a **sufficient degree of control** over premises that he ought to realise that any failure on his part to use care may result in injury to a person coming lawfully there, then he is an 'occupier' and the person coming lawfully there is his 'visitor' ..."

In [William Brown v Morgan Sindall Construction and Infrastructure Ltd [2025] EWHC 2204 (KB)](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ewhc/kb/2025/2204) at [195], the High Court drew out the two features that matter most here:

> "There is authority that the basis for an occupier's liability is 'occupational control, i.e., control associated with and arising from presence in and use of or activity in the premises'. See Wheat v Lacon [1966] AC per Lord Pearson at 552 (HL). The same authority supports the proposition that **that control does not need to be complete**. See per Lord Denning in the same case: '... **In order to be an "occupier" it is not necessary for a person to have entire control over the premises. He need not have exclusive occupation. Suffice it that he has some degree of control.**' (Page 578)."

Three things follow, and they are what an adviser needs:

- **Control, not title.** Ownership, tenancy and residence are evidence of control, not substitutes for it.
- **Control need not be exclusive or complete.** A degree of control suffices.
- **There can therefore be more than one occupier of the same premises at the same time**, each in respect of the aspects they control.

Lord Pearson's phrase is the useful one for a notice: control "associated with and arising from presence in and use of or activity in the premises".

#### 2.5 Applying this to serving a notice on "the occupier"

Where the enabling provision does not define the term, the meaning is taken from that enactment and its purpose. The common law test above is a starting point and an analogy, not a definition that displaces the Act. Four practical steps follow from the material above:

1. **Read the enabling Act as a whole first.** An interpretation section elsewhere in the Act, or a general service-of-notices provision, may define or qualify the term even though the notice power itself does not. The purpose of the particular notice also colours the meaning: a notice about the physical condition of premises points to whoever controls their state, while one about an activity points to whoever controls that activity.
2. **Ask who has control of the relevant premises for the relevant purpose**, using *Wheat v Lacon* as the analogy: presence, use and activity, not title. Check that a control-based reading actually fits what this notice power is for before adopting it.
3. **Do not assume a single answer.** Where control is divided, for example between a landlord who retains common parts and a tenant who controls the let unit, both may be occupiers for different purposes.
4. **Take service from the enabling Act, not from the definition.** Whether a notice may be addressed to "the occupier" at the premises, and whether more than one person can or must be served, is answered by that Act's service provisions and any applicable general rule, not by the number of people who might satisfy a control test.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **England and Wales.** Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 and Occupiers' Liability Act 1984. Neither defines "occupier" independently of the common law.
- **Scotland.** Occupiers' Liability (Scotland) Act 1960, which extends to Scotland only and does contain the formulation "occupying or having control of land or other premises".
- **Status of the case law.** *Juj* is a Court of Appeal decision and *Brown* a first instance decision of the King's Bench Division; both are cited here as accurate statements of *Wheat v Lacon*, which is a decision of the House of Lords and remains the governing authority.
- **Limit of this answer.** *Wheat v E Lacon & Co Ltd* [1966] AC 552 itself could not be retrieved: Find Case Law does not cover 1966, so the authority is reached through modern judgments quoting it. The quoted passages should be checked against the report before the definition is relied on in advice.
- **Limit of this answer.** Confined to the meaning of "occupier". It does not address the separate statutory rules on how a notice must be served, or on whom service is deemed effective.

---

### 4. References

- [Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, s.2 - Extent of occupier's ordinary duty](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/Eliz2/5-6/31/section/2)
