question: please summarise Rex v Evans (Graham) [2025] EWCA.
statements: Whether a person is a public officer for the purposes of misconduct in a public office turns on the actual duties and responsibilities they held at the material time, and not on the formal designation, grade or job title of their role.

The Court of Appeal dismissed Graham Andrew Evans's appeal against his conviction for misconduct in a public office, holding that an operational support grade left alone overnight in charge of a prison block was a public officer acting as such.

The court applied the three questions from R v Mitchell [2014] EWCA Crim 318: what position is held, what is the nature of the duties undertaken in it, and does fulfilling those duties fulfil a responsibility of government in which the public has a significant interest beyond that of anyone directly affected by a failure.

Misconduct in a public office is a conduct offence, so the prosecution does not have to prove that the misconduct caused harm; the appellant's acquittal on gross negligence manslaughter for want of causation did not prevent conviction on the misconduct count.
The appellant was convicted after failing to carry out 24 of the 38 checks required by a prisoner's Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork plan and falsifying the log to record that he had done so.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The case is **[Graham Andrew Evans v R [2025] EWCA Crim 1150](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ewca/crim/2025/1150)** (Court of Appeal, Criminal Division; Holroyde LJ (Vice-President), May J and Wall J; judgment 5 September 2025). **The appeal against conviction was dismissed.**

The appellant was an **operational support grade ("OSG")** at HMP Hewell, convicted of **misconduct in a public office**. Working alone overnight in a prison block, he failed to carry out 24 of the 38 checks required by a prisoner's Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork ("ACCT") plan, and falsified the log to show that he had. The prisoner, Mr Olgun, was found hanging and died a week later. A gross negligence manslaughter count was withdrawn from the jury at half time because causation could not be proved.

**The point of the case is what makes someone a "public officer".** It is not the job title or the formal grade. It is the **actual duties and responsibilities the individual held at the material time**, and whether performing them properly discharges a responsibility of government in which the public has a significant interest going beyond the interest of anyone directly affected. On that test an OSG, alone overnight and responsible for a block of prisoners, was a public officer, even though an OSG has no power of arrest and, save in emergencies, no power to search a prisoner, use force or enter a cell.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The three grounds of appeal

1. That the judge was wrong to rule there was a case to answer, because an OSG is not a public officer.
2. That, the jury having been unable to be sure that any breach caused the death, no jury could find the breach serious enough to amount to the offence.
3. That the judge should not have directed the jury that they could consider the likely consequences of the breach.

All three failed.

#### 2.2 The test for public officer status

The court took the elements of the offence as settled, summarising them (at [21]) as:

> "(1) A public officer acting as such (2) wilfully neglects to perform his duty and/or wilfully misconducts himself (3) to such a degree as to amount to an abuse of the public's trust in the office holder (4) without reasonable excuse or justification."

On who is a public officer, the court adopted the three questions from **R v Mitchell [2014] EWCA Crim 318** at [16], which it described (at [37]) as "a clear and helpful indication of the approach to be taken":

> "First, what is the position held? Second, what is the nature of the duties undertaken by the employee or officer in that position? Third, does the fulfilment of those duties represent the fulfilment of one of the responsibilities of government such that the public have a significant interest in the discharge of that duty which is additional to or beyond an interest in anyone who might be directly affected by a serious failure in the performance of that duty?"

Two features of that approach carry the decision. First, as *Mitchell* emphasised at [17] and this court repeated at [25], **the focus is on the duties and responsibilities of the individual accused, not on the overall responsibility of the employing organisation**. Second, as **R v Cosford [2013] EWCA Crim 466** held at [34], any "strict confinement" of the offence is directed not at the position held but at **"the nature of the duty undertaken"**.

The court also noted (at [37]) that **the categories of activity which may be held to be a public office are not closed**.

#### 2.3 Applying the test to an OSG

The first two *Mitchell* questions were not in dispute. On the third, the court held (at [39]) that proper performance of the appellant's duties

> "would represent the fulfilment of the responsibility of government for the safety and security of persons whom the state had deprived of their liberty."

The reasoning is specific to what this appellant was actually doing that night. He was the **one person present in the block** who held a position of responsibility towards all the prisoners in it, the one person immediately able to assist if a prisoner's health or safety was compromised, and the one person immediately able to ensure compliance with the ACCT plans. The court found it "impossible to regard the appellant's duties and responsibilities as being no more than three discrete duties of care owed to three individual prisoners".

It followed (at [41]) that the judge was "plainly correct" to rule that a reasonable jury could be sure the appellant was a public officer acting as such at the material time.

This is why the defence argument from powers failed. Counsel had argued that an OSG has no more power than a civilian secretary in a prison, and that the offence should not expand simply because the prison authorities found it expedient to give auxiliary staff more functions. That argument addresses the grade; the test addresses the duties.

#### 2.4 Consequences and causation

Grounds 2 and 3 rested on the acquittal on manslaughter. The court accepted the prosecution's position that **misconduct in public office is a conduct offence**: there is no requirement to prove that the misconduct caused harm. That the jury could not be sure the breach caused the death therefore did not prevent them finding the breach serious enough to amount to an abuse of the public's trust, and the judge was entitled to direct the jury that they could take the potential consequences of the conduct into account when judging its seriousness.

#### 2.5 What a summary of this case should not say

The reported outcome is easy to state and easy to state shallowly. A summary that gives only the facts, the offence and the dismissal has missed the reason the case is worth reading: it is authority on **how public officer status is decided**, and it decides it by reference to what the person was actually responsible for, not what they were called.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Jurisdiction.** England and Wales. Misconduct in a public office is a common law offence of the law of England and Wales; it has no direct Scots law equivalent.
- **Status.** A judgment of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), binding on the Crown Court and below.
- **Naming.** The question calls the case "Rex v Evans (Graham)". Find Case Law reports it as "Graham Andrew Evans v R", the appellant being named first on appeal. Both refer to the same judgment.
- **Limit of this answer.** Written from the judgment text alone. *Mitchell* and *Cosford* are described as they are quoted and applied in this judgment; neither was retrieved separately.

---

### 4. References

- [Graham Andrew Evans v R [2025] EWCA Crim 1150](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ewca/crim/2025/1150)

question: are there rules on the level of vitamins contained in margarine sold in the UK?
statements: The vitamin content requirement for margarine in England was removed in 2013, when regulation 3(4) of the Environmental Noise, Site Waste Management Plans and Spreadable Fats etc. (Revocations and Amendments) Regulations 2013 omitted regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) and the Milk and Milk Products (Protection of Designations) (England) Regulations 2008.

In Scotland the requirement remains in force under regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats, Milk and Milk Products (Scotland) Regulations 2008, which requires margarine sold by retail to contain per 100 grams not less than 800 and not more than 1,000 micrograms of vitamin A, and not less than 7.05 and not more than 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D.
The 2013 Regulations amended the England Regulations only and did not remove the equivalent requirement in any other UK jurisdiction.

A question asked about the United Kingdom has different answers in different jurisdictions here, so the answer must say which jurisdiction it covers rather than presenting one jurisdiction's position as the UK position.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**There is no single UK answer.** The requirement was once uniform across the UK but has since been removed in England while remaining in force elsewhere.

- **England: no requirement.** Regulation 4 of the 2008 England Regulations was **omitted** in 2013 and there is now no statutory vitamin content requirement for margarine sold in England.
- **Scotland: requirement in force.** Per 100 grams: **800 to 1,000 micrograms of vitamin A** and **7.05 to 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D**.
- **Wales:** the equivalent 2001 Regulations impose the same levels on the text retrieved.
- **Northern Ireland:** governed by its own instruments, not verified in this retrieval.

An answer that cites the 2013 revocation as having removed the requirement generally is wrong. It amended the **England** Regulations and nothing else.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 England: the requirement was removed in 2013

Regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) and the Milk and Milk Products (Protection of Designations) (England) Regulations 2008 ([uksi/2008/1287, reg 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2008/1287/regulation/4)) is headed "Vitamin content of margarine" and now returns **no operative text**, the database rendering it as omitted.

The instrument that did it is the Environmental Noise, Site Waste Management Plans and Spreadable Fats etc. (Revocations and Amendments) Regulations 2013:

> **Regulation 3 — Amendment of the Spreadable Fats ... (England) Regulations 2008**
> (1) The Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) and the Milk and Milk Products (Protection of Designations) (England) Regulations 2008 are amended as follows.
> (2) In regulation 2(1), omit the definitions of "vitamin A" and "vitamin D".
> (3) In regulation 3 — (a) in paragraph (1), omit the words "Except where paragraph (2) applies,"; (b) omit paragraphs (2) and (3).
> **(4) Omit regulation 4.**
> (5) Omit regulation 6(1)(a).

([uksi/2013/2854, reg 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2013/2854/regulation/3))

Two points a reader is likely to need:

- **It is an amendment, not a revocation.** The separate revocation provision, regulation 2, revokes three environmental-noise and site-waste instruments and says nothing about margarine ([uksi/2013/2854, reg 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2013/2854/regulation/2)). Citing "the 2013 revocation" for the removal of the vitamin rule points at the wrong regulation of the right instrument.
- **Its reach is England.** Regulation 3(1) names only the England Regulations. Nothing in it touches the Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish instruments.

#### 2.2 Scotland: the requirement remains

> **Regulation 4 — Vitamin content of margarine**
> No person may sell by retail any margarine unless it contains in every 100 grams —
> (a) not less than 800 micrograms and not more than 1,000 micrograms of vitamin A; and
> (b) not less than 7.05 micrograms and not more than 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D,
> and a proportionate amount in any part of 100 grams.

([ssi/2008/216, reg 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/4))

Contravention is an offence under regulation 6 and enforcement falls to food authorities under regulation 5 ([ssi/2008/216](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216)).

#### 2.3 Wales

Regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) (Wales) Regulations 2001 imposes the same levels, in the older two-limb drafting:

> (1) Any margarine sold by retail shall contain in every 100 grams of such margarine — (a) not less than 800 micrograms and not more than 1000 micrograms of vitamin A, and (b) not less than 7.05 micrograms and not more than 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D, and a proportionate amount in any part of 100 grams.
> (2) No person shall sell by retail any margarine in contravention of this regulation.

([wsi/2001/1361, reg 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/wsi/2001/1361/regulation/4))

#### 2.4 Northern Ireland

The relevant instruments are the Margarine Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1968 ([nisro/1968/3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/nisro/1968/3)) and the Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1996 ([nisr/1996/47](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/nisr/1996/47)). Their vitamin provisions were not retrieved in this research and the Northern Irish position is therefore **not established** by this answer.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **The question has four answers, not one.** This is the whole point of the question: "the UK" is not a single regulatory area for margarine composition.
- **Verified here:** the England omission (positively, from the text of the amending instrument), the Scottish requirement, and the Welsh requirement as drafted.
- **Not verified here:** whether the Welsh 2001 Regulations have since been amended in the same way as England's, and the Northern Irish position. An answer confidently stating either without retrieval is going beyond the evidence.

question: How are months defined under the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009?
statements: The Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 does not apply to the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, because section 1(1)(a) of the 2010 Act applies Part 1 only to Acts of the Scottish Parliament whose Bills received Royal Assent on or after the day Part 1 came into force, and the 2009 Act preceded that day.

Interpretation of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 is instead governed by the Scotland Act 1998 (Transitory and Transitional Provisions) (Publication and Interpretation etc. of Acts of the Scottish Parliament) Order 1999.
Schedule 2 to that 1999 Order defines "month" as meaning a calendar month.

A provision such as section 35ZA being inserted into the 2009 Act by a later Act does not bring the 2010 Act into play, because the 2010 Act keys its application to the Royal Assent date of the Act being interpreted, not to the date a provision within it was inserted.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**"Month" means calendar month**, and the definition comes from the **Scotland Act 1998 interpretation order of 1999**, not from the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010.

The 2010 Act does **not** apply to the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009. Section 1(1)(a) of the 2010 Act applies Part 1 only to Acts of the Scottish Parliament "the Bills for which receive Royal Assent **on or after** the day on which this Part comes into force". Part 1 came into force on 6 April 2011; the 2009 Act preceded it.

The applicable definition is in Schedule 2 to the 1999 Order: **"'Month' means calendar month"**.

That a provision such as section 35ZA was inserted into the 2009 Act by a later Act makes no difference. The 2010 Act keys its application to the Royal Assent date of the **Act being interpreted**, not to when an individual provision was inserted into it.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The 2009 Act does not define the term

Section 98 of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 is the Act's interpretation section ([asp/2009/12, s.98](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/98)). It defines terms specific to the Act's subject matter, "additional greenhouse gas", "baseline", "baseline year" and so on. It does not define "month". The meaning therefore comes from the general interpretation regime applicable to the Act.

#### 2.2 Which regime applies, and why it is not the 2010 Act

> **Section 1 - Application of Part 1**
> (1) This Part applies to -
>    (a) **Acts of the Scottish Parliament the Bills for which receive Royal Assent on or after the day on which this Part comes into force**,
>    (b) Scottish instruments made on or after that day ...
>    (c) this Act.

([asp/2010/10, s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2010/10/section/1))

This is a **commencement-keyed** application provision, and it is the reason the 2010 Act is the wrong instrument here. The Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 received Royal Assent in 2009. Part 1 of the 2010 Act came into force on 6 April 2011, the date used throughout the associated savings instrument ([ssi/2011/88](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2011/88)). The 2009 Act therefore falls outside section 1(1)(a).

Schedule 1 to the 2010 Act, which carries its definitions of words and expressions ([asp/2010/10, sch 1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2010/10/schedule/1)), is introduced by section 25(1) and sits inside Part 1. It is caught by the same limit.

#### 2.3 The regime that does apply, and the definition

For Acts of the Scottish Parliament passed before 6 April 2011, interpretation is governed by the Scotland Act 1998 (Transitory and Transitional Provisions) (Publication and Interpretation etc. of Acts of the Scottish Parliament) Order 1999 ([uksi/1999/1379](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/1999/1379)). Article 6 deals with statutory interpretation, Schedule 1 with statutory interpretation and operation, and Schedule 2 carries the general definitions.

Schedule 2 provides:

> **"Month" means calendar month;**

([uksi/1999/1379, sch 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/1999/1379/schedule/2))

A calendar month runs from a day in one month to the corresponding day in the next, rather than as a fixed number of days.

#### 2.4 Later insertion does not switch the regime

Section 35ZA was inserted into the 2009 Act by later legislation. That does not bring the 2010 Act into play, for a reason visible on the face of section 1(1)(a): the trigger is the Royal Assent date of the **Bill for the Act**, a single fixed date for the whole Act. It is not a provision-by-provision test, and an amending Act does not give the amended Act a new Royal Assent date.

The practical consequence is that one interpretation regime governs the whole of the 2009 Act, including provisions inserted into it years later. An answer that applies the 2010 Act to section 35ZA because section 35ZA is recent has misread the application provision.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 and the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 extend to Scotland. The 1999 Order is a UK statutory instrument made under the Scotland Act 1998.
- **Limit of this answer.** The 6 April 2011 commencement date for Part 1 of the 2010 Act is taken from the associated savings and transitional instrument rather than from a commencement order retrieved in terms. The reasoning does not depend on the precise date, only on its being later than the 2009 Act's Royal Assent.

---

### 4. References

- [Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010, s.1 - Application of Part 1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2010/10/section/1)

question: With regards to Scotland, what mechanisms could the Scottish Government consider if it wanted to lessen the requirements for a single local authority to provide accommodation to the homeless, include any tangential or related measures which might free up local authority housing supply or budgets
statements: Section 32A of the Housing (Scotland) Act 1987 provides that section 31(2), so far as it requires the accommodation to be permanent accommodation, does not apply in such circumstances as may be prescribed, so the permanent accommodation requirement can be relaxed by the Scottish Ministers through subordinate legislation and does not need an Act of the Scottish Parliament.

The section 33 power to refer a homelessness application to another local authority on local connection grounds is currently suspended between Scottish local authorities by article 2 of the Homeless Persons (Suspension of Referrals between Local Authorities) (Scotland) Order 2022, and the enabling power in section 33A expressly allows such an order to be confined to specified local authorities or descriptions of local authority and to specified circumstances or modifications, so narrowing it to relieve one authority needs no primary legislation.

Which levers are ministerial has to be checked provision by provision rather than inferred from a duty appearing on the face of the Act: sections 32A, 33A and 29(3) each let the Scottish Ministers change how the homelessness duties operate without an Act of the Scottish Parliament, and the standard that interim accommodation must meet is set by order under section 29(3) and can be amended by ministers at any time.

An authority need not use its own housing stock: section 35(1) allows a section 31 or 34 duty to be discharged by securing accommodation from another person or by advice and assistance, section 31(2A) to (2H) allows a private accommodation offer to end the duty in a restricted case, section 35(2) allows reasonable charges to be recovered, and section 38 requires other authorities and registered social landlords to co-operate on request.

In Glasgow City Council v X (Scotland) [2025] UKSC 13 the Supreme Court held that the needs of the household must be taken into account under article 4(b) of the Unsuitable Accommodation Order 2014 but do not all have to be met at the interim stage.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The Scottish Government has levers at three different heights, and the distinction between them is the practical point: **some need an Act of the Scottish Parliament, some can be done by order, and one significant lever is currently switched off by an order the Government itself made.** The single easiest mistake here is to assume that a duty written on the face of the Act can only be changed by an Act. This Act attaches its modification powers in their own sections, so each duty has to be checked against them.

- **Currently switched off.** The section 33 local connection referral power, which is the statutory route by which one authority moves the permanent accommodation duty to another, **cannot presently be used between Scottish authorities**. The Homeless Persons (Suspension of Referrals between Local Authorities) (Scotland) Order 2022 ([ssi/2022/356](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2022/356)) suspends it. Revoking or narrowing that Order is the single quickest way to relieve pressure on one authority, and it needs no primary legislation.
- **Ministerial, by order or regulations.** The standard of interim accommodation is set by the Homeless Persons (Unsuitable Accommodation) (Scotland) Order 2014 ([ssi/2014/243](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/243)), made under section 29(3). It has already been amended to create exemptions and can be amended again. Regulation-making powers in sections 31(3)(b), 32(3), 32(6) and 32B(5) and (6) allow prescribed matters to be varied, and section 32B(6) permits **different provision for different areas**, which is the express route to relieving a single authority rather than all 32.
- **Ministerial, and the most direct lever of all.** Section 32A provides that section 31(2), so far as it requires the accommodation to be permanent, **does not apply in such circumstances as may be prescribed** ([s.32A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/32A)). The permanent accommodation requirement is therefore not fixed by the Act in the way the duty itself is, and reducing it does **not** need an Act of the Scottish Parliament.
- **Check before assuming primary legislation is needed.** The duty in section 31(2) to secure that accommodation becomes available at all, the interim duty in section 29(1) and the definition of homelessness in section 24 have no ministerial modification power attached to them in the text retrieved for this answer. That is a reason to check each one, not a finding: sections 32A and 33A show that this Act attaches its modification powers in separate sections, easily missed by a search aimed at the duty itself.

**Tangential measures already in the Act** are often overlooked and free up stock or budget without changing any duty: section 35(1) lets an authority discharge the duty using **someone else's accommodation**, section 31(2A) to (2H) lets a **private accommodation offer** end the duty in a restricted case, section 35(2) allows **reasonable charges** to be recovered, section 38 compels **co-operation** from other authorities and registered social landlords, section 32(2) funds **prevention** by requiring reasonable steps before homelessness occurs, and section 32(4) preserves an authority's right to **recover vacant possession**.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The duty that would be lessened

Two duties must be kept apart, because they have different levers.

**The interim duty**, section 29(1): where the authority has reason to believe an applicant may be homeless, it "shall secure that accommodation is made available for his occupation" pending inquiries, pending review, and until accommodation under section 31 becomes available. Section 29(2) provides that this duty "arises irrespective of any local connection which an applicant may have with the district of another local authority" ([ukpga/1987/26, s.29](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/29)). Section 29(3) lets the Scottish Ministers specify by order accommodation that does not count.

**The permanent accommodation duty**, section 31(2): where the authority is satisfied the applicant is homeless and not intentionally so, it "shall, **unless they notify another local authority in accordance with section 33** (referral of application on ground of local connection), secure that permanent accommodation becomes available for his occupation" ([s.31](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/31)).

The words in bold are where the single-authority burden is decided. Section 31(2) is drafted with the referral route as its only built-in exit.

#### 2.2 The lever that is currently disabled

> **Article 2 - Suspension of referrals**
> A relevant local authority **may not exercise the power under section 33(1) of the 1987 Act** (referral of application to another local authority) in respect of any other relevant local authority.

([ssi/2022/356, art.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2022/356/article/2))

"Relevant local authority" means a Scottish council ([art.1(2)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2022/356/article/1)), so referrals to authorities in England and Wales, which section 33(1) also permits, are unaffected. Article 3 preserves the position for applications made before the Order came into force.

This matters more than any other single point in the answer. Section 33 sets out the conditions for referral, that neither the applicant nor anyone reasonably expected to reside with them has a local connection with the notified-to authority's district, that one of them does have such a connection with the other district, and that there is no risk of domestic abuse there ([s.33](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/33)); section 34 then moves the section 31(2) duty to the notified authority once the conditions are determined to be met ([s.34](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/34)). All of that machinery is presently unavailable between Scottish councils.

Any analysis that offers section 33 as the answer to "how could one authority's burden be reduced", without noting that it is suspended, is describing a mechanism that cannot be used today. Conversely, the suspension is itself among the cheapest levers, and the enabling power says so in terms.

> **Section 33A - Power to modify section 33**
> (1) The Scottish Ministers may by order made by statutory instrument provide that, for so long as the order is in force, the power of a local authority under subsection (1) of section 33 ... (a) **shall not be exercisable by such local authorities or such descriptions of local authority as are specified in the order, or shall be exercisable ... only in such circumstances, or with such modifications, as are specified in the order**; (b) [the same, in relation to the authorities referred to] ...
> (3) A statutory instrument containing an order under this section is, if made without a draft having been laid before, and approved by a resolution of, the Scottish Parliament, subject to annulment ...

([ukpga/1987/26, s.33A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/33A))

So the power is not simply on or off. Section 33A(1) expressly allows the suspension to be applied to **named authorities or descriptions of authority**, and to be made subject to **specified circumstances or modifications**. Narrowing the 2022 Order to relieve one authority, rather than revoking it nationally, is within the power as drafted. Section 33A(2) allows consequential modification of Part II and transitional provision, and section 33B requires Ministers to publish, and keep under review, a statement of the circumstances and criteria by reference to which the section 33A power is to be exercised ([s.33B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/33B)). That statement is a procedural step to plan for, not a legal obstacle.

#### 2.3 The permanent accommodation requirement is itself ministerial

This is the provision most easily missed, and it changes the shape of the answer.

> **Section 32A - Power of the Scottish Ministers to modify application of sections 31 and 32**
> (1) The provisions of—
> (a) **section 31(2) so far as requiring that accommodation is to be permanent accommodation** (within the meaning of section 31(5)), and
> (b) section 32(5)(b),
> **do not apply in such circumstances as may be prescribed**.
> (2) Where— (a) accommodation has been provided under section 31(2), and (b) by virtue of subsection (1) above, that accommodation is not permanent accommodation ... or does not meet the special needs of the applicant and any other person referred to in section 24(2), section 26 does not apply.

([ukpga/1987/26, s.32A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/32A))

Three things follow.

- **The permanence requirement is severable from the duty.** Section 32A(1)(a) reaches section 31(2) "so far as requiring that accommodation is to be permanent accommodation", and nothing else in it. The duty to secure accommodation survives; what can be switched off by regulations is the requirement that what is secured be permanent.
- **It is done by prescribing circumstances.** The disapplication operates "in such circumstances as may be prescribed", so it is subordinate legislation and it can be targeted rather than general. Which instrument "prescribed" means here, and whether it can be targeted at a single named authority as sections 32(6) and 32B(6) expressly permit for their own regulations, is not stated in section 32A itself and was not traced through the Act's general provisions.
- **Section 32A(2) handles the consequence.** Where accommodation is non-permanent by virtue of subsection (1), section 26 (intentional homelessness) does not apply, so an applicant is not later treated as having made themselves homeless by moving on from it.

What section 32A does **not** do is define the circumstances. That is left entirely to regulations, and this research did not establish whether any have been made. Before relying on the section, check whether the power has been exercised and what is currently prescribed under it. **Section 31(5) sets the boundary the power operates against**: "permanent accommodation" includes accommodation secured by a Scottish secure tenancy, by a short Scottish secure tenancy where paragraph 1, 2 or 2A of schedule 6 to the Housing (Scotland) Act 2001 is satisfied, or by a private residential tenancy ([s.31](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/31)).

#### 2.4 Other ministerial levers inside the Act

**Interim accommodation standards, section 29(3).** The Ministers may specify by order accommodation that does not satisfy the interim duty. The order in force is the Unsuitable Accommodation Order 2014. Article 4 makes accommodation unsuitable "in all circumstances" if it is not wind and watertight, not suitable for occupation by a homeless household taking into account the needs of the household, or not meeting minimum safety standards ([ssi/2014/243, art.4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/243/article/4)). Article 5 adds further disqualifying features, including accommodation outwith the authority's own area in which the household has not agreed to be placed ([art.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/243/article/5)). Articles 6 and 7A carry exemptions, and article 7A is the proof of concept: it already disapplies parts of article 5 for community hosting, rapid access accommodation and shared tenancy accommodation ([art.7A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2014/243/article/7A)). Widening those exemptions enlarges the pool of lawful interim accommodation without touching the duty.

**Prescribed matters, sections 31(3)(b), 32(3), 32(6) and 32B.** Section 32(3) requires advice and assistance "of such type as may be prescribed" to applicants threatened with homelessness who fall outside the section 32(2) duty. Section 32(6) provides that regulations made by virtue of section 31(3)(b) or section 32(3) "may make different provision for different purposes and different areas" ([s.32](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/32)). Section 32B requires assessment for, and provision of, prescribed housing support services where a section 31(2) or 32(2) duty is owed, and section 32B(6) again allows "different provision for different purposes and different areas" ([s.32B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/32B)).

The area-differentiation words are the direct answer to a question about **a single** local authority. They are what allows a targeted, rather than national, adjustment.

#### 2.5 Tangential measures that free up supply or budget

These change nothing about the duty and are available now.

- **Discharge using other people's accommodation, section 35(1).** An authority may perform a section 31 or 34 duty by making its own stock available, "by securing that he obtains accommodation from some other person", or by giving advice and assistance that secures accommodation from some other person ([s.35](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/35)). The duty is to secure accommodation, not to allocate council housing.
- **Private accommodation offers, section 31(2A) to (2H).** In a restricted case the duty ends if the applicant accepts or refuses a private accommodation offer: a short assured tenancy of at least 12 months, made with the authority's approval under arrangements with the landlord, where the authority is satisfied it is reasonable to accept ([s.31](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/31)).
- **Charging, section 35(2).** An authority may require reasonable charges for accommodation it secures, or reasonable amounts in respect of sums it pays another person for accommodation.
- **Compelled co-operation, section 38.** On request, another Scottish, English or Welsh authority, a development corporation, a registered housing association or a social work authority "shall co-operate in rendering such assistance ... as is reasonable in the circumstances" ([s.38](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1987/26/section/38)). This is a lever a single pressured authority can pull without any change in the law.
- **Prevention, section 32(2).** Where an applicant is threatened with homelessness and not intentionally so, the authority must "take reasonable steps to secure that accommodation does not cease to be available". Preventing a homelessness application is cheaper than discharging the duty that follows one.
- **Vacant possession preserved, section 32(4).** Nothing in the section 32(2) duty affects an authority's right to secure vacant possession, whether by contract or by enactment.

#### 2.6 The constraint the Supreme Court has settled

[Glasgow City Council v X (Scotland) [2025] UKSC 13](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/uksc/2025/13) concerned the interim duty under section 29(1) read with article 4(b) of the 2014 Order, and specifically whether interim accommodation is unsuitable unless it meets **all** the needs of the applicant and every member of the household.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the Inner House. The needs of the household must be **taken into account**, but they do not all have to be **met** at the interim stage: the household's need for a five-apartment property "had to be considered but did not have to be met at the interim stage" ([59]).

For this question the decision cuts in the Government's favour: the interim standard is less demanding than it might have been, and the room it leaves is created by the wording of a **ministerial order** that the Government can amend.

#### 2.7 What each option costs

| Lever | Instrument needed |
| --- | --- |
| Revoke, time-limit or narrow the suspension of section 33 referrals, including for named authorities only | Order under section 33A, with the section 33B statement kept up to date |
| Disapply the requirement that section 31(2) accommodation be permanent, in prescribed circumstances | Subordinate legislation prescribing those circumstances under section 32A |
| Widen the exemptions from the unsuitable accommodation standards | Order under section 29(3) |
| Vary prescribed advice, assistance or housing support, including for one area only | Regulations under ss.31(3)(b), 32(3), 32(6), 32B(5)-(6) |
| Remove or qualify the duty in section 31(2) to secure accommodation at all, the section 29(1) interim duty, or the section 24 definition of homelessness | An Act of the Scottish Parliament, unless a modification power attached to them elsewhere in the Act was missed here |

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Jurisdiction.** Scotland. Part II of the Housing (Scotland) Act 1987 as amended, and Scottish statutory instruments made under it.
- **Status.** SSI 2022/356 was in force at the date of research and had not been revoked in the retrieved text. Its duration should be re-checked before advice is given, since a suspension of this kind is the sort of provision that is periodically extended or allowed to lapse.
- **Limit of this answer.** Sets out the statutory levers and what instrument each needs. It does not assess whether any of them would be lawful in a particular case, compatible with the ECHR, or sound as policy.
- **Limit of this answer.** The Housing (Scotland) Act 1987 could not be found by a title search of the legislation service; its provisions were retrieved by identifier from the revised text.
- **Limit of this answer.** Whether anything has yet been prescribed under section 32A, and what circumstances it covers, was not established. The section is described here as an available power, not as one already exercised.
- **Limit of this answer.** Which form of subordinate legislation section 32A's "prescribed" refers to, and whether it can be confined to a single local authority, is not answered by section 32A itself and was not traced through the Act's general provisions.
- **Limit of this answer.** The list of ministerial powers here is what section searches surfaced, not a systematic sweep of Part II. Sections 32A and 33A were both missed by the first round of searches for this answer, so treat any statement that a change needs primary legislation as a prompt to check rather than as a conclusion.

question: What provision enables Scottish Ministers to establish a national bus fare cap scheme?
statements: Section 38 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 empowers the Scottish Ministers to make grants to operators of eligible bus services towards their costs in operating those services, and those grants may be made subject to such conditions as the Scottish Ministers determine.

Section 70 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 gives the Scottish Ministers a general power to make grants or loans to any persons for any purposes relating to transport, and is also available as a basis for a national fare cap scheme.

Section 3C(3)(b) of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 allows a bus services improvement partnership scheme to impose requirements about the maximum fares that may be charged, but that power is held by a local transport authority for its own area rather than by the Scottish Ministers nationally.

A national travel concession scheme under section 40 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2005 provides a reduced or waived fare to persons the Scottish Ministers specify as eligible, which is a different thing from a fare cap applying to passengers generally.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

Two different powers have to be told apart, and the question turns on the word **national**.

**An express maximum-fares power does exist**, at section 3C(3)(b) of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 ([asp/2001/2, s.3C](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/3C)): a bus services improvement partnership scheme may impose requirements about "the maximum fares that may be charged". But it belongs to a **local transport authority** for its own area, not to the Scottish Ministers, so it cannot produce a national scheme.

**For a national scheme the Scottish Ministers must use their grant powers.** The provision to cite is **section 38 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001** ([asp/2001/2, s.38](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/38)): Ministers may make grants to operators of eligible bus services, "subject to such conditions ... as the Scottish Ministers may determine". A cap on the fare charged is such a condition. **Section 70 of the same Act** ([asp/2001/2, s.70](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/70)) is a broader alternative: a general power to make grants or loans to any persons for any purposes relating to transport.

The concessionary travel powers are **not** the answer. A "travel concession" is statutorily defined as a reduction or waiver of the fare **for eligible persons**, which is a different instrument from a cap applying to passengers generally.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Section 38 of the 2001 Act, the operator grant power

> **Section 38 — Grants to bus service operators**
>
> (1) The Scottish Ministers may make grants to operators of eligible bus services towards their costs in operating those services.
> (2) The Scottish Ministers may make provision by regulations as to the method of calculation of grants.
> (3) Subject to any regulations under subsection (2) above, grants under this section shall be of such amount and **subject to such conditions** (including conditions requiring their repayment in specified circumstances) **as the Scottish Ministers may determine**.
> (4) A determination under subsection (3) above may be made either generally or in relation to particular cases or classes of case.
> (5) In this section "eligible bus services" means services of a class using public service vehicles (or such services using a class of public service vehicles) prescribed by regulations made by the Scottish Ministers.

([asp/2001/2, s.38](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/38))

Three features make this the natural vehicle for a fare cap:

- **Conditions are at large.** Subsection (3) does not enumerate permitted conditions. A requirement that a participating operator charge no more than a stated single fare is within the ordinary meaning of a condition of grant.
- **It can be applied generally.** Subsection (4) allows a determination to be made "either generally or in relation to particular cases or classes of case", which is what makes a scheme national rather than operator-by-operator.
- **Repayment is available as enforcement.** Subsection (3) expressly contemplates conditions requiring repayment, so a cap can be enforced by clawback without any further statutory machinery.

The limit is subsection (5): the power bites on "eligible bus services", a class prescribed by regulations. The scope of any cap is therefore bounded by those regulations.

#### 2.2 Section 70 of the 2001 Act, the general transport grant power

> **Section 70 — Grants for transport-related purposes**
>
> (1) The Scottish Ministers may make grants or loans to any persons for any purposes relating to transport.

([asp/2001/2, s.70](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/70))

This is wider than section 38 in two respects: the recipient is "any persons", not only operators of eligible bus services, and the purpose is "any purposes relating to transport", not only operating costs. Where a scheme's design falls outside the "eligible bus services" boundary in section 38(5), section 70 is the fallback. The remainder of the section (subsections (1A) to (1B)) concerns grants for acquiring land blighted by transport orders and is not relevant here.

#### 2.3 The express maximum-fares power, and why it is not national

Section 3C of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 governs the service standards a bus services improvement partnership scheme may impose:

> (3) An operational service standard may, in particular, impose requirements about —
>    (a) the vehicles which are used to provide services,
>    (b) **the maximum fares that may be charged** for particular journeys, or for journeys of particular descriptions on services to which the scheme applies,
>    (c) ticketing and the manner in which entitlement to travel may be evidenced,
>    (d) the pricing of multi-operator travel cards, ...

([asp/2001/2, s.3C](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/3C))

This is a direct power to cap fares, and it is worth citing for that reason. Two limits stop it answering the question as asked:

- **The holder is a local transport authority, not the Scottish Ministers.** A partnership scheme is made under section 3B alongside a partnership plan, and section 3A(1) provides that "**a local transport authority** may, if they consider it appropriate to do so, make a bus services improvement partnership plan ... in relation to the whole or part of their area" ([asp/2001/2, s.3A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/3A)).
- **The reach is the scheme's area.** Section 3C(5) provides that a service standard "has effect only in relation to so much of a local service as is provided in" the scheme area.

A national cap would therefore require every local transport authority to make a scheme in identical terms, rather than a single act of the Scottish Ministers. That is why the grant route in 2.1 and 2.2 is the answer to a question about a **national** scheme.

#### 2.4 What the concessionary travel powers do instead

Two powers create **travel concession schemes**, and neither creates a fare cap.

**Section 40 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2005** ([asp/2005/12, s.40](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2005/12/section/40)) lets the Scottish Ministers "by order, make national travel concession schemes", operating throughout Scotland or in part of it. The defined terms are decisive:

> (7) In this section —
> "**eligible person**" in relation to a national travel concession scheme, means a person who is of such description as the Scottish Ministers may by order specify;
> "**travel concession**", in relation to a journey, means — reduction of the fare ... for the journey below the amount applicable to an adult who is not entitled to any reduction; or waiver of such fare.

A concession is thus defined **by reference to an adult who is not entitled to any reduction**, whose fare the scheme leaves untouched. The instrument reduces or waives the fare for a specified class of person. It does not set a ceiling on what everyone else pays.

**Section 68 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001** ([asp/2001/2, s.68](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/68)) is the local counterpart: the Scottish Ministers may by order require a specified local transport authority, or two or more acting jointly, to make a travel concession scheme for a specified area. It is a power to direct authorities, over an area that is "the whole or any part of the area, or combined area" of those authorities, so it is not a route to a national scheme in its own right.

#### 2.5 A worked example of the concessionary route

The National Bus Travel Concession Scheme for Young Persons (Scotland) Order 2021 ([ssi/2021/175](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2021/175)) shows the concessionary machinery in operation. Article 3 provides that "This Order establishes a national travel concession scheme ... to be known as the National Bus Travel Concession Scheme for Young Persons", and article 2 defines "eligible journey" as having "the same meaning as in section 40(7) of the 2005 Act", confirming the Order operates under section 40 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2005.

Article 5 sets the rate: "The rate of travel concession in the scheme is to be a waiver of the fare". A total waiver for a specified group, not a cap for everyone, which is exactly the distinction in 2.4.

#### 2.6 The parallel with England

Section 38 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 is drawn in near-identical terms to **section 154 of the Transport Act 2000** ([ukpga/2000/38, s.154](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/154)), the England and Wales operator grant power, down to both provisions repealing section 92 of the Finance Act 1965 and section 111 of the Transport Act 1985. The two jurisdictions therefore reach a fare cap by the same statutory route, a conditional operator grant, under separate Acts.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Transport (Scotland) Act 2001 (asp 2) and the Transport (Scotland) Act 2005 (asp 12) both extend to Scotland only. The retrieval returned both in revised (as amended) form.
- **Status of the provisions cited.** Sections 38, 68 and 70 of the 2001 Act and section 40 of the 2005 Act were all returned as current revised text, with no indication of repeal.
- **Limit of this answer.** That the Scottish Ministers hold no power to fix bus fares nationally by order is a conclusion from the searches recorded in `searches.json`, which covered the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001, the Transport (Scotland) Act 2005 and Scottish concessionary travel instruments. It is a negative established by not finding such a power in that material, which is weaker evidence than a positive citation, and it is the point most worth a reviewer's attention. The express but local power at section 3C(3)(b) is by contrast positively established.
- **Out of scope.** Whether any fare cap has actually been established in Scotland, and on what terms, is a question of policy and administrative action rather than legislation, and the legislation database cannot answer it.

---

### 4. References

- [Transport (Scotland) Act 2001, s.3C — Partnership schemes: service standards](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/3C)
- [Transport (Scotland) Act 2001, s.38 — Grants to bus service operators](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/38)
- [Transport (Scotland) Act 2001, s.68 — Travel concession schemes](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/68)
- [Transport (Scotland) Act 2001, s.70 — Grants for transport-related purposes](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/70)
- [Transport (Scotland) Act 2005, s.40 — National travel concession schemes](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2005/12/section/40)
- [The National Bus Travel Concession Scheme for Young Persons (Scotland) Order 2021](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2021/175)

question: What legislation and specific provision did UK Ministers use to establish the £3 bus fare cap scheme in England?
statements: Section 154 of the Transport Act 2000 empowers the Secretary of State, with the approval of the Treasury as respects England, to make grants to operators of eligible bus services towards their costs in operating those services.

Section 154(3) of the Transport Act 2000 allows those grants to be of such amount and subject to such conditions as the Secretary of State determines, which is the mechanism by which a maximum single fare is imposed on participating operators.

Section 113E(5)(a) of the Transport Act 2000 allows an advanced quality partnership scheme to specify requirements as to the maximum fares that may be charged, but that power is held by a local transport authority for the services its scheme covers rather than by the Secretary of State nationally.
The £3 fare cap operates through conditions attached to grant funding rather than through a statutory instrument that fixes fares.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

The provision is **section 154 of the Transport Act 2000** ([ukpga/2000/38, s.154](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/154)).

It empowers the Secretary of State, with the approval of the Treasury as respects England, to make grants to operators of eligible bus services towards their costs in operating those services. Critically, subsection (3) provides that such grants are "of such amount and **subject to such conditions** ... as may be determined by" the Secretary of State. The fare cap is **a condition of that grant funding**, so there is no statutory instrument establishing it.

The Act does contain **express maximum-fares powers**, and they should be distinguished rather than overlooked. Section 113E(5)(a) lets an advanced quality partnership scheme specify "requirements as to the maximum fares that may be charged" ([ukpga/2000/38, s.113E](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/113E)), and a local service contract under a franchising scheme fixes terms "including in particular as to frequency, **fares** and standard of service" ([ukpga/2000/38, s.123A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/123A)). Both belong to **local transport authorities** over their own areas, not to the Secretary of State, so neither can deliver a national cap. That is why a nationwide scheme runs on grant conditions instead.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Section 154, the operative provision

> **Section 154 — Grants to bus service operators**
>
> (1) The Secretary of State with the approval of the Treasury (as respects England) or the National Assembly for Wales (as respects Wales) may make grants to operators of eligible bus services towards their costs in operating those services.
> (2) The Secretary of State ... may make provision by regulations as to the method of calculation of grants.
> (3) Subject to the provisions of any such regulations, grants under this section shall be of such amount and **subject to such conditions** (including conditions requiring their repayment in specified circumstances) as may be determined by —
>    (a) the Secretary of State with the approval of the Treasury (as respects England), or
>    (b) the National Assembly for Wales (as respects Wales).
> (4) A determination under subsection (3) may be made either generally or in relation to particular cases or classes of case.
> (5) In this section "eligible bus services" means bus services of a class (or using vehicles of a class) prescribed by regulations made by the Secretary of State (as respects England) or the National Assembly for Wales (as respects Wales).

([ukpga/2000/38, s.154](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/154))

Four features of the section carry the scheme:

- **The condition power is unenumerated (subsection (3)).** Nothing narrows what a condition of grant may require, so a maximum single fare is within it.
- **A determination can be made generally (subsection (4)).** This is what makes a scheme national in effect rather than a series of individual funding decisions.
- **Enforcement is by repayment (subsection (3)).** Conditions "requiring their repayment in specified circumstances" are expressly contemplated, so an operator that breaches the cap can be made to repay. No separate enforcement provision is needed.
- **Treasury approval is a precondition as respects England (subsections (1) and (3)(a)).** It is part of the power, not an administrative formality.

The boundary of the power is subsection (5): it operates on "eligible bus services", a class prescribed by regulations, so the cap reaches only services within that prescribed class.

#### 2.2 The express maximum-fares powers, and why they are not national

**Advanced quality partnership schemes.** Section 113E(5) provides:

> (5) The standard of services which may be specified in a scheme may also include —
>    (a) **requirements as to the maximum fares that may be charged** for particular journeys, or for journeys of particular descriptions, on services to which the scheme applies,
>    (b) requirements as to the ways in which passengers may pay for journeys, ...

([ukpga/2000/38, s.113E](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/113E))

Three limits keep this out of the answer to the question as asked:

- **The holder is a local transport authority.** Section 113C(1) provides that "a local transport authority whose area is in England, or two or more such authorities acting jointly, may make an advanced quality partnership scheme" ([ukpga/2000/38, s.113C](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/113C)).
- **Operators hold a veto.** Section 113E(7): a scheme "may include a requirement falling within subsection (4)(b) or (5)(a) only if there are **no admissible objections** to the requirement from relevant operators."
- **The reach is the scheme's services**, not the country.

The Secretary of State's role here is confined to making regulations about the content or operation of schemes containing such a requirement (s.113N(1)(b)(i)), not to setting fares.

**Franchising schemes.** Section 123A(5)(b) defines a local service contract as one under which the operator "undertakes to provide the local services on such terms (including in particular as to frequency, **fares** and standard of service) as may be specified". Again the power is the franchising authority's, and section 123A(4) defines that as "a local transport authority whose area is in England".

#### 2.3 Why the national cap is a grant condition and not an instrument

The searches recorded in `searches.json` covered the Transport Act 2000, the Transport Act 1985 and the Concessionary Bus Travel Act 2007, and returned no provision empowering **the Secretary of State** to set, cap or otherwise fix the fare a bus passenger is charged nationwide. Central government's powers over fares are exercised by **funding** (section 154, and section 154A below) or by **conferring a concession on a class of person** (2.4 below); the direct fare-fixing powers in 2.2 sit with local transport authorities.

That is the structural reason the answer to this question is a section of an Act plus a funding condition, rather than a named statutory instrument. A reader looking for an SI called something like "The Bus Fare Cap Regulations" will not find one, and its absence is not evidence that the citation is wrong.

#### 2.4 The concessionary regime is a different mechanism

The Concessionary Bus Travel Act 2007 ([ukpga/2007/13](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2007/13)) creates "the national concession" (s.1), with reimbursement of operators (s.3) and a power to vary its scope (s.8). Section 145A of the Transport Act 2000 ([ukpga/2000/38, s.145A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/145A)) provides for mandatory concessions in England for journeys not beginning on the London bus network.

A concession is an **entitlement held by a class of eligible person** (in the national concession's case, older and disabled passengers), reimbursed to the operator. A fare cap changes the maximum price payable by **any** passenger on a participating service. The two regimes are funded and enforced differently and should not be conflated.

#### 2.5 The parallel local grant power

**Section 154A of the Transport Act 2000** ([ukpga/2000/38, s.154A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2000/38/section/154A)) gives a local transport authority whose area is in England power to make grants to operators of local services with one or more stopping places in its area. Subsection (3) mirrors section 154(3): grants are "of such amount and subject to such conditions (including conditions requiring their repayment in specified circumstances) as may be determined by the authority".

Where the authority is a mayoral combined authority or mayoral CCA, subsections (4) and (5) make the function exercisable only by the mayor on the authority's behalf. Subsections (6) to (8) let the Secretary of State issue guidance, to which authorities and mayors must have regard.

Section 154A matters for this question because it means a capped fare in a particular area may rest on the **local** authority's power rather than on section 154. A national cap funded by central government rests on section 154.

#### 2.6 The parallel with Scotland

Section 154 is drawn in near-identical terms to **section 38 of the Transport (Scotland) Act 2001** ([asp/2001/2, s.38](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2001/2/section/38)), down to both provisions repealing section 92 of the Finance Act 1965 and section 111 of the Transport Act 1985. The equivalent Scottish question is therefore answered by the same statutory route under a different Act, with section 70 of the 2001 Act available as a wider alternative that section 154 does not have a direct counterpart to.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Transport Act 2000 is stated as extending to the United Kingdom, but section 154 is drawn on its face as an England and Wales provision, allocating the power between the Secretary of State (as respects England) and the National Assembly for Wales (as respects Wales). The Concessionary Bus Travel Act 2007 extends to England and Wales. This answer addresses England only.
- **Status of the provisions cited.** Sections 154, 154A and 145A of the Transport Act 2000 were returned as current revised text, with no indication of repeal. Section 154A and the mayoral CCA references in it are later insertions.
- **Limit of this answer.** That the Secretary of State holds no power to fix bus fares nationally is a negative established by not finding one across the three Acts searched. It is weaker evidence than a positive citation, and it is the proposition most worth a reviewer's attention. The express but local powers at sections 113E(5)(a) and 123A(5)(b) are by contrast positively established.
- **Out of scope.** The amount of funding allocated, the operators participating, the dates the £2 and then £3 caps ran, and the departmental announcements establishing them are administrative rather than legislative and cannot be confirmed from the legislation database.

---

question: are there any requirements for the level of vitamins in margarine for sale in Scotland?
statements: The requirements for margarine sold by retail in Scotland are in regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats, Milk and Milk Products (Scotland) Regulations 2008.

Margarine sold by retail in Scotland must contain, in every 100 grams, not less than 800 and not more than 1,000 micrograms of vitamin A, and not less than 7.05 and not more than 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D, with a proportionate amount in any part of 100 grams.

The Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) (Scotland) Regulations 1999 are the predecessor instrument and were revoked by the 2008 Regulations, so the 1999 Regulations are not the current source of the requirement.
Contravention of the vitamin content requirement is an offence under regulation 6 of the 2008 Regulations, enforced by food authorities under regulation 5.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

Yes. The requirement is in **regulation 4 of the Spreadable Fats, Milk and Milk Products (Scotland) Regulations 2008** ([ssi/2008/216](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/4)).

Margarine sold by retail in Scotland must contain, in every 100 grams:

- **vitamin A:** not less than 800 and not more than 1,000 micrograms
- **vitamin D:** not less than 7.05 and not more than 8.82 micrograms

with a proportionate amount in any part of 100 grams. Contravention is an offence under regulation 6, enforced by food authorities under regulation 5.

The instrument to cite is the **2008** Scottish Regulations. The Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) (Scotland) Regulations 1999 are their revoked predecessor and are not the current source of the rule.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The requirement

> **Regulation 4 — Vitamin content of margarine**
> No person may sell by retail any margarine unless it contains in every 100 grams —
> (a) not less than 800 micrograms and not more than 1,000 micrograms of vitamin A; and
> (b) not less than 7.05 micrograms and not more than 8.82 micrograms of vitamin D,
> and a proportionate amount in any part of 100 grams.

([ssi/2008/216, reg 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/4))

The obligation is framed as a prohibition on **retail sale**, not on manufacture or import, so it bites at the point of sale to the consumer.

#### 2.2 Offence, enforcement and exemptions

- **Offence and penalty:** regulation 6 ([ssi/2008/216, reg 6](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/6)).
- **Enforcement:** regulation 5, by food authorities ([reg 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/5)).
- **Exemptions:** regulation 3 ([reg 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/3)).
- **Revocations and transitional provision:** regulations 8 and 9 ([reg 8](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2008/216/regulation/8)).

#### 2.3 The 1999 Regulations are the predecessor, not the current rule

The Spreadable Fats (Marketing Standards) (Scotland) Regulations 1999 contained a materially identical regulation 4 ([ssi/1999/34, reg 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/1999/34/regulation/4)), with its own offence, enforcement and revocation provisions. They were superseded by the 2008 Regulations, whose regulation 8 deals with revocations.

Because the figures are the same in both, an answer citing the 1999 Regulations will state the **right numbers from the wrong instrument**. That is a citation error rather than a substantive one, but it is the error to watch for here.

#### 2.4 Contrast with England

The equivalent English requirement was **removed in 2013**: regulation 3(4) of the Environmental Noise, Site Waste Management Plans and Spreadable Fats etc. (Revocations and Amendments) Regulations 2013 omitted regulation 4 of the England Regulations ([uksi/2013/2854, reg 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2013/2854/regulation/3)). The Scottish requirement was untouched by that instrument. An answer that reasons from the English position to Scotland will get this backwards.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The 2008 Regulations extend to Scotland (regulation 1, citation, commencement and extent). The database returned them in revised form.
- **Currency.** Regulation 4 was returned as current operative text, unlike its English counterpart, which returns as omitted.

---

### 4. References

question: Can the requirements under section 35A and section 35ZA of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 be run concurrently?
statements: The requirements under section 35A and section 35ZA of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 can run concurrently.

Section 35ZA requires the Scottish Ministers to carry out a public consultation, for a period of no less than 6 months, to inform the proposals and policies to be set out in a climate change plan laid under section 35(1)(b), and to lay a statement about that consultation before the Parliament beforehand.

Section 35A requires the Scottish Ministers, before laying a climate change plan under section 35, to lay a draft of the plan before the Parliament for 120 days, of which no fewer than 60 must be days on which the Parliament is not dissolved or in recess.

Both sections are expressed as preconditions of the same event, the laying of the plan under section 35, and neither is expressed as a precondition of the other, so neither contains language displacing the other.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**Yes, they can run concurrently.**

Both sections are drafted as preconditions of the **same event**, the laying of a climate change plan under section 35. Neither is expressed as a precondition of the other, and neither contains any language of displacement or sequencing that would require one procedure to finish before the other begins.

- **Section 35ZA** requires a public consultation of **no less than 6 months** to inform the proposals and policies to be set out in the plan, with a statement laid before the Parliament first.
- **Section 35A** requires a **draft** of the plan to be laid before the Parliament for **120 days**, of which no fewer than 60 must be sitting days.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Section 35ZA, the consultation stage

> **Section 35ZA - Preparation of climate change plan: public consultation**
> (1) The Scottish Ministers must carry out a public consultation to inform the proposals and policies to be set out in a climate change plan laid under section 35(1)(b).
> (2) Before carrying out a consultation under subsection (1), the Scottish Ministers must lay a statement before the Parliament setting out -
>    (a) the methodologies the Scottish Ministers plan to use to consult ...
>    (c) the period of time for which the Scottish Ministers plan to consult, **which must be a period no less than 6 months**,
>    (d) such other information as the Scottish Ministers consider appropriate.

([asp/2009/12, s.35ZA](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/35ZA))

The consultation is tied to the plan **"laid under section 35(1)(b)"**, that is, to the final laying. It is not tied to the section 35A draft.

#### 2.2 Section 35A, the draft scrutiny stage

> **Section 35A - Climate change plan: further procedure**
> (1) The Scottish Ministers must, **before laying a climate change plan under section 35** before the Scottish Parliament -
>    (a) lay a draft of the plan before the Parliament for a period of 120 days, of which no fewer than 60 must be days on which the Parliament is not dissolved or in recess,
>    (aa) request the views of such persons as they consider appropriate with [specified expertise],
>    (b) have regard to - (i) any representations on the draft plan made to them, (ii) any views ... (iii) any resolution relating to the draft plan passed by the Parliament, and (iv) any report relating to the draft plan published by any committee ...

([asp/2009/12, s.35A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/35A))

Subsection (1A) additionally requires Ministers to publish a response to any such resolution or committee report.

#### 2.3 Why they can run together

**Both are preconditions of the same act.** Section 35ZA(1) attaches to the plan "laid under section 35(1)(b)"; section 35A(1) attaches to the moment "before laying a climate change plan under section 35". The gateway each guards is the laying of the plan, not the other procedure.

**Neither refers to the other.** Section 35A does not require the section 35ZA consultation to have concluded, and section 35ZA does not require the section 35A draft period to be complete or not yet begun. Neither contains "after", "once", or any comparable sequencing word directed at the other section.

**Nothing in the subject matter forces an order.** Section 35ZA informs "the proposals and policies to be set out in" the plan, and section 35A subjects a draft to parliamentary scrutiny and requires Ministers to have regard to representations. Both are inputs to the same final document, and Ministers can be receiving consultation responses and parliamentary representations over overlapping periods, having regard to both when settling the plan.

**The practical reading.** Running the 6-month consultation and the 120-day draft period concurrently is permissible on the text. What Ministers cannot do is lay the plan under section 35 before both have been completed, because each is independently a precondition of that act.

#### 2.4 The contrary reading, and why it does not hold

It can be argued that a consultation which "informs the proposals and policies to be set out in" the plan must logically precede a draft that already contains those proposals and policies, so the two must be sequential. That reasoning has intuitive force but no textual anchor: it derives a mandatory order from the subject matter rather than from words in either section, and section 35A(1)(b) expressly contemplates Ministers continuing to receive and have regard to input after the draft is laid. An answer that concludes the sections must be sequential is reading in a restriction the Act does not impose.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009 extends to Scotland. Both sections were returned as current revised text.
- **Insertion history.** Both sections are later insertions into the 2009 Act, which is why they carry the 35ZA and 35A numbering. Which interpretation regime governs the Act as a result is addressed separately, in the answer to question 15.
- **Limit of this answer.** This is a question of construction on which the text does not speak directly. The conclusion rests on the absence of sequencing language plus the shared gateway in section 35, which is a strong but not conclusive basis.

---

### 4. References

- [Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, s.35 - Climate change plan](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/35)
- [Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, s.35ZA - Preparation of climate change plan: public consultation](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/35ZA)
- [Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, s.35A - Climate change plan: further procedure](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2009/12/section/35A)
