question: I am looking at the process for the reporting and publishing of Scottish Water's annual and interim reports and accounts. I am wanting to create a basic timeline of the statutory requirements of various actors including Scottish Water, the Scottish Ministers and the Auditor under the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 and the Public Finances and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000. I also want a more detailed note on each step and what each report and set of accounts is required to contain. Can you provide me with this information?
statements: Section 45(1) of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 requires Scottish Water to keep proper accounts and accounting records, to prepare for each financial year a statement of accounts giving a true and fair view of the state of its affairs and its income and expenditure, and to send that statement to the Auditor General for Scotland for auditing by such time as the Scottish Ministers may direct, with section 45(2) requiring the statement to comply with any ministerial direction as to its content, presentation and the methods and principles used.

Section 21(2) of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000 requires an account that must be sent to the Auditor General for auditing to be sent not later than 6 months after the end of the financial year to which it relates, which supplies the deadline the 2002 Act leaves to direction.

Section 57(3) of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 requires Scottish Water to prepare a report on its activities from the beginning of each financial year to 30 September in that year and a report on its activities for the whole of each financial year, as soon as practicable after the end of the period to which the report relates, with section 57(4) requiring the interim report to include a statement of accounts for that period and section 57(5) requiring the whole-year report to describe how Scottish Water complied with its duties under sections 26, 28, 50 and 51 and the reasons for any failure under sections 26 and 28.

Section 57(6) of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 requires Scottish Water to send a copy of each report to the Scottish Ministers, the Commission, every water services provider and sewerage services provider and Consumer Scotland, and to publish the report, and section 57(8) requires the Scottish Ministers to lay a copy before the Parliament.

Section 22(5) of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000 requires the Scottish Ministers to lay before the Parliament every account and report sent to them by the Auditor General and, except where they have been published by Scottish Water, to publish them, not later than 9 months after the end of the financial year to which the account relates.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

There are **two tracks**, and the question asks about both.

- **Accounts.** Section 45 of the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002, with the deadline supplied by section 21(2) of the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000.
- **Reports.** Section 57 of the 2002 Act, which carries the interim report to 30 September, the whole-year report, what each must contain, who gets a copy, publication, and laying before the Parliament.

An answer that reads section 45 alone covers the accounts and misses the reporting timetable entirely.

Cited to the subsection that carries each requirement:

| Requirement | Timing | Provision |
|---|---|---|
| Keep proper accounts and accounting records | continuing | 2002 Act, **s.45(1)(a)** |
| Prepare a statement of accounts for each financial year giving a true and fair view | each financial year | 2002 Act, **s.45(1)(b)** |
| Comply with Ministers' directions on content, presentation, and methods and principles | as prepared | 2002 Act, **s.45(2)(a)-(c)** |
| Send that statement to the Auditor General for Scotland for auditing | by such time as Ministers direct, and in any event **not later than 6 months** after the year end | 2002 Act, **s.45(1)(c)**; 2000 Act, **s.21(2)** |
| Audit by the Auditor General or a qualified person | after receipt | 2000 Act, **s.21(3)** |
| Auditor's report to set out findings on regularity | on reporting | 2000 Act, **s.22(1)** |
| Prepare an interim report on activities from the start of the year to **30 September** | as soon as practicable after 30 September | 2002 Act, **s.57(3)(a)** |
| Prepare a report on activities for the **whole** financial year | as soon as practicable after the year end | 2002 Act, **s.57(3)(b)** |
| Send a copy of each report to Ministers, the Commission, providers and Consumer Scotland, and **publish** it | on preparation | 2002 Act, **s.57(6)** |
| **Lay** a copy of each report before the Parliament | on receipt (Scottish Ministers) | 2002 Act, **s.57(8)** |
| **Lay** the account and audit reports before the Parliament, and publish them unless Scottish Water has already published them | **not later than 9 months** after the year end | 2000 Act, **s.22(5)** |

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Section 45(1): the three duties

> **Section 45 - Accounts and audit**
> (1) Scottish Water must -
>    **(a)** keep proper accounts and accounting records,
>    **(b)** prepare for each financial year a statement of accounts giving a true and fair view of the state of its affairs and its income and expenditure, and
>    **(c)** send the statement of accounts, **by such time as the Scottish Ministers may direct**, to the Auditor General for Scotland for auditing.

([asp/2002/3, s.45](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/section/45))

These are three distinct obligations, not one: a continuing record-keeping duty (a), an annual preparation duty with a substantive standard, "a true and fair view" (b), and a transmission duty (c).

#### 2.2 Section 45(2): what Ministers may direct about the statement

> (2) Every statement of accounts prepared by Scottish Water in accordance with this section must comply with any direction given by the Scottish Ministers relating to -
>    **(a)** the information to be contained in the statement of accounts,
>    **(b)** the manner in which that information is to be presented, or
>    **(c)** the methods and principles according to which the statement of accounts is to be prepared.

Subsection (2) is what makes the content of the statement largely a matter of ministerial direction rather than of the Act. An answer that asks "what must the accounts contain?" and looks only at the 2002 Act will find the direction-making power, not a list.

#### 2.3 The deadline is in the 2000 Act, not the 2002 Act

Section 45(1)(c) fixes no date; it defers to ministerial direction. The backstop is general:

> **Section 21 - Audit of accounts**
> (1) This section and section 22 apply in relation to any account which is, by virtue of any enactment or prerogative instrument, required (in whatever words) to be - ... (b) **sent to the Auditor General for auditing**.
> **(2) The account must be sent to the Auditor General not later than 6 months after the end of the financial year to which the account relates.**
> (3) The account is to be audited by - (a) the Auditor General, or (b) a qualified person appearing to the Auditor General to be suitable for appointment to audit the account ...

([asp/2000/1, s.21](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/21))

Section 45(1)(c) is an enactment requiring an account to be sent to the Auditor General for auditing, so section 21(1)(b) is engaged and section 21(2) applies. A ministerial direction under section 45(1)(c) may set an earlier date but cannot go beyond the 6 months.

#### 2.4 What the auditor must report on

Section 22(1) requires the auditor's report to set out findings on whether the expenditure and receipts shown in the account were incurred or applied in accordance with the enactment authorising them, the Budget Act or Acts for the year, and sections 4 to 7 of the 2000 Act; and, where sums were paid out of the Scottish Consolidated Fund to meet that expenditure, whether they were applied accordingly ([asp/2000/1, s.22](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/22)).

This is a regularity audit sitting alongside the true and fair requirement in section 45(1)(b).

---

#### 2.5 The reporting track: section 57

Section 45 is about accounts. The reports the question asks about are in section 57, and there are two of them:

> **Section 57 - Information and reports**
> (3) Scottish Water must prepare -
>    (a) a report on its activities during the period from the beginning of each financial year **to 30th September** in that year, and
>    (b) a report on its activities during **the whole of each financial year**,
> as soon as practicable after the end of the period to which the report relates.
> (4) A report prepared under subsection (3)(a) **must include a statement of accounts** for the period to which the report relates; and subsection (2) of section 45 applies to such a statement of accounts as it applies to a statement of accounts prepared in accordance with that section.
> (5) A report prepared under subsection (3)(b) must include -
>    (a) a description of the manner in which Scottish Water has complied ... with its duties under **sections 26, 28, 50 and 51**, and
>    (b) the reasons for any failure ... to comply with its duties under sections 26 and 28.
> (6) Scottish Water must -
>    (a) send a copy of each report prepared under subsection (3) to the Scottish Ministers, the Commission, every water services provider and sewerage services provider and Consumer Scotland, and
>    (b) **publish** the report.
> (7) A report prepared under subsection (3) must set out - (a) any directions under section 56 given to Scottish Water during the period, and (b) the extent to which Scottish Water has complied with any requirements made under section 13(2) or 15(1) or (5) of the Water Services etc. (Scotland) Act 2005.
> (8) **The Scottish Ministers must lay a copy of a report sent to them under subsection (6) before the Parliament.**

([asp/2002/3, s.57](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/3/section/57))

Three points that a timeline has to carry. The **interim** report is dated to 30 September and, uniquely, must itself contain a statement of accounts, prepared to the same ministerial directions as the annual one under section 45(2). The **content** requirements for the whole-year report are express, not left to direction: compliance with sections 26, 28, 50 and 51 and the reasons for any failure under sections 26 and 28. And publication and laying are both duties here: Scottish Water publishes under section 57(6)(b), the Scottish Ministers lay under section 57(8).

#### 2.6 The last dated step: laying and publishing the account

> **Section 22 - Audit of accounts: further provisions**
> (4) The Auditor General must send to the Scottish Ministers the account, the auditor's report on the account and any report prepared by the Auditor General under subsection (3) **in sufficient time to enable the Scottish Ministers to comply with subsection (5)**.
> (5) The Scottish Ministers must -
>    (a) **lay before the Parliament** a copy of every account and report sent to them under subsection (4), and
>    (b) except where the account and the report are published by the body or office-holder in question, **publish** every such account and report, **not later than 9 months after the end of the financial year** to which the account relates.

([asp/2000/1, s.22](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2000/1/section/22))

This closes the accounts track: 6 months to the Auditor General under section 21(2), then 9 months to laying and publication under section 22(5). Section 22(5)(b) makes the Ministers' publication duty a fallback, biting only where Scottish Water has not published the account and report itself.

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** Both Acts extend to Scotland and were returned in revised form.
- **Publication and laying.** Section 45 itself requires only preparation and transmission to the Auditor General. The publication and laying duties sit elsewhere: section 57(6)(b) and 57(8) of the 2002 Act for the reports, and section 22(5) of the 2000 Act for the account and the audit reports.
- **Relationship to question 7.** That question asks the same shape of question about the Water Industry Commission for Scotland without naming the Public Finance and Accountability (Scotland) Act 2000. Here the user names it. The 6-month deadline in section 21(2) is the same in both.

question: is the care reform (Scotland) Act 2025 in force?
statements: The Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 is partly in force: section 30 and the final Part came into force the day after Royal Assent under section 39(1), and the remaining provisions come into force on days appointed by the Scottish Ministers by regulations under section 39(2).

The Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1) Regulations 2025 (SSI 2025/388) have been made under section 39(2), so an answer stating that no commencement regulations have been made is wrong.

SSI 2025/388 commenced sections 1, 9(1) and (2), 10(1) and (2), 11, 13, 14 (except for the insertion of section 78G of the Public Services Reform (Scotland) Act 2010), 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 33 and 34 on 7 January 2026, section 14 for its remaining purposes on 31 March 2026, sections 31 and 32 on 1 April 2026, and section 36 on 30 April 2026.
The Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 22 July 2025, so the provisions commenced by section 39(1) came into force on 23 July 2025.
Answering whether the Act is in force requires checking for commencement regulations made under section 39(2), not just reading the commencement section itself.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**Partly.** The Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 is **not** wholly in force, and it is **not** wholly uncommenced.

The Act received Royal Assent on **22 July 2025**. Section 39 brought **section 30 and the final Part into force on 23 July 2025**, the day after. Everything else comes into force only when the Scottish Ministers appoint a day by regulations.

The failure this question exists to catch is stopping there. Reading section 39 tells you the substantive provisions await commencement regulations. It does **not** tell you whether those regulations have since been made. **They have.** The **Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1) Regulations 2025, SSI 2025/388**, made 4 December 2025, appointed four further commencement dates, all of which have now passed. Most of the Act's substantive provisions are in force.

An answer that reads section 39 and then volunteers that no commencement regulations have been made turns a failed search into a false negative, on a question where the user is relying on the answer to know whether a duty currently binds them.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The commencement provision

> **Section 39 - Commencement**
> (1) The following come into force on the day after Royal Assent: **section 30 and this Part**.
> (2) The other provisions of this Act come into force on such day as **the Scottish Ministers may by regulations appoint**.

([asp/2025/9, s.39](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/39))

The Act's own metadata records an enactment date of **22 July 2025**, so subsection (1) operated on **23 July 2025**. The Act has 56 provisions and is held in revised form with Scotland extent.

Section 39 splits the Act into two populations:

| Population | Status | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Section 30, and the Part containing section 39 (the final, general Part: [s.37 Ancillary provision](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/37), [s.38 Regulation-making powers](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/38), s.39 itself and [s.40 Short title](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/40)) | **In force 23 July 2025** | s.39(1) |
| All other provisions, including the substantive care reform duties | In force **only when appointed** by regulations | s.39(2) |

Subsection (2) is where the answer is decided, and SSI 2025/388 is the instrument that decides it.

Note the shape of subsection (1). It commences the machinery, the ancillary provision power and the short title, plus one substantive section. This is the ordinary pattern for a Scottish Act, and it is exactly the pattern that misleads: an Act can be "commenced" in the sense that some of it is live while none of the provisions a user cares about are.

#### 2.2 The commencement instrument: SSI 2025/388

Section 39(2) is a **pointer to a further instrument**, not an answer. The instrument is the Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1) Regulations 2025, **SSI 2025/388 (C. 31)**, made 4 December 2025, laid 8 December 2025, in force 7 January 2026. It appoints four dates:

| Date appointed | Provisions | Authority in the instrument |
|---|---|---|
| **7 January 2026** | ss.1, 9(1) and (2), 10(1) and (2), 11, 13, 14 (all purposes except the insertion of s.78G of the Public Services Reform (Scotland) Act 2010), 16, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 33, 34 | reg.2(1) and Part 1 of the schedule |
| **31 March 2026** | s.14, for all remaining purposes | reg.2(3) |
| **1 April 2026** | ss.31 and 32 | reg.2(4) and Part 2 of the schedule |
| **30 April 2026** | s.36 | reg.2(5) |

All four dates have passed, so those provisions are now in force. What is left uncommenced is everything not in that list and not commenced by section 39(1).

#### 2.3 Why this instrument is hard to reach, and what that means

**SSI 2025/388 is not in the LEX corpus.** Retrieving it by identifier returns HTTP 404, and none of the four searches run here reached it, by full title, by short title, or by subject. Its terms above are taken from the official text at [legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2025/388](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2025/388), not from the research tools.

The retrieval makes the shape of the gap concrete. The same searches readily returned commencement instruments for two other Acts of the same session:

- The Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1) Regulations 2025 (`ssi/2025/106`)
- The Victims, Witnesses, and Justice Reform (Scotland) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1 and Transitional Provision) Regulations 2025 (`ssi/2025/393`)

So the search tool does surface commencement SSIs when it holds them. It does not hold this one. That is a **corpus gap, not a research failure**, and it is a real finding about this question: a response working only from these tools cannot reach the correct current answer. It is still the correct current answer, and the reference states it.

#### 2.4 How the answer should be framed

- **Correct.** "Partly in force. Section 30 and the final Part came into force on 23 July 2025. SSI 2025/388 then commenced most of the substantive provisions on 7 January 2026, with section 14 completed on 31 March 2026, sections 31 and 32 on 1 April 2026 and section 36 on 30 April 2026."
- **Acceptable.** The same, saying plainly which provisions could not be confirmed.
- **Wrong.** "The substantive provisions are not in force and no commencement regulations have been made."

The difference between the second and the third is one clause, and it is the whole question: **not found** is a fact about the search, **not made** is a claim about the law, and here the claim would be false.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** Scotland. `asp/2025/9`, held in revised form, 56 provisions, extent Scotland.
- **Royal Assent.** 22 July 2025, so section 39(1) took effect 23 July 2025.
- **Currency.** Commencement is a moving target. This answer states the position as at 10 September 2026, on the basis of SSI 2025/388. A further Commencement No. 2 or later instrument may since have been made, and a correct answer says which day it speaks as at.
- **Source of the commencement detail.** SSI 2025/388 is not held by the LEX corpus, so its terms come from the official text at legislation.gov.uk. Everything about the Act itself, sections 37 to 40 included, is from the retrieval.
- **Not addressed.** Which provisions remain uncommenced is not listed exhaustively here; the instrument's schedule lists what was commenced, and everything else outside section 39(1) awaits a further instrument.

---

### 4. References

- [Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025, s.39 - Commencement](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/39)
- [Care Reform (Scotland) Act 2025, s.37 - Ancillary provision](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/9/section/37)

final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**Partly.** The Social Security (Amendment) (Scotland) Act 2025 (**2025 asp 2**) is in force in part, and the answer must say which parts.

Three commencement steps have happened:

| Step | Provisions | When | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Act commenced itself | ss.24, 25, 26, 27 and 28 | day after Royal Assent | [s.27(1)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/27) |
| Commencement No. 1 | ss.**2, 9, 17, 20, 21, 22 and 23** | **10 May 2025** | SSI 2025/119 |
| Commencement No. 2 | **s.18**, for the consultation purpose only | **15 December 2025** | SSI 2025/377 |

Everything else awaits further regulations under section 27(2). So substantive provisions, including the section 17 inflation uprating duty, **are** in force, and an answer saying the substantive provisions all await commencement is wrong.

The failure this question exists to catch is not a wrong date. It is **not finding the Act at all**, including after being handed its full title and the citation 2025 asp 2, and then not finding the commencement instruments. An answer that reports the Act does not exist, or that its commencement cannot be established, is wrong on both counts.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 The Act exists and is retrievable

The Act is held as `asp/2025/2`, **Social Security (Amendment) (Scotland) Act 2025**, in revised form, extent Scotland. Its section 28 confirms the short title:

> **Section 28 - Short title**
> The short title of this Act is the Social Security (Amendment) (Scotland) Act 2025.

([asp/2025/2, s.28](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/28))

This is worth stating plainly because the recorded failure was a claim that the Act could not be found. It can be, by title and by identifier.

#### 2.2 What the Act commenced itself

> **Section 27 - Commencement**
> (1) This section and **sections 24, 25, 26 and 28** come into force on the day after Royal Assent.
> (2) The other provisions of this Act come into force on **such day as the Scottish Ministers may by regulations appoint**.
> (3) Regulations under this section may - (a) include transitional, transitory or saving provision, (b) make different provision for different purposes.

([asp/2025/2, s.27](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/27))

Subsection (1) commences only the tail of the Act: [s.25 Ancillary provision](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/25), [s.26 Regulation-making powers](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/26), s.27 itself and [s.28 Short title](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/28), plus s.24. **None of the substantive social security provisions is commenced by section 27(1).**

Subsection (3)(b) matters for how the answer must be phrased. Because regulations may "make different provision for different purposes", a provision can be in force for some purposes and not others. "Is the Act in force?" therefore has no single yes or no answer, and a correct response says so.

#### 2.3 The commencement instruments

**SSI 2025/119**, the Social Security (Amendment) (Scotland) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 1 and Saving and Transitional Provisions) Regulations 2025, brings **sections 2, 9, 17, 20, 21, 22 and 23** into force on **10 May 2025**. Retrieving it by identifier returns HTTP 200 with the instrument's title and description but **no section text**, so its effect is established from that description:

> These Regulations bring sections 2, 9, 17, 20, 21, 22, and 23 of the Social Security (Scotland) (Amendment) Act 2025 ("the Act") into force on 10 May 2025.

Those sections can be matched to their subject matter from the Act itself:

- [s.2 Care experience assistance](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/2)
- [s.17 Duty to uprate assistance for inflation](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/17)
- [s.20 Scrutiny of regulations by the Commission](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/20)
- [s.21 Removal of Commission's status as body corporate](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2025/2/section/21)

Because the section text was not returned, the **saving and transitional provisions** the instrument also contains could not be read, and their effect is not stated here.

**SSI 2025/377**, the Commencement No. 2 Regulations 2025, brings **section 18** into force on **15 December 2025 for one purpose only**: enabling the Scottish Ministers to consult in accordance with section 87B(6) of the Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018. This is section 27(3)(b) in action, a provision in force for some purposes and not others.

`ssi/2025/377` returns HTTP 404 from the research tools and was not returned by any search, so its terms come from the official text at [legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2025/377](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2025/377). That instrument's own note as to earlier commencement regulations independently confirms the seven sections and the 10 May 2025 date for SSI 2025/119.

#### 2.4 What a correct answer looks like

- **Correct.** "Partly in force. Sections 24 to 28 came into force the day after Royal Assent. SSI 2025/119 brought sections 2, 9, 17, 20, 21, 22 and 23 into force on 10 May 2025, and SSI 2025/377 brought section 18 into force on 15 December 2025 for the consultation purpose only. The rest awaits further regulations."
- **Acceptable.** The same, saying plainly which instrument could not be read and what therefore could not be confirmed. Reporting a retrieval limitation is not the same error as the next line.
- **Wrong.** "The Act cannot be found." "The Act is not in force." "The Act is fully in force." "No commencement regulations have been made."

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** Scotland. `asp/2025/2`, held in revised form.
- **Partly retrievable commencement trail.** SSI 2025/119 is retrievable by identifier, but only its title and description come back, not its section text; SSI 2025/377 is not in the corpus at all. Neither was returned by any title search. Commencement instruments for this Act are therefore hard to reach, which is the underlying cause of the recorded failure.
- **Source of the commencement detail.** The effect of SSI 2025/119 is from its retrieved description. The effect of SSI 2025/377 is from the official text at legislation.gov.uk, since the corpus does not hold it.
- **Currency.** Commencement continues. This answer states the position as at 10 September 2026, and a correct answer says which day it speaks as at and points the user to check for later instruments.
- **Not addressed.** The saving and transitional provisions in SSI 2025/119 are not stated: the instrument's section text was not returned, only its description.

question: Is the Scotland Act 1998 in force?
statements: The Scotland Act 1998 is in force: every provision requiring commencement had been commenced by 1 April 2000, and the Act remains in force as amended.

Section 130(1) of the Act put only sections 19 to 43, Parts II to V, sections 117 to 124 and part of section 125 on an appointed-day footing, so the remainder of the Act came into force on Royal Assent on 19 November 1998.

The Scotland Act 1998 (Commencement) Order 1998 (SI 1998/3178) commenced the remaining provisions, with article 2(1) and article 3 bringing all provisions not already in force into effect on the principal appointed day of 1 July 1999, except those in Schedule 5 to the Order, which came into force on 1 April 2000.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**Yes. Every provision of the Scotland Act 1998 requiring commencement had been commenced by 1 April 2000, and the Act remains in force as amended.**

The route to that answer is the Act's own commencement provision read with the commencement order made under it:

- **Section 130(1)** put only part of the Act on an appointed-day footing: sections 19 to 43, Parts II to V, sections 117 to 124 and part of section 125. Everything else came into force on Royal Assent, 19 November 1998.
- **The Scotland Act 1998 (Commencement) Order 1998 ([uksi/1998/3178](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/1998/3178))** then commenced the rest. Article 2(1) brought all remaining provisions into force on **1 July 1999**, except those in Schedule 5, and article 3 names 1 July 1999 as **the principal appointed day**. The Schedule 5 provisions followed on **1 April 2000**.

**In-force status rests on legislation.** It is established by a commencement provision, a commencement instrument, or the absence of any commencement requirement, and by checking that the Act has not been repealed. A judgment applying the Act is legitimate corroboration and an answer is right to offer it as such; what it cannot do is carry the answer on its own, because most statutes have never been litigated and a judgment shows only that the provisions it considered were operative at the time of those events.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 Section 130: what needed commencing and what did not

> **Section 130 - Commencement**
> (1) Sections 19 to 43, Parts II to V, sections 117 to 124 and section 125 (except so far as relating to paragraphs 10, 11, 19 and 23(1) and (6) of Schedule 8) shall come into force on such day as the Secretary of State may by order appoint.
> (2) Different days may be appointed under this section for different purposes.

([ukpga/1998/46, s.130](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/130))

This is a **partial** commencement provision, and reading it correctly matters. It does not say that the Act comes into force on an appointed day. It lists the provisions that do. Anything outside that list was in force on Royal Assent, without any order being needed, including the core provisions establishing the Scottish Parliament in Part I.

Section 132 confirms the citation, "This Act may be cited as the Scotland Act 1998" ([s.132](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/132)), and section 131 records that section 25 extends only to Scotland ([s.131](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46/section/131)); the Act otherwise extends across the United Kingdom.

#### 2.2 The commencement order

The power in section 130(1) was exercised by the Scotland Act 1998 (Commencement) Order 1998:

> **Article 2 - Appointed days**
> (1) All the provisions of the Act, so far as not then in force, shall come into force on 1st July 1999, except the provisions specified in Schedule 5 to this Order.
> (2) The provisions of the Act, specified in column 1 of any of the Schedules to this Order ... shall, so far as not then in force, come into force on the day appointed in relation to that Schedule in the Table below ...

([uksi/1998/3178, art.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/1998/3178/article/2))

The Table sets the appointed days as 25 January 1999 (Schedule 1), 1 April 1999 (Schedule 2), 6 May 1999 (Schedule 3), 20 May 1999 (Schedule 4) and 1 April 2000 (Schedule 5). Article 3 provides that "**The principal appointed day is 1st July 1999**" ([art.3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/1998/3178/article/3)).

The staging follows the devolution timetable. Schedule 3 (6 May 1999) commenced sections 19 to 22 on the Presiding Officer, administration and proceedings, for the first election. Schedule 4 (20 May 1999) commenced section 27 on the participation of the Scottish Law Officers. Schedule 5, the last tranche, commenced section 120 on accounts and audit and part of section 125 on 1 April 2000.

The combined effect of article 2(1) and Schedule 5 is that **no provision of the Act remained uncommenced after 1 April 2000**.

#### 2.3 Why the case law route is the wrong route

A search of Find Case Law for Supreme Court judgments on the Scotland Act returns a substantial body of decisions applying it. In [For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers [2025] UKSC 16](https://caselaw.nationalarchives.gov.uk/uksc/2025/16), for instance, the Court set out how "Section 29 of the Scotland Act provides that a provision of an Act of the Scottish Parliament is outside the legislative competence of the Scottish Parliament if it relates to reserved matters", and how Schedule 5 specifies those matters, including "Equal opportunities" (section L2). That is a court treating sections 29 and Schedule 5 as operative in 2025. It is consistent with the Act being in force, and nothing more.

The reasoning does not run the other way, for three reasons:

1. **Absence proves nothing.** The great majority of statutes have never been the subject of a reported judgment. If a judgment were needed to show an Act was in force, most of the statute book could not be shown to be in force.
2. **A judgment is evidence of the past, and only of what it considered.** *For Women Scotland* shows the court treating section 29 and Schedule 5 as operative. It says nothing about section 130, section 120, or any other provision the court had no reason to look at, and nothing about a provision repealed since.
3. **It answers a different question.** Courts decide the disputes in front of them. Commencement is decided by Parliament in the Act, and by the Minister in the commencement instrument.

A statement that the Act is in force, supported **only** by a judgment that cites it, can be a correct conclusion reached by an unsound route. The correct answer, on the correct route, is section 130 plus the 1998 Order, with the case law as corroboration if the answer wants it.

#### 2.4 A note on searching for the Act

Searching the legislation service for the phrase "Scotland Act 1998" returns instruments **made under** the Act, including the Commencement Order, but not the Act itself at [ukpga/1998/46](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/46). Its provisions retrieve normally once requested by identifier. An answer that concludes the Act cannot be found, or that turns to case law because a title search came back without it, has drawn the wrong conclusion from a search limitation.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** The Scotland Act 1998 is an Act of the United Kingdom Parliament. It extends to the whole United Kingdom, except section 25 which extends only to Scotland (s.131).
- **Status.** In force as amended. Royal Assent 19 November 1998; every provision needing an appointed day had been commenced by 1 April 2000.
- **Amendment.** The Act has been amended many times since, notably by the Scotland Acts 2012 and 2016. "In force" is a statement about commencement and repeal, not about the Act remaining in its original terms.
- **Limit of this answer.** Establishes commencement. It does not verify provision by provision that nothing has since been repealed, which for a specific provision should be checked on the revised text.

question: I am looking for scottish statutory instruments, made under the powers in section 95 of the Social Security (Scotland) act 2018, which feature a £ symbol within their text
statements: The complete list of Scottish statutory instruments made under section 95 of the Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018 cannot be produced from the available legislation search tools, and a correct answer says so rather than presenting a partial or invented list as complete.

Section 95 of the Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018 is the ancillary provision power, letting the Scottish Ministers by regulations make incidental, supplementary, consequential, transitional, transitory or saving provision.
Instruments cannot be found by their enabling power using these tools, because the preamble reciting the powers exercised is not part of the retrievable text of an instrument.

Because section 95 is an ancillary power rather than a subject-matter power, instruments made under it share no common subject and are typically made under several powers at once, so no topic search will collect them.
final_answer:
### 1. Summary Answer (BLUF)

**The complete list cannot be produced with the available legislation tools, and the correct answer says so.**

The question asks for an intersection of two sets: instruments **made under section 95** of the Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018, and instruments whose text **contains a £ symbol**. The second set is testable, because instrument text is retrievable. The first is not, for a specific and checkable reason:

> **The preamble that recites the powers exercised ("in exercise of the powers conferred by section 95...") is not part of the retrievable text of an instrument.** Retrieved text begins at section 1. No search can therefore find instruments by their enabling power.

So the population cannot be enumerated, and an answer that offers a list as if it were complete is misrepresenting the search it ran. The reviewers put the population at **33 instruments**; that figure comes from a source other than these tools.

One instrument gets as close as these tools allow: **SSI 2024/311** is an ancillary-provision instrument under the 2018 Act whose retrieved text contains the £ symbol. Its preamble is not retrievable either, so even here the enabling power cannot be read off the text.

---

### 2. Detailed Analysis

#### 2.1 What section 95 actually is

> **Section 95 - Ancillary provision**
> The Scottish Ministers may by regulations make any **incidental, supplementary, consequential, transitional, transitory or saving provision** they consider appropriate for the purposes of, or in connection with, or for giving full effect to this Act or any provision made under it.

([asp/2018/9, s.95](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2018/9/section/95))

This shapes the whole question, and it is the first thing a correct answer should establish. Section 95 is **not** a subject-matter power. It does not authorise a scheme of assistance, so no instrument made under it has "section 95" or anything like it in its title. It is the general tidying-up power, exercised alongside other powers whenever an instrument needs consequential amendments, revocations or savings.

Two consequences follow:

1. Instruments made under section 95 are almost always made under **several** powers at once, with section 95 supplying only the ancillary provisions. They are not "section 95 instruments" in any natural sense.
2. They are scattered across every subject area of the Act, so **no topic search will collect them**. They have nothing in common except the ancillary power.

This also explains why the population is as large as 33: an ancillary power is exercised routinely over the life of a major Act.

#### 2.2 Why the population cannot be retrieved

The decisive point is what the tools return. Retrieving an instrument's text gives the operative provisions from section 1 onwards. It does **not** give the preamble. Checked against three instruments:

| Instrument | Text retrieved | Preamble reciting enabling powers |
|---|---|---|
| SSI 2024/311 | ~30,000 characters, from "Section 1) Citation and commencement" | **Absent** |
| SSI 2025/105 | Present, from section 1 | **Absent** |
| SSI 2025/119 | "No text content available" | **Absent** |

The enabling power is recorded only in that missing preamble. Section searching does not help either: it searches provision text, which likewise starts at section 1.

This is a **tool limitation, not a gap in the law**. The information exists on legislation.gov.uk; it is simply not in what these tools return. That distinction belongs in the answer, because it tells the user where to go instead rather than leaving them thinking the question is unanswerable in principle.

#### 2.3 What can be confirmed, and what still cannot

**SSI 2024/311**, the Disability Assistance (Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance) (Consequential Amendment, Revocation and Saving Provision) Regulations 2024, was retrieved in full and **its text contains the £ symbol**. Its title is the signature of an ancillary-power instrument: "Consequential Amendment, Revocation and Saving Provision" tracks the language of section 95 almost word for word.

What the retrieval does **not** show is that it was made under section 95. Its preamble is missing in exactly the way described at 2.2, so the enabling power is inferred from the title and subject matter, not read. That is the same limitation this answer relies on elsewhere, and it applies here too.

Its opening provision:

> **Section 1 - Citation and commencement**
> These Regulations may be cited as the Disability Assistance (Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance) (Consequential Amendment, Revocation and Saving Provision) Regulations 2024 and come into force on 21 March 2025.

The instrument amends the Social Security (Invalid Care Allowance) Regulations 1976, the Council Tax (Discounts) (Scotland) Regulations 1992 and others, in each case consequentially on the introduction of Scottish adult disability living allowance under section 31 of the 2018 Act. That is exactly the shape section 95 exists to authorise.

Confirming one member of a set is not enumerating the set. It shows the answer is not empty; it does not make it complete.

#### 2.4 What a correct answer looks like

- **Correct.** Explain that section 95 is the ancillary provision power; explain that instruments cannot be searched by enabling power because the preamble is not retrievable; give any instruments that can be confirmed, flagged as examples rather than a complete list; point the user to the legislation.gov.uk "enabling power" listing.
- **Also acceptable.** State plainly that the complete population cannot be established and stop.
- **Wrong.** Present a list of instruments as the answer without evidence that each was made under section 95. This is the same failure as question 13 inverted: there, no instrument existed and three were invented; here, 33 exist and none can be found.
- **Also wrong.** Exhaust the tool-call budget searching, then return nothing without explaining why the search could not succeed.

---

### 3. Jurisdiction & Status

- **Extent.** Scotland. `asp/2018/9`, Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018, held in revised form.
- **The £ criterion.** Testable only once an instrument is identified. It cannot be used to narrow a search, because the tools do not offer full-text search across instruments.
- **Population size.** The figure of 33 instruments is the reviewers' count and is not derived from the retrieval here. It is recorded to show the scale of what is being missed, not cited as a retrieved fact.
- **Not addressed.** How many of the 33 contain the £ symbol is not stated. Only SSI 2024/311 was retrieved and checked.
- **Outside the audit trail.** The reviewer's record has SSI 2024/311 made under section 95, and the population at 33 instruments. Neither can be read from the retrieval here, so both are recorded for the reviewer and are not part of what a response is scored against.

---

### 4. References

- [Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018, s.95 - Ancillary provision](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2018/9/section/95)
- [Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018, s.99 - Commencement](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2018/9/section/99)
- The Disability Assistance (Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance) (Consequential Amendment, Revocation and Saving Provision) Regulations 2024, `ssi/2024/311` (full text retrieved; contains the £ symbol; preamble, and so the enabling power, not retrievable)

Regulation 2 of the Financing, Management and Monitoring of Direct Payments to Farmers (Amendment) Regulations 2020 (SI 2020/90) amends Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 in so far as it relates to CAP direct payments.
Regulation 2 of the Agriculture (Legislative Functions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/748) amends Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 in accordance with regulations 3 to 27.
The Agriculture (Retained EU Law and Data) (Scotland) Act 2020 confers power on the Scottish Ministers to modify the retained Regulation as it applies in Scotland.
Where a complete list of amending instruments cannot be established, the answer says so rather than presenting a partial list as exhaustive.
final_answer:
### Summary Answer (BLUF)

**This answer is not a complete list, and the question asks for one.** What follows are instruments
confirmed from their own text to amend Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013, plus the Scottish framework
that governs how it may be modified. The limits of the list are stated below and are part of the
answer.

Three instruments are confirmed direct amenders, each by its own regulation 2 headed "Amendment of
Regulation (EU) 1306/2013":

- **The Common Agricultural Policy (Financing, Management and Monitoring) (Miscellaneous
  Amendments) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/763)**, [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/763/regulation/2), amending it
  **insofar as it relates to common organisation of the markets and rural development measures**,
  in accordance with regulations 3 to 11.
- **The Financing, Management and Monitoring of Direct Payments to Farmers (Amendment) Regulations
  2020 (SI 2020/90)**, [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2020/90/regulation/2), amending it
  **in so far as it relates to CAP direct payments**, in accordance with regulations 3 to 11.
- **The Agriculture (Legislative Functions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/748)**,
  [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/748/regulation/2), amending it
  **without any aspect limitation**, in accordance with regulations 3 to 27.

Note the shape of the first two. Each is drafted to bite on one aspect of the Regulation rather than
on the whole of it, which is why an answer that finds one and stops has found half the picture.

### Detailed Analysis

#### How the Regulation applies in Scotland

Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013, the "Horizontal Regulation", was retained in domestic law and is
amended aspect by aspect: SI 2019/763 addresses it as it relates to the common organisation of the
markets and rural development, SI 2020/90 as it relates to CAP direct payments, and SI 2019/748
without any such limitation. The reviewer's understanding is that this reflects two retention
routes, the **Direct Payments to Farmers (Legislative Continuity) Act 2020** for direct payments and
the **European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018** for the rest. Neither Act was retrieved by this
research, so that framing is recorded for the reviewer and is not part of what a response is scored
against; describing the two as parallel mechanisms is an equally reasonable reading.

#### Confirmed direct amendments

**SI 2019/763, [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/763/regulation/2).** Provides that Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 on the financing,
management and monitoring of the common agricultural policy "is amended, insofar as it relates to
common organisation of the markets and rural development".

**SI 2020/90, [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2020/90/regulation/2).** Provides that the Regulation "in so far as it relates to the Common
Agricultural Policy ('CAP') direct payments" is amended.

**SI 2019/748, [regulation 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/uksi/2019/748/regulation/2).** Provides that Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 "is
amended in accordance with regulations 3 to 27". This is a direct amendment on the face of the
retrieved text: regulation 2 contains no aspect limitation and applies the amendments in
regulations 3 to 27.

#### The Scottish modification framework

The **Agriculture (Retained EU Law and Data) (Scotland) Act 2020 (asp 2020/17)** is the Scottish
vehicle: it [defines the Horizontal Regulation](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2020/17/section/1) and confers power on the Scottish Ministers to
[simplify, improve or update](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2020/17/section/2), [continue or end the operation of](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2020/17/section/3) and
[modify financial provision in](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2020/17/section/4) the retained CAP legislation. It was commenced by SSI 2020/315 (No. 1) and SSI 2020/373 (No. 2). The
**Agriculture and Rural Communities (Scotland) Act 2024 (asp 2024/11)** amends and expands that
framework, restating those powers at [sections 22](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2024/11/section/22), [23](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2024/11/section/23) and [24](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2024/11/section/24) and
[repealing section 5 of the 2020 Act](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2024/11/section/25).

#### Supplementing and implementing acts

Amendments also reach the Regulation indirectly through its supplementing and implementing acts,
notably **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 907/2014** and **Commission Implementing
Regulation (EU) No 908/2014**, both of which are expressly made under Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013.
An instrument amending those does not amend 1306/2013 itself.

#### What could not be established

The question asks for **every** amending instrument. That could not be established from the
legislation tools available:

1. **Regulation (EU) No 1306/2013 itself was not retrievable.** Searching for it returns amending
   instruments, not the Regulation, so its amendment history could not be read off the consolidated
   text.
2. **There is no way to search by "what amends X".** The tools search by title and by text within a
   named instrument, so an exhaustive list would require reading every candidate instrument in turn.

A correct answer should therefore either give a list and say plainly that it is not verified as
complete, or say that completeness could not be established. Presenting a partial list as exhaustive
is wrong. A response naming amending instruments beyond the three confirmed here is going further
than this answer, not contradicting it.

### Jurisdiction & Status

Scotland, within a largely UK-wide instrument set. SI 2019/763, SI 2020/90 and SI 2019/748 are
UK-extent and in force, status "revised". The Agriculture (Retained EU Law and Data) (Scotland) Act
2020 and the Agriculture and Rural Communities (Scotland) Act 2024 extend to Scotland and are in
force, status "revised".

question: Can you identify duties or functions conferred on procurator fiscals, prosecutors, or the Lord Advocate under the Victims and Witnesses (Scotland) Act 2014?
statements: Section 4 of the Victims and Witnesses (Scotland) Act 2014 requires the Lord Advocate to make and publish rules for reviewing a decision not to prosecute.
Section 6 of that Act imposes a duty to disclose information about criminal proceedings on request, which is a different duty from the section 4 review rules.

Section 1 requires the Lord Advocate to have regard to the general principles when carrying out functions relating to victims and witnesses, and section 2 requires standards of service to be set and published.
Sections 9D and 9E confer duties to enable a victim to avoid contact with the offender and to protect a victim's privacy.
Procurators fiscal are brought within these duties through the definition of prosecutor and the interpretation provision in section 32, rather than being named in each operative section.
final_answer:
### Summary Answer (BLUF)

The Victims and Witnesses (Scotland) Act 2014 confers duties on these office-holders in three
groups: **overarching duties** on the Lord Advocate (ss.1, 1A, 2), a set of **victims' rights
duties** (ss.3B to 3I, 9A to 9E), and two **prosecution-specific duties**, the duty to make rules
for reviewing a decision not to prosecute (s.4) and the duty to disclose information about criminal
proceedings (s.6).

Procurators fiscal are reached in two different ways, and the distinction matters: some duties bind
them because they fall within the **definition of "prosecutor"**, and others reach them through the
**interpretation provision in section 32**.

### Detailed Analysis

#### Overarching duties on the Lord Advocate

- **[s.1](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/1) (General principles)**: the Lord Advocate must have regard to the general principles when
  carrying out functions relating to victims and witnesses.
- **[s.1A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/1A) (Further general principles applicable to victims)**: further principles applying to
  victims specifically.
- **[s.2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/2) (Standards of service)**: the Lord Advocate must set and publish standards of service
  relating to the functions covered by the Act.

#### Victims' rights duties

- **[s.3B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3B) (The Victims' Code for Scotland)**.
- **[s.3C](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3C) (Victims' right to receive information)**.
- **[s.3D](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3D) (Referral to providers of victim support services)**.
- **[s.3E](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3E) (Victims' right to understand and be understood)**.
- **[s.3F](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3F) (Victims' right to interpretation and translation)**.
- **[s.3H](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3H) (Victims' right to reimbursement of expenses)**.
- **[s.3I](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/3I) (Victims' right to return of property)**.
- **[s.9A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/9A) (Victims' right to protection during criminal investigations)**, **[s.9B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/9B) (individual
  assessment of victims)**, **[s.9C](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/9C) (measures to assist victims)**.
- **[s.9D](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/9D) (Right to avoid contact between victim and offender)**.
- **[s.9E](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/9E) (Victims' right to protection of privacy)**.

#### Prosecution-specific duties

- **[s.4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/4) (Rules: review of decision not to prosecute)**: the Lord Advocate must make and publish
  rules establishing a procedure by which a person may request a review of a decision not to
  prosecute.
- **[s.6](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/6) (Disclosure of information about criminal proceedings)**: a duty to disclose information
  about criminal proceedings to a person who requests it.

**These two are distinct duties and must not be conflated.** Section 4 is about reviewing a decision
not to prosecute; section 6 is about disclosing information about proceedings. An answer that
attributes the review procedure to section 6 has the Act wrong.

#### Other relevant provisions

- **[s.5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/5) (Restorative justice)**.
- **[s.8A](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/8A) (Certain medical examinations: additional information to be provided)**.
- **[s.18](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/18) (Review of arrangements for vulnerable witnesses)** and **[s.23](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/23) (Victim statements)**.
- **[s.27B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/27B) (Provision of information to person supporting victim)**.
- **[s.29B](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/29B) (Application of Act where victim's death caused by offence)**.

#### How procurators fiscal are caught

[Section 32](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2014/1/section/32) is the interpretation provision and is the key to reading the duties correctly. Rather
than naming procurators fiscal in every operative section, the Act reaches them partly through the
defined term "prosecutor" and partly through section 32's interpretation of how the victims' rights
provisions apply. An answer that lists duties without explaining this mechanism has not answered the
question as asked, because the question is specifically about procurators fiscal and prosecutors as
well as the Lord Advocate.

### Jurisdiction & Status

Scotland. The Victims and Witnesses (Scotland) Act 2014 (asp 2014/1) extends to Scotland and is in
force, status "revised". It has been commenced in stages by a series of commencement orders,
including SSI 2020/405 (No. 7), SSI 2021/39 (No. 8) and SSI 2022/22 (No. 9).

question: How soon after birth must a bovine animal be officially identified in Scotland?
statements: A dairy animal must have its first ear tag applied within 36 hours of birth and its second within 20 days of birth, under Schedule 1 paragraph 1 of the Cattle Identification (Scotland) Regulations 2007.
Any bovine animal other than a dairy animal or a bison must have both ear tags applied within 20 days of birth.
A bison must be tagged within 9 months of birth or when separated from its mother, whichever is sooner.
The governing instrument in Scotland is the Cattle Identification (Scotland) Regulations 2007 (SSI 2007/174).
The deadline for recording a birth in the holding register, 7 days for a dairy animal and 30 days otherwise, is separate from the deadline for applying ear tags.
final_answer:
### Summary Answer (BLUF)

Under **[Schedule 1, paragraph 1](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/schedule/1) of the Cattle
Identification (Scotland) Regulations 2007 (SSI 2007/174)**, the deadline for applying ear tags depends on the type of animal:

| Animal | Deadline |
| --- | --- |
| **Dairy animal** | first tag **within 36 hours of birth**; second tag **within 20 days of birth** |
| **Bison** | **within 9 months of birth**, or when the animal is separated from its mother, whichever is sooner |
| **Any other animal** | both tags **within 20 days of birth** |

So for a typical beef animal the answer is **20 days**; for a dairy animal the first tag is due much
sooner, **within 36 hours**.

### Detailed Analysis

#### The governing provision

[Schedule 1 to SSI 2007/174](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/schedule/1) is headed "Application of ear
tags". Paragraph 1 sets the time limits for
a keeper to apply ear tags to an animal born on the keeper's holding, in accordance with Article
4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000.

The three limbs are:

- **dairy animals**, at sub-paragraph (a): "within 36 hours of birth for the first tag; and within
  20 days of birth for the second tag";
- **bison**, at sub-paragraph (b): "within 9 months of birth or when the animal is separated from
  its mother, whichever is sooner", in accordance with Articles 1 and 2 of the relevant Commission
  Regulation extending the maximum period for bison;
- **any other animal**, at sub-paragraph (c): "within 20 days of birth".

Paragraph 1(4) adds that a keeper whose animal is born on an additional holding must apply ear tags
indicating the unique numeric identity either of that keeper's principal holding or of the
additional holding on which the animal was born.

#### Related deadlines, which are not the identification deadline

Two other deadlines sit close to this and are easily confused with it.

**Cattle passport.** ([regulation 7](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/regulation/7) and
[schedule 3](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/schedule/3).) An application for a cattle passport runs from a starting point that itself
varies by animal: for a bison, the birth of the animal; for a dairy animal, the date the second ear
tag is applied; and in any other case, the date the ear tags are applied.

**Holding register.** ([Schedule 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/schedule/4).) The birth must be
recorded in the holding register **within 7 days** in the
case of a dairy animal, and **within 30 days** in the case of an animal other than a dairy animal.

#### Replacement tags

([Schedule 1, paragraph 3](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/schedule/1); see also
[regulation 5](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174/regulation/5).) Where an ear tag on an animal born on or
after 1 January 1998 is removed, lost or becomes illegible,
the keeper must apply a replacement bearing the same identification code **within 28 days** of
ascertaining that fact. No ear tag may be removed, modified or replaced without permission.

#### Currency of the figures

The Regulations have been amended, including by [SSI 2007/312](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/312),
[SSI 2011/412](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2011/412) and [SSI 2017/133](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2017/133). Nothing
retrieved shows the Schedule 1 paragraph 1 time limits being altered by those instruments, so the
figures above stand.

### Jurisdiction & Status

Scotland. The [Cattle Identification (Scotland) Regulations 2007 (SSI 2007/174)](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ssi/2007/174)
extend to Scotland
and are in force, status "revised".

question: can scottish public authorities refuse a freedom of information request because it would cost too much to deal with, is there a cost limit and how is the cost worked out?
statements: A Scottish public authority is not obliged to comply with a request where the projected cost of complying exceeds the prescribed amount, under section 12(1) of the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002.
The prescribed amount for the purposes of section 12(1) is £600, set by regulation 5 of the Freedom of Information (Fees for Required Disclosure) (Scotland) Regulations 2004 (SSI 2004/467).
Projected costs are the total direct and indirect costs the authority reasonably estimates it will incur in locating, retrieving and providing the information, under regulation 3 of SSI 2004/467.
Any estimate of the cost of staff time must not exceed £15 per hour per member of staff.
An authority relying on section 12(1) must give the applicant a notice saying so within the time allowed by section 10 for complying with the request.
final_answer:
### Summary Answer (BLUF)

Yes. Under **[section 12(1)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/12) of the Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002** a Scottish public
authority is not obliged to comply with a request if the projected cost of complying exceeds the
amount prescribed in regulations. The Act sets no figure itself.

The figure is set by **[regulation 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/5) of the Freedom of Information (Fees for Required Disclosure)
(Scotland) Regulations 2004 (SSI 2004/467)**, which prescribes **£600** for the purposes of section
12(1).

The cost is worked out under **[regulation 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/3)**: projected costs are the total costs, direct or
indirect, the authority reasonably estimates it is likely to incur in **locating, retrieving and
providing** the information, and any estimate of staff time **must not exceed £15 per hour per
member of staff**.

### Detailed Analysis

#### The power to refuse (section 12 FOISA)

[Section 12(1)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/12) provides that a Scottish public authority is not obliged to comply with a request
where the authority estimates that the cost of complying would exceed the amount prescribed for
the purposes of that subsection in regulations made by the Scottish Ministers. The section is a
power to decline to comply, not an exemption, and it fixes no monetary figure of its own.

#### The prescribed amount (regulation 5, SSI 2004/467)

[Regulation 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/5) is titled "Excessive cost, prescribed amount" and provides that the amount prescribed
for the purposes of section 12(1) of the Act is **£600**. Answering the question therefore requires
following the reference out of the Act and into the Regulations; the £600 exists nowhere in FOISA
itself.

#### How the cost is calculated (regulation 3, SSI 2004/467)

[Regulation 3](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/3)(1) defines "projected costs" as the total costs, **whether direct or indirect**, which
the authority reasonably estimates it is likely to incur in **locating, retrieving and providing**
the information.

Regulation 3(2) governs the estimate. Any estimate of the cost of staff time in locating, retrieving
or providing the information **shall not exceed £15 per hour per member of staff**.

The three permitted activities are exhaustive of what the estimate may cover. Costs of deciding
whether the authority holds the information, or whether the applicant is entitled to it, are not
among them.

#### Fees below the limit (regulation 4)

[Regulation 4](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/4) deals with the separate question of charging where the cost is under the limit. Where
projected costs do not exceed **£100**, no fee is payable. Where they exceed £100 but do not exceed
the prescribed amount, the fee must not exceed **10% of the difference between the projected costs
and £100**.

#### The procedural duty (section 16(4))

Where an authority claims that section 12(1) applies, it must under [section 16(4)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/16), **within
the time allowed by or by virtue of [section 10](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2002/13/section/10)** for complying with the request, give the applicant a notice stating that it
so claims.

#### Aggregating related requests

[Regulation 6](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2004/467/regulation/6) allows costs to be aggregated across two or more requests where the conditions
there are met, including that the authority estimates the total cost of complying with all of them
would exceed the prescribed amount.

### Jurisdiction & Status

Scotland. The Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 (asp 2002/13) is in force, status
"revised". SSI 2004/467 is in force, status "final". This is the Scottish regime and is distinct
from the UK Freedom of Information Act 2000 and its own cost limits.

question: at what contract value do the duties under the Procurement Reform Scotland act 2014 apply . what are the minimun values for goods , services and work contracts to count as a "regulated procurement"
statements: The threshold for a public contract other than a public works contract is £50,000, under section 3(2) of the Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014.
The threshold for a public works contract is £2,000,000, under section 3(2) of the same Act.
A contract is a regulated contract only if it is a public contract, its estimated value meets or exceeds the contract threshold, and it is not an excluded contract, under section 3(1).

The thresholds in section 3(2) of the 2014 Act are distinct from the higher thresholds of the Public Contracts (Scotland) Regulations 2015 and the Procurement Act 2023, which apply to higher value regulated procurements as defined in section 41.
The estimated value of a contract is the total consideration expected to be payable, excluding value added tax, under section 5(1).
final_answer:
### Summary Answer (BLUF)

The duties in the Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 bite on a **regulated procurement**, and a
procurement is regulated when the contract is a **regulated contract**. Under
**[section 3(1)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/3)** a contract is a regulated contract if it is a public contract, its estimated value is equal to or
greater than the contract threshold, and it is not an excluded contract.

**[Section 3(2)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/3)** sets the contract threshold:

| Type of contract | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| Public contract (other than a public works contract) | **£50,000** |
| Public works contract | **£2,000,000** |

So goods and services contracts are caught at **£50,000** and works contracts at **£2,000,000**.
These are the 2014 Act's own thresholds. They are not the thresholds of the Public Contracts
(Scotland) Regulations 2015 or of the Procurement Act 2023, which are higher and govern a
separately defined category.

### Detailed Analysis

#### Regulated procurement and regulated contract

[Section 2](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/2) defines a regulated procurement as any procedure carried out by a contracting authority in
relation to the award of a proposed regulated contract, including seeking offers and selecting
economic operators, and the award of a regulated contract.

[Section 3(1)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/3) makes a contract a regulated contract where all three of the following hold:

1. it is a public contract;
2. the estimated value of the contract (see [section 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/5)) is equal to or greater than the contract
   threshold; and
3. it is not an excluded contract.

All three are required. Meeting the financial threshold alone is not enough.

#### The threshold figures

[Section 3(2)](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/3) states the contract threshold in a table: **£50,000** for a public contract other than
a public works contract, and **£2,000,000** for a public works contract.

#### Estimated value

[Section 5](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/5)(1) provides that the estimated value of a contract is the value of the total consideration,
**not including value added tax**, which the contracting authority expects to be payable under or by
virtue of the contract. Section 5(2) lets the Scottish Ministers make further provision by
regulations about how estimated value is determined.

#### Whether the figures have changed

The Act contains a power to amend the table in section 3(2) by order. Nothing retrieved shows that
power having been exercised to change the £50,000 or £2,000,000 figures, so they stand as enacted.

The nearest instrument, the Public Procurement (Agreement on Government Procurement) (Thresholds)
(Miscellaneous Amendments) (Scotland) Regulations 2023 (SSI 2023/300), amends threshold figures in
the [Public Contracts (Scotland) Regulations 2015](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2023/300/regulation/2), the [Utilities Contracts (Scotland)
Regulations 2016](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2023/300/regulation/3) and the [Concession Contracts (Scotland) Regulations 2016](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ssi/2023/300/regulation/4), for example
substituting "£5,372,609" for "£5,336,937" in the Concession Contracts Regulations. It does not touch section
3(2) of the 2014 Act.

#### The neighbouring regimes, and why they are not the answer

[Section 41](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/41) defines a **higher value regulated procurement** as a regulated procurement to which the
Public Contracts Regulations or **section 115A of the Procurement Act 2023** apply. A number of
duties in the 2014 Act are then expressly disapplied for higher value regulated procurements.

Two other figures in the Act are easy to mistake for the threshold and are not it.
[Section 25](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/25) applies where the estimated value is **£4,000,000** or more (community benefit
requirements), and under [section 15](http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/asp/2014/12/section/15) an authority has significant procurement expenditure in a
year where the sum of estimated values of its regulated procurements reaches **£5,000,000**
(procurement strategy duties).

### Jurisdiction & Status

Scotland. The Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 (asp 2014/12) extends to Scotland only and is
in force, status "revised".
